en: We pay homage to Sarasvatī for the removal of the obstruction of impediments,
in whom the supreme consciousness resides within the minds of those whose thoughts are one-pointed. (1)
O Lord of Obstacles, homage to you! Dispel the host of obstacles;
bring about a great accumulation [of merit] and grant the purification of the intellect. (2)
His eyes were like hundred-petaled lotuses with unblinking petals;
he was a friend of Sugrīva and a worthy vessel for most wonderful deeds;
his body possessed a complexion identical to that of a brilliant blue sapphire.
I worship Rāma, the lord of the lineage, whose consort is Kamalā. || 3 ||

Born of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Govinda, he was like the moon in the ocean of Viśvāmitra’s lineage—an unbroken treasury of all arts; his speech, though composed of every word, was nectar itself; he was surrounded by disciples and grand-disciples, and was the sole sun for the blossoming of the lotuses of knowledge.
Like the number one among numbers, the illustrious Bhaṭṭarāmeśvara reigns supreme. || 4 ||
Because it was inhabited by him, that city Vārāṇasī is not the greatest;
for another city has attained the status of being a "city of gold. || 5 ||
Nārāyaṇa, his son, who had studied the scriptures under his own father and had reflected upon the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and the customs of the land, [resided] in Avimukta.
He establishes this bridge for the triad of sacred sites.
If it is said that you are possessed of a multitude of virtues in this treatise,
who indeed does not say that their own treatise is possessed of a multitude of virtues? Therefore, O virtuous ones, I entreat you with palms joined upon my head.
That which is to be purified is here described by me as being both existent and non-existent.
This is merely the desire of the wicked; as for their wickedness, let it remain yours alone.
Let there be no thought in your minds toward finding fault here, even though this is an ornament for you. 8.
The common procedure for visiting sacred sites (tīrtha) is first correctly explained; thereafter follows the procedure for the triad beginning with Prayāga—this is the summary here. (9)

(1) Indeed, for those revolving in this wheel of saṃsāra, four aims of human life—known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—are heard of in all the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts as objects to be pursued. Accordingly, there is a statement by Bhīmasena to Yudhiṣṭhira in the Mahābhārata: "O best of speakers, a wise man who knows the proper time should divide his time accordingly and pursue all three—dharma, artha, and kāma."

"Or liberation (*mokṣa*) is the supreme good for those who seek happiness, O King. (MBh III.34.41–42b) (1) In this context, since only the absence of pleasure and pain is the object of desire independent of any external qualification, it possesses the primary status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being sought after by the person; however, its means possess only a secondary status. (2) This being the case, *dharma* and *artha* possess a figurative status as human goals because they are, as appropriate, the means for achieving pleasure and the absence of pain. (3) For this very reason, the elders have stated that both types of *dharma*—consisting of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)—are means for attaining the human goal.
"In the dharma designated as *pravṛtti* (active engagement), the fruit is considered to be worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*);
in the dharma designated as *nivṛtti* (renunciation), the fruit is considered to be the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Thus [it is said].
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Since from dharma one obtains both happiness and knowledge,
therefore a wise person, having renounced everything else, should practice dharma.
Since whatever happiness exists in both worlds is obtained through dharma, one should therefore practice dharma alone for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims. 12.
O Draupadī, in this world, dharma alone is the raft for those going to heaven, and nothing else. 13.
And so forth. [It has been said: "By means of dharma, one removes evil through dharma" (MBh III.32.22a-b). This also establishes that dharma is a means for the cessation of suffering. 14.

(1) Thus the Śruti declares that [liberation] comes through the removal of sin, which is the cause of suffering. And in the Skanda Purāṇa: "O you whose wealth is austerity, by practicing penance for a long period of time..."
The desires of those whose sins have been shaken off by the Dharma are fulfilled. || 15 ||
Manu says:
For with dharma as his companion, one crosses over that darkness which is difficult to cross.
A person for whom dharma is paramount, whose defilements have been destroyed by austerity.
[It] quickly leads the embodied soul to the radiant world beyond.

Furthermore, the fact that dharma—such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*)—is a means for the absence of suffering by way of the destruction of evil deeds (*durita*) is well-established in all the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*.
(2) That wealth (*artha*) is also a means for achieving pleasure and the absence of pain is established by experience and established by scripture; as it is said:
"Those who give gold ornaments stand in heaven;
those who give horses abide with the sun."
Givers of gold partake in immortality; O Soma, givers of clothing extend their lifespan. 17.
From the wording of the mantra, "RV X. 107.2," [it is known that] one is purified immediately by gold. 18.

And because of this traditional authority (*smṛti*). (1) Furthermore, scriptural passages enjoining gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others also serve as authoritative evidence in this regard. (2) Thus, it is established that for dharma and artha, the status of being human goals (*puruṣārthatā*) is only figurative (*aupacārikī*).
(3) Desire (*kāma*), however, is a primary human goal precisely because its nature is pleasure (*sukha*). And that its nature is pleasure is heard in the *Āraṇyaka-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata*:
The pleasure that arises from contact with a physical object is desire, which is a mental volition; its physical form is not perceived. (19)
And likewise,
O King, a man seeking wealth desires the great dharma.
One who desires wealth seeks it for the sake of sensual pleasure; one who desires sensual pleasure seeks nothing other than sensual pleasure.
"For one desire is not accomplished by means of another desire; that [desire] is itself merely a fruit.
(MBh III.34.31–32b) And of the five senses, of the mind, and of the heart...
The pleasure that arises for those dwelling among sense objects—
It is my conviction that he is desire, the supreme fruit of actions.
And thus it is said in Mahābhārata III.34.37;
for here indeed—
Joy, affection, delight, and exhilaration. || 22 ||

Because desire (*kāma*) is designated by the word *prīti* (joy), which is a synonym for happiness as set forth in the *Amarakośa* 4.24(1) and other lexicons; because it is stated that there is no other fruit [for its fulfillment]; and because it is stated to be of the nature of a fruit, desire is of the nature of happiness. For this very reason, it is said in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇavārtika*:
"Whatever is connected with dharma and liberation originates from the Veda."
"But that which has wealth and pleasure as its object is preceded by worldly convention" (TV 1.3.1.2, p.
166). Thus, desire (*kāma*) is already included by the very word "pleasure" (*sukha*).
Also in the section concerning explanatory passages (arthavāda):
"The result is the comprehension of dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa, adharma, anartha, duḥkha, and saṃsāra, along with their means and ends, which consists of taking up and abandoning [them]. (Sūtra 24)

In this regard, at TV 1.2.1.7 (p. 116), the author of the Vārttika, by stating that suffering is the counter-correlate of desire, indicates that he accepts pleasure alone as the human goal consisting of desire (*kāma-puruṣārtha*).
As for what is stated in the Bhāgavata:
The gratification of the senses is not the attainment of desire; one should live only as long as necessary. || 25 ||
[Page 6] (1)—This refutation is made even while conceding that desire is a means for attaining the fruit of happiness known as sensory pleasure (*indriya-prīti*);
and as it is stated elsewhere:
"From dharma comes wealth, from wealth comes desire, and from desire comes unsurpassed pleasure. || 26 ||

(1) This statement regarding the means of accomplishing joy (*prīti*) is to be explained by accepting a figurative sense of "desire" (*kāma*), since it serves as a means to the pleasure known as desire when one experiences its objects. (2) Alternatively, even in that context, the word "desire" refers exclusively to pleasure itself. (3) However, the term "satisfaction of the senses" (*indriyaprīti*) alone refers to the gratification of the senses, because joy—which is a synonym for pleasure—cannot be an inherent property of the sense organs.

(4) Thus it is established that desire possesses the status of a primary human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because its nature is pleasure. (5) Liberation (*mokṣa*), moreover, according to different philosophical views, consists either of pleasure or the absence of suffering; therefore, it too possesses the status of a primary human goal.

(6) However, the conventional usage of the term "human goal" with respect to all four [aims] is figurative—like the word "umbrella-bearer" applied to a group consisting of both those with and without umbrellas, or like the word "creature" applied to a group consisting of both living and non-living beings.

(7) Among these four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), Dharma is the foremost, because it is the cause of the other aims of life and the cause of knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth. As it is said in the *Kaurma Purāṇa*:
"From Dharma, indeed, wealth (*artha*) is born; from Dharma, desire (*kāma*) arises.
From Dharma alone comes the Supreme Brahman; therefore, one should practice Dharma. (27)
As stated in KūP 1.2.52: (1) ‘The supreme Brahman’ is liberation.
Likewise—
With arms upraised I cry out, yet no one listens to me;
since from dharma come both wealth and pleasure, why then is it not practiced? (28)
Likewise: "In the dharma known as cessation (nivṛtti), the fruit is considered to be the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). (29) (= 11)
In the *Bhārata*:
"Learning, wealth, physical form, valor, noble birth, and freedom from disease—the cause for the eradication of worldly existence is proclaimed to arise from dharma alone. (30)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"From righteousness come kingdom, wealth, and happiness; from unrighteousness arises the birth of suffering.
Therefore, for the sake of happiness, one should practice righteousness and avoid sin. (31)
Yājñavalkya:
One should practice dharma with effort through action, mind, and speech. (32)
Manu (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.156):
Dharma alone, when violated, destroys; dharma, when protected, protects.
Therefore, dharma must not be destroyed; lest dharma, being slain, slay us. (33)
Manu 8.15, etc.
(1) "But since wealth (*artha*) is also experienced as a cause of dharma, how can dharma alone be considered primary? As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:"
In every respect, wealth has its root in dharma, and dharma is sustained by wealth. || 34 ||
Likewise: "O King, the world has dharma as its root; nothing excels dharma."
And Dharma, O King, can be practiced by means of great wealth.
In the *Bhāgavata*:
“And [he taught] dharma, which has dharma as its sole fruit. (36) Thus it is said.

(1) It is not so; for although some religious duties such as sacrifice (*yāga*) or giving (*dāna*) are accomplished through wealth (*artha*), it is not the case that all [duties] are accomplished through wealth. (2) This is because dharma arises even without wealth from practices such as silent recitation (*japa*), pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), and fasting (*upavāsa*); whereas without dharma, not even a trace of wealth can arise. (3) Thus, since dharma is primary, it alone should be practiced primarily. As it is said in the *Āraṇyaka*:
"One should practice dharma first, wealth in the middle, and desire last. (37)

In that regard as well, because dharma consisting of sacrifice, giving, and so forth is accomplished through abundant material wealth and involves a multitude of constituent parts (*aṅga*), it cannot be performed in its entirety by people of the present age; furthermore, because it must be performed with one's wife and accomplished with the assistance of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, and because it does not confer eligibility upon those born of mixed castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) or those belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*), the dharma of pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) is far easier than that, owing to its distinction from the aforementioned causes. Thus it is said in the *Bhārata* and the *Mātsya*:
"Sacrifices have been proclaimed by the seers (*ṛṣi*) even in the Vedas, according to their proper order."
And the fruit, according to reality, in its entirety both after death and in this world.
O lord of the earth, those sacrifices cannot be attained by a poor man;
for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
These are attained by kings or by men who are prosperous; they are never attained by those deficient in wealth, by the lowly, by those who act alone, or by those who are not united.
O Lord of Men, O Ruler of the Earth, learn now that rite which even the poor are able to perform,
yet which is equal in merit to the fruits of sacrificial offerings.
"O best of the Bharatas, this supreme secret of the seers— that pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha) is meritorious and even excels sacrifices— is thus [declared]. MBh 3.80.34–38.

(1) ‘By those without attendants (*avagaṇaiḥ*)’ means by those who are without companions. (2) ‘By those who are single (*ekātmabhiḥ*)’ means by those who are without wives. (3) ‘By those who are unassociated (*asaṃhataiḥ*)’ means by those who are devoid of a collective assembly such as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the like.

(4) It will be established in the determination of the qualified [performers] that there is eligibility here even for Śūdras, those of mixed caste (*saṃkīrṇa*), renunciants (*pravrajita*), and others.

(5) "Is it not the case that religious duties such as recitation (*japa*) and fasting (*upavāsa*) certainly exist independently of wealth? How then can pilgrimage alone be considered superior? (6) True; nevertheless, because those [other] duties are mostly accomplished through physical exertion, because they cannot be performed by those afflicted with diseases such as constipation or bile disorders, and because they are not accessible to all qualified persons, pilgrimage is superior due to its distinct nature. As it is said: "While wandering, one indeed finds honey. || 39 ||
This meaning is to be determined from such indicative marks (*liṅga*) as those beginning with *aitbr* 33.3.5(1).

Thus ends the determination of the duties to be performed on a pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*), composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara Sūri, in the *Tristhalīsetu*.
Now, a general praise of sacred fords (*tīrtha*): Śaṅkha says—
All sacred fords are always meritorious and destroyers of the sins of men.
The wise have declared them to be mutually independent. || 40 ||
Śaṃkha 8.13 (1):
"Mutually" means that each [of these] individually destroys sin.
Likewise—
All springs are meritorious, and all mountain peaks are meritorious;
all rivers are always meritorious, but the Ganges is especially so.
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, Śaṅkha (8.14) states:
"That man who, having renounced his sons, wealth, and other possessions, goes to a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*)."
Indeed, the deities beginning with Brahmā grant him satisfaction and nourishment.
In the Bhārata (2.26.13):
Likewise, there are sacred fords and sacred shrines.
Having worshipped and obtained merit, one becomes a partaker of the world of the immortals.
Likewise:
"By glorifying the sacred ford, by bathing there, and by offering libations to the ancestors, those who [perform these acts] at a sacred ford shake off their sin and go to supreme bliss. (44)
Regarding the sacred fords (tīrthas) in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"O best of sages, wherever bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, ancestral rites, charity, and so forth are performed—even individually—they purify one's lineage up to the seventh generation. (45)

In the *Bhārata* and *Mātsya*, after stating from “The sacrificial rites were proclaimed by the seers” up to “one is distinguished even by sacrifices,” it is said: “Without fasting for three nights and without visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*),” [one does not attain the fruit].
By not giving gold and cattle, one is born as what is called a poor man.
One does not obtain that fruit by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees which one obtains by visiting sacred fords.
“By the phrase ‘without fasting’ (*anupoṣya*), the meaning is that the fruit of each of the four [types of fasting], beginning with the three-night fast (*trirātropavāsa*), is the absence of poverty;
likewise—”
Those sacred fords that are inaccessible, difficult to reach, and rugged—
one should visit them mentally, with the intent of beholding all sacred fords.
These [worlds] are inhabited by the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Maruts, and the Aśvins, as well as by the ṛṣis who are like gods and who seek the fruits of their good deeds. || 47 ||
Likewise:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this path has been traveled by royal sages who performed meritorious deeds."
O Great King, pilgrimage to sacred fords yields great fruit, as declared by Manu and others.
Likewise, MBh 3.90.10 states:
"Even for one who, through ignorance, might undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords and the like in this world..."
With all his desires fulfilled, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
He shall always obtain a dwelling abounding in wealth and grain;
endowed with sovereignty and knowledge, he is ever righteous.
By him, his fathers and great-grandfathers are delivered from hell. Thus it is said.
(1) “By ignorance” means even in the absence of such knowledge as “this is to be performed here” or “by this, this result is obtained,” as in the case of a child and so forth.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: “The hero, full of faith and concentrated, while visiting sacred fords... [p. 11]
One who has committed evil deeds would be purified; how much more so one who performs pure actions?
He shall not go to the womb of an animal, nor is he born in an evil land;
indeed, the Brahmin dwells in heaven and finds the path to liberation.
Enough, then, of this [discussion], since the greatness of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is well-established in all the Purāṇas.
Now, the nature of the sacred ford (*tīrthasvarūpa*).

In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "That which is occupied by Arhats—who are free from passion and darkness (*rajas* and *tamas*) and whose impurities have been shaken off through austerity—is indeed declared to be a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). (51)
In Bhārata— by virtue of their possessions, by the splendor of the earth,
and by the power of the waters, those [sages] were exceedingly partakers of merit. (52)
(1) ‘By splendor’ means by power.
That is of two kinds. This has been stated in the *Bhārata*:

In this world, there are two kinds of sacred fords (tīrtha): those created by gods according to their own will, and those that are self-arisen, such as Prabhāsa, which are fashioned by the gods. || 53 ||
Furthermore, it is fourfold. This has been stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Nārada said:
O Lord of the Gods, how many are those sacred fords (tīrthas), and what are their fruits? Among all these sacred fords, which one is always preeminent? (54)
Brahmā said: "O tiger among sages, there are four kinds of sacred fords (tīrthas) in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld:
those belonging to the gods, those belonging to the asuras, and those belonging to the ṛṣis."
Among the worlds, those renowned as human are created by the gods beginning with the Suras;
that which is fashioned by the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva is called divine.
Since that which is one is born from the three, they know nothing beyond this. || 54 ||
Just as Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, and other such sites are most excellent because they were born from the three [fires],
so too are the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, and Veṇikā.
The Tāpī and Payoṣṇī are proclaimed to be on the southern side of the Vindhya.
The Bhāgīrathī, the Narmadā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī,
as well as the Viśokā and the Vitastā, all take their source from the Himavat mountains.
These rivers are declared to be the most meritorious, divine sacred fords (devatīrtha). || 55 ||
Likewise: "That which was not made by anyone is remembered as 'devakhāta' (a divine excavation). (BrP 70.33–35b) Thus it is said.

(1) Those established by Asuras such as Gayaka and Kolāsura are "Asura" [tirthas]; (2) those established by sages such as Vasiṣṭha are "Ārṣa" [tirthas]; (3) those established by kings such as Māndhātṛ, Ambarīṣa, and Hariścandra are "Mānuṣa" [tirthas]. (4) As for the Bhāgīrathī and others, although they possess a divine nature, they are exceptionally distinguished because they are the very forms of deities such as Viṣṇu. Thus it is said in the Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The form of Sarasvatī is Brāhmī; the form of Gaṅgā is Vaiṣṇavī; Narmadā is Śāṅkarī. These three rivers are the three deities. (57)
There too is the Gaṅgā—
this Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, the granter of all desires,
who belongs to the three deities; O best of sages, hear now of her origin.

(1) Because it possesses a multitude of qualities such as being presided over by three deities, as established by the collection of statements beginning with "ityādi," its status as most excellent will become clear in the section on the majesty of the Gaṅgā.

(2) Furthermore, it is of three kinds according to the distinction of being located on earth, in the intermediate space, or in the three worlds. (3) Among these, Naimiṣa is terrestrial, Puṣkara is situated in the intermediate space, and Kurukṣetra is situated in the three worlds. As it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Naimiṣa is meritorious on earth, and Puṣkara in the intermediate space."
O lord of the people, Kurukṣetra is equal to all three worlds.
In the Brāhma [section],
I have proclaimed to you the mental pilgrimage site (tīrtha) of those who belong to the earth.
"And Puṣkara, situated in the intermediate space, is difficult to attain for my world.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, Mahādeva says:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme majesty of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*)."
Naimiṣa is the sacred ford on earth, and Puṣkara is the one in the intermediate space.
"Kedāra and Prayāga," and so forth. 61.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Prayāga, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara;
Gaṅgādvāra, Kubjāmra, Badarī, and the ocean at the Indus. (62)
Thus the description of the sacred fords (tīrthas) has been made. In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa:
"First is the king of sacred fords, called Prayāga, which is very extensive. (63)
The sacred sites (tīrthas) are described in the sixth chapter beginning with Kākh 6.21ab:
"In Vārāṇasī [one worships] Mahādeva, but at Prayāga, Maheśvara."
By such passages, sixty-eight sacred sites (*tīrtha*) are enumerated in the Śiva Purāṇa.
Likewise, a description of sacred sites is provided in the twelfth chapter of the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Similarly, in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa:
Listen, O large-eyed goddess, for a sacred ford (tīrtha) has been declared to be a linga;
even in a body of water, it receives the name "ford" by virtue of assuming a formal embodiment.
The forms [of the deities] beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, Śiva, and Vighneśvara,
as well as that which is known as the Śaiva Liṅga— wherever these are found, that very place is a sacred ford (tīrtha).
"In Vārāṇasī, Mahādeva is said to be the first sacred site (tīrtha)," and so forth.
Also elsewhere [in the Kālikākhaṇḍa, 97.5–7b]:
The Śoṇa, the Sindhu, the Hiraṇyākṣa, the Poṣya, the Lohita,
the Ghargharā, and the Śatadru— these seven rivers are purifying and are the daughters of Brahmā.
And so forth.
[p.15] Now, regarding the secondary sacred sites (*gauṇatīrtha*):
"The field, fire, water, the gods, the Brahmins, the cow, and the teacher are said to be sacred sites."
It purifies through dwelling there, performing fire-sacrifices, ritual bathing, worship, nourishing, and satisfying [the deity]. || 67 ||
In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa:
"O Brahmin, even mental holy places such as Truth (satya) and the rest are indeed bestowers of liberation; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (68)
Likewise, in Kākh 6.26:
the wife of equal dharma said:
O Mahāmati, you have mentioned those sacred sites that are mental;
you should explain here which ones they are.
The sage said:
Listen, O sinless one, as I speak of the mental sacred fords (tīrthas) of mine;
by bathing properly in these, a man attains the supreme goal.
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
compassion for all beings is a sacred ford, and straightforwardness indeed is a sacred ford.
Generosity is a sacred ford, self-restraint is a sacred ford, contentment is said to be a sacred ford;
celibacy is the supreme sacred ford, and kind speech is also a sacred ford.
Knowledge is a sacred ford, fortitude is a sacred ford, and austerity is declared to be a sacred ford;
yet among all sacred fords, that which is the supreme purity of the mind is the true sacred ford.
One whose body is merely drenched with water is not said to have bathed;
he alone is truly bathed who has bathed in self-restraint and whose mental impurities are purified by faith.
He who is impure, slanderous, cruel, hypocritical, and devoted to sensual objects—
though he may bathe in all the sacred fords, that sinner remains indeed defiled.
A person does not become stainless merely by discarding the impurities of the body;
rather, when the impurities of the mind are abandoned, one becomes perfectly pure within.
Leeches are born and die only in the waters;
yet they do not go to heaven, for they are not free from the impurities of the mind.
Excessive attachment toward sense objects is called the mental impurity;
indeed, detachment from those very same objects is declared to be its purification.
A mind that is corrupted within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
even if washed with water hundreds of times, it remains as impure as a vessel that once held liquor.
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, purity, visiting sacred fords, and likewise the study of the Vedas—
all these are without merit if one’s inner disposition is not stainless.
Wherever a man dwells who has restrained the collection of his senses,
for him that place is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford, which is purified by meditation and filled with the water of wisdom that removes the stains of passion and hatred, attains the supreme goal.
This, O Goddess, has been told to you: the characteristic of the mental sacred site (tīrtha).
In the *Mātsya*:
Truth is a sacred ford, compassion is a sacred ford, and restraint of the senses is a sacred ford.
Even in the home of those belonging to the castes and stages of life, tranquility is declared to be the true sacred ford.
Vyāsa says:
The self is a river filled with the waters of restraint, having truth as its pool, exceedingly tranquil, and possessing waves of compassion.
"Therefore, O son of Pāṇḍu, perform the consecration there; for the self is not purified by water. (71)
In the *Dānadharma* section of the *Bhārata*:
"One should bathe in the mental sacred ford (tīrtha), which is unfathomable, stainless, pure, with truth as its water and fortitude as its lake, by taking hold of eternal goodness (sattva). (72)
Likewise: "But one who knows reality and is free from the notion of 'I' is said to be the most excellent sacred ford. (73)
Likewise: "He who bathes in the sacred ford of the mind— that is the true bath for those who perceive reality."
But one who has established purity and is always concentrated in being—
A man who is always endowed with virtues and pure alone [is truly such]. || 74 ||

The intended meaning here is that truth and the other virtues possess a secondary status as "tīrthas" because the fruit of a tīrtha is attained precisely when truth and the rest are present, and because they purify the inner being (*sattva*).
Having thus described the tīrthas, it is stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
This, O Goddess, has been told to you regarding the characteristics of mental holy places (tīrtha). Now hear the cause for the merit even of those holy places that exist on the earth.
Just as certain parts of the body are remembered as most meritorious, so too certain regions on earth are remembered as most meritorious. (75)

(1) Regarding the reading "and the waters are meritorious" in the *Mahābhārata*: the merit of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is traditionally held to arise from the extraordinary power of the earth and the water, from their majestic splendor, and from the acceptance [of those places] by sages. (= 263)
(2) "By the brilliance, power, and efficacy of the water"—this is the meaning.
Therefore: "He who constantly bathes in both types of sacred sites—those on earth and those in the mind—attains the supreme goal. (75) Thus it is said.

In the *Mahābhārata* as well, Bhīṣma said this very same thing using a different form of address: "O King, this has been told to you. It is also stated in the *Dānadharma* section: [KāKh 6.42–45] (3).
There are sacred bathing places (tīrthas) belonging to both the mind and the earth;
he who bathes in both shall swiftly attain perfection.
Just as strength devoid of action, or action bereft of strength,
does not accomplish any task here, but when they are joined together, success is achieved.
"Thus, endowed with both bodily purity and purity through sacred fords, one who is pure attains success; this twofold purity is supreme. (MBh 13.111.19–21)
Now, regarding those entitled to go on pilgrimages:
whatever pilgrimages have been performed, undertaken, or approved by the lords of sages—
The student, being well-restrained and duly appointed by his teacher, performs that [rite] according to the rule.

(1) Thus, according to the statement in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, the qualification belongs only to the student (*brahmacārin*) who has been commissioned by his teacher. (2) And this [qualification] occurs for the *upakurvāṇaka* student precisely through the teacher’s commission, provided it does not conflict with the study of the Vedas; as Yājñavalkya, having introduced the subject of the student, states:
"And he should attend upon the teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study" (78).
(1) Because of the restrictive rule, "Thus one should attend only upon the teacher for the sake of Vedic study" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.26 c-d);

and (2) because of the hearing of the general statement, "The lifelong student, commissioned by the teacher," there is indeed eligibility even for the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate), provided he has received permission from his teacher.
Even for a householder:

those men who, having obtained a well-nourished body and youth free from decay, do not go to the Gaṅgā and other holy places, and having bathed there, do not behold Hari and Maheśvara—they are indeed the lowest of men, robbed by fate. (79)
Thus it is from the traditional authority (*smaraṇa*).

(1) Now, it may be objected that by this statement a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) cannot be enjoined for a householder, because the word [“householder”] is not heard therein. (2) Nor can its purport be established on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as “having attained youth,” and so forth. (3) For that [indicative mark] is also consistent with having as its subject the stages of life beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*), since it does not contradict other scriptural statements. To illustrate: in the *Brahma Purāṇa* it is said: “For one who has the qualification for the duties of sacrifice, the home and all the duties of the householder are excellent.”

Thus, for one established in the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) was prohibited by those of old. We declare that even all sacred fords are certainly not equal to the *agnihotra* sacrifice. (80) Likewise, in that very same place:
Or else, even if his entitlement to perform sacrifices has ceased, a Brahmin should wander among sacred fords (tīrthas);
for it has been declared by the lords of sages, whose natures are stainless, that the fruit of sacrifice is fully obtained at sacred fords.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Indeed, he who abandons his own duties and resorts to sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) finds that those sites bear no fruit for him, neither in this world nor in the next. (82)

(1) It is said: because of the specific qualification, "He who has the entitlement to the duties of sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) and all the duties of a householder," and because of the statement, "He who abandons his own duties," pilgrimage is not contradictory even for a poor householder who lacks the capacity to perform sacrifices and the like, and thus possesses no entitlement [to ritual duties]. (2) For this very reason, in the *Mahābhārata*, after beginning with the words, "Sacrifices were proclaimed by the sages," the previously cited verses such as "They cannot be performed by a poor man" and so forth are stated.
(3) Or rather, the entitlement belongs only to a householder who maintains the sacred fires and has a wife; or he may go to the sacred fords together with his wife and the fire, self-restrained.
Thus liberated from all sins, he shall attain the destination as described. || 83 ||
According to the statement in the Kūrma Purāṇa (KūP 2.42.22):
"One who has performed penance should go to a sacred ford, even if separated from his wife."
Or one who is ineligible for sacrifices, or one who practices mantra-attainment.
Or he may go to the sacred fords together with his wife and his sacred fire, remaining self-controlled.
And because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), for that very reason there is the narrative of the Vaiśya Kr̥kala in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
a certain Vaiśya named Kr̥kala, having completed his pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*),
considered himself to have achieved his purpose, thinking, "I have delivered my ancestors."

Thinking thus, he set out for his own home; on the way, he saw his ancestors who shared his dharma. They said to him, “You have no fruit from the holy sites (tīrtha). He asked, “Why has no fruit from the holy sites arisen for me? How is it that my ancestors have not been delivered?”
Having fallen into such thought, Dharma said to him:
"Indeed, for one who departs after abandoning a wife who is pure and most meritorious, all his fruit of merit becomes in vain; it is not otherwise."
Having spoken much in this manner,
because you performed bathing and giving of gifts at the sacred ford here without her,
your ancestors have indeed been bound by that very fault.
"You have been deceived by her, O fool; you have committed the act of a thief.
These ancestors are thieves as well, for they enjoyed her company without her."
The wife cooks food with her own hand that is like nectar;
and the ancestors, with joyful minds, eat that very food.
"Therefore, no success is found for a man without a wife. When Dharma had spoken thus, Krkalāsa asked, "How then may my father's liberation come to pass? Dharma replied:
"Go home, O illustrious one, [to your wife] who is a partaker of sorrow without you."
For the sake of perfect enlightenment, [praise] that practice of Dharma which is most meritorious and bears excellent fruit.
Having gone to her house, perform the śrāddha offering with your own hand;
remembering the sacred fords (tīrthas), worship the supreme deities.
And in this way, the success achieved through pilgrimage to sacred fords shall also be yours. || 85 ||

Thus it has been stated in such passages as PadPu BhKh 59.8, 26, 30b–c, 31–32, and 60.2–3. By this, it is established that the qualification for the rite belongs only to a householder who is accompanied by his wife. (2) By this, the view that “the qualification belongs only to a householder who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*), and not to one who maintains them (*sāgni*)” is refuted.

(3) Furthermore, even for a widower (*vidhura*), there is qualification, because of the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “Even in the case of the qualification for sacrifice, or rather, [it applies] when [the wife] has passed away. [81]
(4) Even a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should practice residence at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) after having discharged his three debts,
provided he has established a means of livelihood for his wife and entrusted [his family] to his sons. || 86 ||
Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* (2.42.23):

“Having entrusted [his wife] to his sons. This refers to the case of one who is without a wife; in the option of forest-dwelling (*vānaprastha*), having placed his wife with his sons, he goes to the forest accompanied by her. || 87 ||
This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu (Manu 6.3c-d). (1) However, according to the view that [the term] means "accompanied by her," it applies only to one who has a wife.
(2) Furthermore, even for an ascetic (yati), there is eligibility [to perform this rite].

Those seeking liberation, the best of the twice-born desiring the fruits thereof, and likewise a son wishing to cast off the bones of his mother or father, should indeed undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords. 88.

Thus, from the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, beginning with the topic of renunciation (saṃnyāsa): "Dwelling for one night in a village, and staying five nights in a city, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or in a hermitage. || 89 ||
And because it is permitted by Kātyāyana thus:
(1) "A Kṣatriya also has the entitlement; even upon the loss of all his possessions, that king, having placed the Brāhmaṇas at the very forefront—" || 90 ||

(1) Because even a king, preceded by Brāhmaṇas, heard that [instruction] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*; (2) because the pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*) of Bhīṣma, Balabhadra, the Pāṇḍavas, and others is set forth in the *Mahābhārata*; (3) likewise, because there is the account of the Vaiśya Kr̥kala in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, and because of the statement to be cited; and (4) because even for Śūdras, with reference to Puṣkara in the *Mahābhārata*—
O best of kings, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, those who have bathed in this tīrtha of the Great-souled One do not go to a degraded birth. 91.
This is indicated by the mark [of the word] "iti" at MBh 3.80.51, and because the previously cited statements are common [to both].
As for that which Manu [says]:
Recitation, austerity, pilgrimage, renunciation, the practice of mantras,
and the propitiation of deities— these six lead to the downfall of women and Śūdras.
(Atri 136c–137b)
Likewise, for a Śūdra, the service of Brāhmaṇas alone is the distinguished characteristic of his duty;
for whatever else he performs, that becomes fruitless for him. (93)

(1) Thus, this refers to the fact that one should not perform such acts as pilgrimages to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*) continuously if they conflict with service to Brahmins. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"But a Śūdra who practices a duty (*dharma*) that conflicts with service to the twice-born..."
"In the same way, one is cooked in hell for hearing and reciting the Vedas. Thus also Śātātapa says:
"Constant service to sacred fords, renunciation, and the practice of mantras—"
The worship of deities and meditation [performed by them] brings about supreme sin. || 95 ||

(1) Thus, having referred to Śūdras and those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*) by the word "them" (*teṣām*), [the text] immediately thereafter prohibits their resorting to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth. In the explanation of the phrase "whatever else than this," the prohibition of others is for the purpose of praising service to Brāhmaṇas. 96.

Medhātithi has stated [in his commentary on] 10.123: (1) Therefore, even for a Śūdra, there exists the right to pilgrimage provided it does not conflict with service to the twice-born. (2) Even among those born of mixed unions, such as the Mūrdhāvasikta and others who are born in the natural order (anuloma), there is eligibility, because they possess the status of being born from the twice-born and thus have the right to the duties of the twice-born. (3) And there is also [eligibility] for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
But all those born from the inverse order of castes are recorded in tradition as having the same duties as Śūdras.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) in *Manu* 10.41c-d. (1) "Born of transgression" (*apadhvaṃsaja*) means born of adultery. (2) Women also have the right [to perform these rites], as stated in the *Mahābhārata* concerning Puṣkara:
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth, it is entirely destroyed as soon as one has arrived at Puṣkara. || 98 ||
This is evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in MBh 3.80.54. Regarding that, specifically for a widow:
bathing, giving gifts, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and the frequent chanting of Viṣṇu’s name. (99)

For it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, Brahmakhaṇḍa 2.7.72c-d, in the context of describing the duties of widows: "In that regard as well, [she should not act] independently, but only with the consent of her sons, kinsmen, and so forth;
whether she be a woman in her youth or middle age, or even one who is old."
One should not perform any action independently, even within one's own home. || 100 ||
As stated in Manu 5.147: "The father shall protect the maiden; the husband [shall protect her] while she is young; and the sons, however, in old age."
In their absence, those [male relatives] are the cognizers; a woman has no independence anywhere.
And because of the statement by Yājñavalkya,
"Yāj 1.85," a married woman [must perform rites] together with her husband alone, not separately.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
she who serves her husband is exalted in heaven because of that. 102.

(1) Because the sacrifices and other rites mentioned by Manu in 5.155 are intended as illustrative examples; (2) because the previously cited statement of Manu, "The six causes of downfall for women and Śūdras,"—applied here according to the principle governing Śūdras—refers specifically to the abandonment of service to one's husband;

and (3) because the aforementioned statement, "One who intends to cast the bones of his mother or father," applies to anyone at all who desires to throw the bones of a mother or similar relative into a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).
(4) However, for the purpose of removing that [sin], everyone who has committed evil is entitled [to visit it];
for men who have committed sins, the sacred ford shall be the pacifier of sin.
As has been stated, the sacred ford becomes the bestower of fruit for men of purified soul. 103.
Because it is stated thus:
"The wise man should likewise perform penance; such is the householder who follows the *yāyāvara* way of life. (Kākh 6.62 = 127, 178) [p.24]
One should practice the service of sacred fords, as well as other people who are like them.

And because of the statement in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "KūPu 2.42.21," [it follows that] regarding a pilgrimage to a sacred site for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), even a householder who is without his wife has the right [to go], as it is said:
"One seeking expiation should go to a sacred site, even if separated from his wife"—105 (= 84).
Because of this statement, and because of the prohibition against contact with others by one who has not performed penance; [p.
25] now, Śaṅkha states the causes for the gradation of the fruits of sacred bathing sites (tīrtha).
Having reached a sacred ford (tīrtha) by chance, one should perform a bath at that tīrtha;
one obtains the fruit arising from the bath, but not the fruit resulting from a pilgrimage.
“By way of incidental attachment” (*prasaṅgena*) means by way of attachment to trade, service to the king, and so forth. As for what Paiṭhīnasi says:
“Half the fruit of the sacred ford belongs to him who goes there by way of incidental attachment.”

"He who goes for the sake of another obtains a sixteenth part"—(107). Here, (1) "incidentally" (*prasaṅgena*) means by way of visiting other pilgrimage sites (*tīrthāntara*). (2) "For the sake of another" (*parārthena*) means having accepted a fee (*vetana*). In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*, however, the reading is "he who goes on another's food" (*parānnena gacchati*) [PraKh 1.28.35d]. In that case, it means one who eats another's food.
From the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*—
And whoever else, being able, should likewise cause a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrthayātrā) for another, using his own wealth and vehicles, his merit is fourfold. || 108 ||
If the eyes are distinguished [in their gaze], the fruit is eightfold. This was said in the *Mahābhārata* concerning Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Because you are the leader of the sages, for that reason your fruit is eightfold. (109) Thus it is said.
Now,
regarding the gradation of results produced by the specific nature of the vehicle, Mārkaṇḍeya says concerning the Fish and the Tortoise:
O child, I shall describe to you in due order the procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā),
according to the ancient scriptural injunctions, exactly as it was seen and heard.
Listen to the fruit that belongs even to that man who, desiring to go on a pilgrimage to the Prayāga tīrtha, travels somewhere while mounted upon a bull.
Indeed, the anger of cows is terrible; such an embodied being dwells in a horrific hell, and his ancestors do not accept even water. 110.
As it is stated in that very same place: MaPu 106.3–5; KūPu 1.35.1–3. Just as there—
If a man should go by vehicle out of greed for power or out of delusion, that sacred ford becomes fruitless for him; therefore, he should abandon the vehicle. || 111 ||
Likewise— MaPu 106.7; KūPu 1.35.5.
Killing a cow is said to occur when traveling by ox-cart; however, it is fruitless when traveling by horse-carriage.
When traveling by human carriage, the sin would be half of that, and when traveling on foot, it is four times that amount. (112)
(1) "With the feet" means with the bare feet alone.
(2) By this [it is shown that] there is a greater merit in discarding shoes; however, wearing them is not a fault, but rather a necessity:
one should always carry an umbrella and a staff against rain and heat, as well as during nights and in forests.
Indeed, one should always walk wearing shoes according to the procedure for protecting the body. || 113 ||

Thus, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* (3.12.38), by the force of the word "always" (*sadā*), it is indicated that even during a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*), the protection of the body is necessary, as there is no prohibition [against it]; for it is said:
"Wandering to sacred sites on foot is here declared to be the highest austerity."
By performing that very act with a vehicle, one obtains the fruit of merely bathing. || 114 ||

Some maintain that this is because (1) in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* (PraKh 1.28.72), it is stated that one should proceed on foot and traveling by vehicle is censured; and (2) even when wearing shoes, there is no impairment of walking on foot, and thus shoes themselves do not constitute a vehicle.
This is not correct.
A second meal shall take a third part of the merit of visiting sacred sites;
and vehicles, religious duties, as well as umbrellas and sandals, shall take a fourth part.
Therefore, even one devoid of these [qualities] shall obtain the full fruit of all sacred fords.
Thus, because it contradicts the words of Jābāli: "A vehicle destroys half the fruit; an umbrella and sandals destroy half of that;
trade likewise destroys three parts; and possession destroys everything. (116)

And because of the contradiction with this statement: (1) let there be no fault here regarding the application of the vehicle; however, that which is mentioned as a specific case will be like the umbrella. (2) Furthermore—if putting on shoes were mandatory, then how could there be an abundance of fruit upon their abandonment? On the contrary, there would surely be demerit (*pratyavāya*).

(4) Nor should it be argued that, "Just as in the case of [the injunction] 'The king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should cause each other to sacrifice,' because the conjunction obtainable through a *dvandva* compound is intended to be expressed, there is no deficiency of one-fourth in the wearing of the sandals alone"; for there is a disparity between the two cases. (5) For in that instance, the intention to express the conjunction arises because it resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), who is the factor to be enjoined (*upādeya*). (6) Here, however, because it resides in the subject (*uddeśya*), there is no intention to express conjunction, just as in the case of [the statement] "He whose two sacrificial cakes are burnt. (7) Therefore, the wearing of the sandals alone is indeed defective.

(8) "Even so, there remains a contradiction: for one who walks on foot, the merit is fourfold; for one wearing sandals, it is less by a fourth part; and for one using another vehicle, it is even less than that. Thus, whose would the full fruit be? (9–10) It is replied: in the phrase "fourfold" (*caturguṇa*), the word *guṇa* refers to a quarter-part (*caturthāṃśa*), which is synonymous with a foot (*pāda*), as in the expression "dharma is fourfold in the Kṛta age. (11) Therefore, the meaning is: "for one walking on foot, that fruit is fourfold, [that is,] complete with all four quarters."
(12) However, others say that in the final [verse], the mention of fourfold merit is intended to praise walking on foot, and not for the sake of the fruit [of the journey].
Gobhila says:
"He who undertakes a pilgrimage to sacred sites by means of a vehicle yoked with oxen..."
He goes to a terrible hell for as many years as there are hairs on the cow's body.

(1) All of that should be understood as referring to traveling by vehicle for the purpose of traversing the entire path. (2) However, when traveling by vehicle for only a short distance, the gradation of results should be inferred by calculating in terms of *krośas*, *yojanas*, and so forth.
Regarding this, it is said in the *Mātsya*:
"O Blessed One, by what procedure should those who have reached certainty in the Dharma proceed?"
O high-minded one, tell me that ritual which has been prescribed for Prayāga.

In the *Mādhavīya-purāṇa* (MaPu) 106.2(1), when Yudhiṣṭhira asks this question, Mārkaṇḍeya begins by saying, “I shall tell you,” and continues with the passage starting, “Desirous of a pilgrimage to the holy site of Prayāga” [110]. Since it is understood from this that the context concerns Prayāga, the prohibition of travel and the statement regarding the fruitlessness of traveling apply exclusively to Prayāga alone. However, in other holy sites (*tīrtha*), there is merely a slight reduction in the fruit—so it is stated in the *Kalpataru*.

(3) This must be considered: since the statements of Gobhila, Jābāli, and others refer to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in general, it is appropriate that the statements of the *Matsya Purāṇa*—following them—should also break the immediate context (*prakaraṇa*) and refer to both the specific and general sacred fords; (4) or else, they may be included within the context itself as a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*). (5) However, some maintain that because of the general statement, “That sacred ford is fruitless for him” [111], the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) overrides the context; thus, they accept that even the phrase “one desiring a pilgrimage to the Prayāga ford” [110] is intended to indicate sacred fords in general, and thereby conclude that the *Matsya Purāṇa* refers to all sacred fords whatsoever.

(6) That is not so; for just as in the case of the scriptural mentions of *vrīhi* (rice), the *Āgneyī*, and so forth, since it is possible for the scripture consisting of the word "tīrtha" to be consistent with the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no contradiction with the sūtra’s term *samavāya* (inherence/connection), which is based on the determination that [the rite] serves the purpose of results such as stability mentioned in the direct Vedic text (*śruti*)—as in the case of the recitation of the twenty-one [verses], where the context that establishes it as an auxiliary to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is set aside. (7) Otherwise, even in the case of the words *vrīhi* and *Āgneyī*, it would be possible for them to refer to all *vrīhi* and *Āgneyī* verses by setting aside the context; thus, what Mīmāṃsaka could prevent the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of rice intended for eating from being considered non-contextual, or the *Āgneyī* verse from being used for the *agnīdh* priest's worship? (8) Enough of this further elaboration—we shall return to the subject at hand.
As it is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "A Brahmin may go to those holy places such as Kurukṣetra that are accessible by chariot; indeed, there is no fault in using a vehicle for them. (119)
That refers to one who is incapable; however,
one who is unable [to walk] may perform a pilgrimage to sacred fords by means of a vehicle.
Thus it is said: "One who practices dharma according to one's own capacity attains that fruit. || 120 ||
(1) Thus, because Gobhila permits the use of vehicles for the three [classes],
so it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Human vehicles, as well as chariots accompanied by mules, horses, and the like."
For those who are unable to undertake pilgrimages on foot, traveling by vehicle does not cause any fault. || 121 ||
In this case,
"traveling by boat" would be "not traveling."

(1) Some say: "Because of this statement, there is no fault in traveling by boat. This is not so. Since a boat is indeed a vehicle (*yāna*)—by virtue of being a means for reaching another location through an intentional act that cannot be accomplished by the direct operation of one's own body—it follows that it would be subject to prohibition and thus to be avoided in all cases. However, since travel without a boat is simply impossible in places such as the Śaṅkhoddhāra [pass] or the Gaṅgā-Sāgara [confluence], and because travel is impossible along any stretch of road occupied by a river or similar obstacle except by means of a boat, the statement serves to establish the absence of fault in those specific instances. Yet, even regarding a pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*) accessible on foot, there is no evidence for the absence of fault in traveling by boat; rather, (2) there is evidence to the contrary, as it possesses the status of a vehicle.

(3) However, someone might say: "Just as there is the statement, 'Other animals than cows and horses—such as goats and the like—are indeed non-animals; cows and horses alone are animals,' which speaks of them as non-animals for the sake of praising cows and horses, so too here, although the boat is a means of transport, its status as a non-vehicle is proclaimed for the sake of praising horse-drawn vehicles and the like. (4) That is not so, because when the possibility of [the passage] being a primary injunction (*vidhi*) as previously stated is available, it is improper to assume it is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*). (5) Furthermore, if it were for the sake of praising horse-drawn vehicles and the like, it would follow that one must travel by those [vehicles] alone. (6) Alternatively, if the intention were that since horse-drawn vehicles and the like are praised as vehicles, the fault incurred from traveling in them does not apply to the boat, even in the slightest degree; (7) in that case, the effort expended to establish it as an *arthavāda* is wasted, because since there is no greater exertion required compared to other vehicles, it is more appropriate that the boat should incur a greater fault due to defects such as contact with the boatman. (8) Nor is there syntactic unity with a prohibition of other vehicles, by virtue of which it could be considered an *arthavāda*.

(9) "Then why does this not have as its object that which is incapable? (10) It does not, because by the previously stated words there is no negation of other vehicles for such a person, and because this [vehicle] specifically is inexpressible; (11) and because it would entail the consequence of being a mere reiterative statement (*avayutyānuvāda*). (12) Therefore, its object is exactly as we have described it; enough of further elaboration.
By this, a vehicle (*yāna*) is defined as that which, having become a support, causes one to reach another place by its own motion.
But chariots, boats, and the like are not so; therefore, they are not vehicles, and thus there is no fault in traveling by them. || 123 ||

(1) Thus, the statement of the author of the *Mahārṇavaprakāśa* is refuted, because the definition [of a "boat"] applies to chariots as well; (2) furthermore, it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to flowing water and the like—this is the general direction [of the argument]. (3) Therefore, traveling by boat is indeed a fault.

(4) Even in that case, one should not go by twice-born men (*dvija*) to those holy sites (*tīrtha*) situated on oceans or islands that can only be reached by traveling by boat for many days; for a twice-born man who travels by sea on a boat, there is exclusion from society even after he has been purified. || 124 ||

This is because [these places] are enumerated among those forbidden during the Kali age. (1) Since no sin would attach to merely traveling a short distance there, it would be impossible to apply the purification known as *prāyaścitta*; therefore, the prohibition applies to journeys lasting many days that do entail such sin.
(2) Furthermore, although travel to regions such as Aṅga and Vaṅga is forbidden, there is no prohibition against going there for the purpose of pilgrimage.
As it is said: "In Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, and in Saurāṣṭra and Magadha..."
One who has traveled without going on a pilgrimage to sacred sites must undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again. || 125 ||
Thus, according to the Smṛti. (1) The same should be understood regarding the border regions as well.
Thus ends the discussion on the journey (*yānavicāra*) in the *Tristhalīsetu* composed by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭarāmeśvarasūri.
Now, following the context of the gradation of fruits, [we shall discuss] the gradation of *yojanas* in a pilgrimage for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
In order to explain the gradations of results, the substitutes for pilgrimage (*tīrtha-pratyāmnāya*) are stated.

(125.2) First, the foundational scriptural statements regarding the purpose of pilgrimage as the destruction of sin are presented. Among these, the passages beginning with "visiting sacred fords" (*tīrthāny anusaran*) have been cited in the section on the praise of sacred fords.
[The pilgrimage was undertaken] by the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of obtaining a kingdom and for the pacification of their misfortunes.
By Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārada, Vyāsa, Śrīkaṇṭha, Indrājin, and Romaśa.
Likewise, led by Mārkaṇḍeya, Paulastya, Aja, and the Seven Sages,
they performed ascetic penances with devotion for twelve years each.
The story is heard in the Ādipurāṇa: "The holy fords performed [the rites]," and so forth. || 126 ||
(1) From the accounts in the *Tyādi-purāṇas*, it is understood that pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) serves as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for penances such as the *Prājāpatya* and *Kṛcchra*.
And in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"For men who have committed sins, a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) shall be the pacifier of their sin" (127).
Likewise, one who has committed an offense should go to a sacred ford (tīrtha), even if he is separated from his wife— thus [it is said]. (Kākh 6.62ab = 103, 178) || 128 ||
Devala said:
Having visited the sacred fords and holy shrines, [he attained his goal].
Those ascetic Brahmins who are devoted to austerity are liberated from evil.

"All rivers flowing to the ocean are meritorious; all excellent mountains are meritorious; every sacred site (*āyatana*) is meritorious; and all forest retreats are meritorious. (1) Thus, the method described in the *Smṛtyarthasāra* and other texts regarding the performance of a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is set forth here. (2) In that regard, for one who travels sixty *yojanas* on foot according to the rules of expiation after making a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), bathing in the Bhāgīrathī is equal to six years of *kr̥cchra* penance. (3) Here, for each *yojana* of the journey, there is an increase—

An increase in the *kṛcchra* penance should be calculated accordingly: (4) since six years are required for one who has come from sixty *yojanas*, the penance for one year applies to one who has come from ten *yojanas*. (5) Likewise, for one who has come from more than a third of a *krośa*, a single *kṛcchra* is accomplished by bathing in the Bhāgīrathī according to the prescribed rite, provided there is no obstruction such as mountains along the way. (6) In the absence of such obstructions, and when the path is not difficult to traverse, a single *kṛcchra* is accomplished by bathing in the Gaṅgā for one who is capable and has come from one *yojana*. (7) However, for one who is incapable, it is calculated as follows: for one who has come from half a *yojana*; and even for one who is capable, if the path is difficult to traverse, it is likewise calculated for one who has come from half a *yojana*.

(8) Formerly, the rivers were born from the fear of the *saptamātṛkā* demons. When that fear had passed, they became deities; thereafter, the rivers dried up, and upon those dry grounds the Bhāgīrathī appeared. (9) Bathing in those Gaṅgās, which bear the names of the seven mothers beginning with Viṣṇu and Gaṅgā, is equal to six years of *kṛcchra* penance for one who has traveled sixty *yojanas*. (10) At Prayāga, Vārāṇasī, Gaṅgādvāra, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, it is double [the merit]. (11) Bathing in the Yamunā is equal to two years of penance for one who has traveled twenty *yojanas*. (12) At Mathurā, it is double. (13) In the Sarasvatī, it is equal to four years of penance for one who has traveled forty *yojanas*. (14) At Prabhāsa and Dvāravatī, it is double. (15) For every increase of one *yojana* in the journey to the Yamunā and Sarasvatī, an increase of one-quarter of a *kṛcchra* should be calculated. (16) Conversely, a decrease should be calculated according to the aforementioned method, based on the absence of mountains and such, or whether the path is easy or difficult to traverse.

(17) Here too, the number of days for bathing should be determined as follows: water from the Sarasvatī purifies after seven days, that of the Yamunā after three days, that of the Gaṅgā immediately, and that of the Narmadā simply by sight. 130.
According to the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa* (PadPu Ādikhaṇḍa 13.7):
"(1) [The rivers] Dṛśadvatī, Śutudrī, Vipāśā, Vitastā, Śarāvatī, Marudvṛddhā, Madhumatī, Payasvinī, Ghr̥tavatī, and so forth..."

A bath in the divine rivers for one who has traveled fifteen yojanas is equal to thirty *kṛcchra* penances. (2) [These include] the Candrabhāgā, Vetravatī, Śarayu, Gomati, Devikā, Kauśikī, Mandākinī, Nityajalā, Sahasravaktrā, Paunaḥpunyā, Pūrṇapuṇyā, and Bāhudā.

(3) Bathing in divine rivers such as the Vāruṇī and Gaṇḍakī for one who has traveled fifteen *yojanas* is equal to fifteen *kṛcchra* penances. (4) At the confluence of these great rivers with one another, bathing for one who has traveled one *yojana* is equal to one *kṛcchra*. (5) At the confluence of the aforementioned divine rivers with great rivers flowing to the ocean, bathing for one who has traveled one *yojana* yields the fruit of six *kṛcchras*.

(5) In places not specifically mentioned, the number of *kṛcchra* penances should be understood according to the number of *yojana*s traveled. (6) At great rivers (*mahānadī*), the fruit is half that of a great river. (7) At the Śoṇa and Mahānadī, however, the fruit is half that of the Gaṅgā. (8) At ordinary rivers, the fruit is half that of a river. (9) At Māhiṣmatī and other such places, when an oblation is made in a fire that is constantly visible, it is ten times the fruit of the original rite (*prākṛta*). (10) The same applies at Jvālāmukhī. (11) [The same applies at] Gaṇa, Mahānadī, Setu, Rāmeśvara, Padmanābha, Śrīraṅga, Puruṣottama, Kurukṣetra, and Naimiṣa.

By visiting and serving the sacred fields of liberation (muktikṣetra)— such as Vadarī, Āśrama, Puṇyāraṇya, Kedāra, Śrīśaila, Mahālaya, Rudrakoṭi, Puṣkara, Narmadā, Amrātakeśvara, Kubjāmra, Prabhāsa, Kokāmukha, Vijayeśapura, Indraprastha, Pañcanada, Gokarṇa, Mathurā, Ayodhyā, Dvāravatī, Gayā, Kāñcī, Śālagrāma, Śambhalagrāma, Saṃnihitī, and others— one obtains a fruit equal to that of the Gaṅgā.

(12) Bathing at the Narmadā after traveling twenty-four *yojanas* yields the fruit of twenty-four *kṛcchra* penances. (13) At the confluence of the Kubjikā, it is double that. (14) At Śuklatīrtha, it is fourfold. (15) Bathing at the Tāpī after traveling eight *yojanas* is equal to eight *kṛcchras*. (16) It is the same at the Payoṣṇī. (17) At the confluence here, it is double.

(18) For one who has traveled sixty *yojanas* to the Godāvarī, bathing at the three-year *kr̥cchra* [penance] is equal [in merit]. (19) For one who has traveled thirty *yojanas* to the eleven sacred fords (*tīrtha*), bathing in the reverse and direct order (*pratiloma-anuloma*) is equal to sixty *kr̥cchras*. (20) At the confluence of the Vañjarā, it is double that. (21) At Bhīmeśvara on the Saptagodāvara, it is triple. (22) At Kuśatarpaṇa on the Vañjarā, for one who has traveled twelve *yojanas*, it is equal to twelve *kr̥cchras*. (23) At the Praṇītā, for one who has traveled eight *yojanas*, it is equal to eight *kr̥cchras*. (24) At the Pūrṇā, it is half of that. (25) On the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the number of *kr̥cchras* is according to the number of *yojanas*. (26) The same applies to the Tuṅgabhadrā as well. (27) At the confluence of the Pampā, it is double. (28) At Harihara, it is triple. (29) On the Bhīmarathyā, the number of *kr̥cchras* is according to the number of *yojanas*. (30) At the confluence of the Kakudminī, for one who has traveled ten *yojanas*, there are fifteen *kr̥cchras*. (31) On the Malāpahāriṇī, the number of *kr̥cchras* is according to the number of *yojanas*. (32) The same applies to the Nivṛti as well.

(33) On a pilgrimage to the Godāvarī, for every increase of one *yojana* in distance, there is an increase of one *pādakṛcchra*. (34) When Jupiter is in Leo, [the river] is everywhere equal to the Jāhnavī (Ganges). (35) When Jupiter is in Virgo, at the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, it is everywhere half of the Jāhnavī. (36) At the Tuṅgabhadrā, when the Sun is in Libra and in Cancer, it is half of the Gaṅgā. (37) At the confluence of the Kṛṣṇaveṇā with the Malāpahāriṇī, for one who has come from thirty *yojanas*, it is equal to thirty *kṛcchras*. (38) At the confluence of the Bhīmarathī, it is double. (39) At the confluence of the Tuṅgabhadrā, it is triple. (40) At the Nivṛtti confluence, it is quadruple. (41) At Brahmeśvara, it is quintuple.

(42) Near Mallikārjuna, at the Pātālagaṅgā, for one who has traveled thirty *yojanas*, it is equal to six years. (43) To the east of that, it is equal to sixty *kṛcchra* penances. (44) At a shrine of the Liṅga, it is double that. (45) And likewise at the confluence of the ocean.

[p.34] (46) On the Kāverī, a great river, for one who has traveled ten *yojanas*, it is fifteen *kṛcchras*. (47) On the Tāmraparṇī, Kīrtimālā, and Payasvinī, within twelve *yojanas*, it is twelve *kṛcchras*.

(48) Rivers originating from the foothills of the Sahya mountain have streams that flow without interruption for one *yojana*; according to their length, they yield the fruit of one, two, or three *kṛcchra* penances for one who has traveled [that distance]. (49) Those originating from the Vindhya and Śrīśaila mountains yield double that amount. (50) Those originating from the Himālaya yield triple that amount. (51) Small streams (*kulyā*) not mentioned in any way in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth, yield the fruit of a three-night fast for one who has traveled [that distance]. (54) Great rivers (*mahānadī*) yield the fruit of three *kṛcchras*. (55) Streams (*sravantī*) are those ranging from flowing for one *yojana* up to six *yojanas*; these are small channels (*kulyā*). (56) Beyond that, those flowing for up to twelve *yojanas* are minor rivers (*alpanadī*). (57) Beyond that, those flowing for up to twenty-four *yojanas* are rivers (*nadī*). (58) Those flowing for more than that number of *yojanas* are great rivers (*mahānadī*). (59) And those that flow into the ocean. (60) Wherever the designation "great river" is applied in the *Purāṇas* and other texts, those too are great rivers. (61) A bath in a great river performed while observing a fast yields a result equal to a *kṛcchra* even if it is within one *yojana* [of the source]. (62) Rivers with contemptible names such as "Śūnyā" and others, as well as "Pāpanadī," "Karmaṇāśā," and so forth, are to be avoided.

(63) A bath in the ocean should be performed everywhere on the new moon day (*darśa*). (64) It may also be done at all times near a deity, or at the confluence of a lake and a river. (65) For one who has traveled fifteen *yojanas* for the purpose of bathing in the ocean, the merit is equal to that of performing a *kṛcchra* penance. (66) If it is near a well-known deity, the merit is doubled. (67) Having bathed there and beheld that deity, the merit is tripled.
(68) For one who has traveled thirty *yojanas* to behold the Setu (the Bridge), the merit is equal to thirty *kṛcchra* penances. (69) Having bathed there and beheld Rāmeśvara, the merit is doubled.

(70) For those from the Vindhya region, [the merit] at Setu-Rāmeśvara on the Gaṅgā is threefold. (71) For those from that same region, it is likewise threefold at Jāhnavī-Kedāra. (72) For those from the Deccan, it is sixfold on the Gaṅgā. (73) For those from the Gaṅgā region, it is sixfold at Setu-Rāmeśvara. (74) Upon seeing Skanda, for one who has come from thirty *yojanas*, it is equal to twenty *kṛcchra* penances. (75) It is the same even where there is the name "Gaṅgā."

(76) In all cases, when there is an obstruction by differences in dialect, mountains, and so forth, or when the path is difficult to traverse, the results such as *kṛcchra* and others should be calculated by reducing the number of *yojanas* from the stated distance, due to the greater exertion required. (77) At Śrīraṅga, Padmanābha, Puruṣottama, Cakrakoṭi, Mahālakṣmī, and at Loṇāra—the site for beholding [the deity]—for one who has traveled thirty *yojanas*, the result is equal to thirty *kṛcchras*. (78) At all Vaiṣṇava, Māheśvara, Saura, and Śākteya *pīṭhas*, the number of *kṛcchras* is determined by the number of *yojanas* traveled. (79) At those that are renowned, it is double.

(80) In cases where no specific number is mentioned, the number of *kṛcchra* penances should be understood according to the number of *yojana*s. (81) Even in those instances, a distinction—whether by way of deficiency or otherwise—should be understood based on specific differences in the deity to be seen, the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the particular rules.
(82) Furthermore, whatever has been specifically stated in the *Purāṇas* and other such texts, as well as the extent thereof, should be accepted exactly as it is.

(83) Even for one staying at the bank of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), having bathed according to the rules even without traveling from a distance of one *yojana*, and having put on washed garments, one must bathe again once the hair has dried. (84) In this manner, twelve baths constitute one *kṛcchra* penance. (85) In this [penance], the previously mentioned observances (*niyama*)—such as eating only one meal a day, sleeping on the ground, celibacy during the seasons, and so forth—are to be adopted. (86) [The observances also include] bathing and offering libations (*tarpaṇa*) at the sacred ford. (87) And the worship of the respective deities; it should be understood that the pilgrimage to a sacred ford (*tīrthayātrā*) everywhere concludes with these [acts].
(88) In this context, the *kṛcchra* known as *prājāpatya* mentioned by Yājñavalkya is to be understood. As it is said:
"By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for, and by fasting—one quarter of the *kṛcchra* is thus proclaimed."
"In whatever manner [performed], this threefold [penance] is called the *prājāpatya*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.318–319b).
Thus, when the one-quarter *kṛcchra* that is accomplished in four days is repeated three times, it becomes accomplished in twelve days and nights.
And as for the measurement of a yojana: eight barley grains across, or three rice grains upwards, is said to be the measure of one *aṅgula*;
twelve *aṅgulas* constitute a *vitasti*.
Two *vitastis* make a *hasta*; four *hastas* make a *daṇḍa*;
two thousand of those [daṇḍas] make a *krośa*; and four of those [krośas] make a *yojana*. Thus ends the section on the substitutes for visiting sacred sites (*tīrtha-pratyāmnāya*).
Now, regarding the purification of time for a journey:

one should not travel on the sixth, eighth, or twelfth lunar days, nor on a day that touches three [consecutive] days; nor on the full moon, the first day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon, the *rikta* days, or on days of waning. (133)
In the *Ratnamālā*:

"The lunar mansions Hasta, Indu, Maitra, Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Puṣya, Pauṣṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, and Punarvasu are the most excellent for a new journey; one should avoid the three, five, first, and seventh stars."
The constellations Citrā, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Āśleṣā, Svāti, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Abhijit are remembered as unfavorable for journeys; they are neither desired nor censured. (134)
Likewise, in the *Ratnamālā* (15.8, 13):
"The days of Mercury, the Moon, Saturn, Mars, and the Sun are said to bring inauspiciousness during a journey. (135)
Likewise—the days of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus bring success in all undertakings. (136)

Likewise— the Vyatīpāta yoga, half of the Parigha yoga, the Vaidhṛti yoga, the Viṣṭi karaṇa, the equality of the solar and lunar courses (krāntisamatva), Kulika, and the Avama- and Gaṇḍāntas are not auspicious. || 137 ||

Lalla says: When [a planet] is in its sign of debilitation, in retrograde motion, in extreme velocity, or set like a child or an old man, there should be renunciation, pilgrimage to sacred sites, the performance of vows and observances, ear-piercing, or initiation.

The tying of the muñja-grass girdle, the rites of tonsure and marriage, and the consecration of a house or a deity should be diligently avoided by the virtuous when Jupiter, the preceptor of the thirty gods, is situated in the sign of Leo. (138)
Likewise:
"When Jupiter has entered the solar domain (Leo) or when the Sun has entered the domain of Jupiter (Sagittarius), one should avoid all ritual acts, as well as vows and rites for prosperity. (139)
Likewise:
When Jupiter is in the Sun, when Jupiter is in Leo, and when Venus has set, one should avoid travel, great gifts, religious vows, and visiting deities. (140)
Likewise:
when Jupiter is in the Sun, when Jupiter is in Leo, when Venus has set, during the intercalary month, during the southern solstice, and while Hari is asleep, one should avoid all ritual acts. (141)
Likewise:
[the construction of] ponds, wells, and tanks; going to sacrifices; shaving; consecrations; vows; learning; building a temple; piercing the ear; great gifts; and resorting to the forest.
One who desires to live should avoid from afar bathing at sacred fords, marriage ceremonies, visiting temples, reciting mantras, and beholding the gods when Venus has set.
One should carefully avoid Jupiter when it is situated in Leo or established in the Maghā constellation;
elsewhere, in other parts of Leo, marriage and other ceremonies are prescribed.
Likewise:
"Whether Jupiter is in its childhood or its old age, or when Venus has set, one should avoid visiting the deity during these times, as if it were an intercalary month. (143)
(1) In this context, the vision of a hitherto unknown deity is prohibited.
For this very reason, Gārgya said:
"If one sees an unprecedented deity when Bhārgava has vanished, there shall be sorrows."
"Even during an intercalary month, one should abandon a pilgrimage to a sacred site that does not involve returning [to it].
Thus, "a pilgrimage to a sacred site that does not involve returning" refers to a pilgrimage to a sacred site never before visited.
Likewise—
If Jupiter, having entered a sign of transgression, does not return to that same sign again, it should be known as a "lost year" (lupta-saṃvatsara), which is censured in all ritual acts. || 145 ||
The exception to this is stated:
"If Jupiter is in excessive transit (atīcāra) in Taurus, Aries, Pisces, or Aquarius, there shall be no lapse of the proper time for marriage there," so said the sage Gālava. (146) Thus.
In the *Ratnamālā*:
"In whichever direction it rises, in whichever it sets, or through whichever gates of the directions it wanders by mistake while moving within the circle of the stars..."
In this context, the sages have declared that the threefold presence of the white [element] is to be abandoned with effort as soon as it has arisen.
Even the slightest matter certainly does not reach fulfillment for those wishing to travel during the period of *pratiśukrā*. (147)
In the *Ratnāmālā* 15.17–18b,
there is an exception stated in the *Vṛttaśata*:
"There is no inauspiciousness for those who travel on a Friday if they belong to the Vatsa, Bhṛgu, or Aṅgiras [lineages]."
Those born in the lineages of Bhāradvāja, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśyapa, as well as those in the lineage of Atri—
during a famine, a flood in the region, at a wedding, when traveling to sacred fords, or in a single city or village, O gentle one, there shall be no obstruction. || 148 ||
(1) In some places, however, the absence of defects such as the guru’s ignorance is stated:
"At the Godāvarī, at Gayā, at Śrīśaila, and during the two eclipses, the defect of ignorance does not exist even in the gurus of the gods and the asuras. (149)
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "At Gayā, one should offer the piṇḍa according to the prescribed rule at all times—
even during an intercalary month (adhimāsa), on one's birthday, or when Jupiter and Venus are eclipsed."
The Śrāddha at Gayā must not be abandoned even when Jupiter is situated in Leo. || 150 ||
(1) Regarding this, some maintain that because the *śrāddha* is preceded by a pilgrimage (*yātrā*), the pilgrimage itself is not prohibited.
Likewise:
"In an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), on one's birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*), and when Jupiter and Venus have set..."
A pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) should not be undertaken, except to Gayā and the Godāvarī.
