(1) Other factors conducive to a journey, such as the purity of the *lagna* and its *navāṃśa*, should be learned from the treatises on astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) and those who know them; however, they are not mentioned here for fear of prolixity.
Thus ends the section on the purification of time for pilgrimage in the *Tristhalīsetu*. [p.
40] Now follows the procedure for going on pilgrimage.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
One desiring to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā) should first observe a fast at home and worship Gaṇeśa, the ancestors, the Brahmins, and virtuous men according to one's capacity.
Having completed the breaking of the fast, the practitioner, joyful and firm in his observance, should go forth again;
having returned and honored the ancestors, he shall partake of the fruit as it has been described.
(1) Regarding the phrase “having returned” (*āgatya*): the meaning is that after performing a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), one who has returned home must perform the *śrāddha* rite once again.
Likewise, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:

Whoever should go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), being well-restrained, having first observed a fast at his own home, pure and vigilant, he should worship Gaṇeśa with devotion and humility.
A wise Brahmin, according to his means and with great effort, should diligently honor the gods, the ancestors, and virtuous Brahmins;
and having returned from his journey, he should likewise again worship the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins.
Acting in this manner, he shall obtain the fruit that was described for that sacred ford; there is no doubt about this. || 153 ||
(1) On the day following the fast,
on an auspicious lunar date, under a favorable weekday, and with strength in the ascendant, the twice-born,
having fasted for one night and performed the *śrāddha* ceremony in the morning, [should proceed].
Having bowed to Gaṇeśa and the Brāhmaṇas and having eaten, the wise man proclaimed [the following].

Thus, from the *Skānda-purāṇa*, in the narrative of Śivaśarman (*Śivaśarmopākhyāna*), we observe another meaning [of the passage]: (1) here, the syntactical connection is "having set out on an auspicious lunar day and so forth. (2) In the phrase "having bowed to Gaṇeśa and the Brahmins," the sequence is not intended to be significant, because, being in the form of a narrative (*upākhyāyikā*), the order of recitation is not prescriptive. (3) Alternatively, what is mentioned here is merely the worship of Gaṇeśa and others prior to the *śrāddha*, distinct from the *śrāddha* itself which occurs before that.
(4) After the *śrāddha*, one should also adopt the attire of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭika*).
One who is intent on going to Gayā, having performed the *śrāddha* according to the rules,
having donned the attire of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭī*), and having circumambulated the village;
Then, having gone to another village, he should eat the remnants of a *śrāddha* offering;
thereafter, he should travel every day, avoiding the acceptance of gifts. (155)

This is according to the statement in the *Vāyupurāṇa* (GaPu 1.84.1–2). (1) Some, however, say: "This rule is to be performed only during a pilgrimage to Gayā, because the injunction begins specifically with 'having undertaken [the journey to] Gayā'; it does not apply to pilgrimages to other sacred sites (*tīrtha*). (2) Others say that on the day of fasting, one should perform the shaving of the head even prior to the *śrāddha*.
At Prayāga, during a pilgrimage, or due to the loss of a father or mother, one should perform the shaving of the hair; one should not remain with disheveled hair for no reason.

Thus, according to the statement of Viṣṇu: (1) some say, "And this [is prescribed] only for a pilgrimage performed for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because that is what is ordained therein"; (2) others say, "That applies when traveling to a sacred site (*tīrtha*) in the guise of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭika*). And the *śrāddha* must be performed as a *pārvaṇa* rite—consisting of six, nine, or twelve deities according to different opinions—specifically within the category of *tīrtha-śrāddha*. (4) And this [rite] consists of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) alone as its substance.
He who is about to travel to another country should perform a *śrāddha* with clarified butter;
this is declared to be for the purpose of a journey, and it applies equally upon his return—of this there is no doubt. (157)

This is because of the statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. (1) Some maintain that [the word *sarpiṣā*] means "with clarified butter as the principal substance," for otherwise, if there were association with another substance, the instrumental case in *sarpiṣā*—which conveys the status of being an independent means of accomplishment, as in the injunction *yajeta vrīhibhiḥ* ("one should sacrifice with rice")—would be contradicted. (2) That is not correct; since clarified butter alone cannot be eaten independently, it is impossible for it to be a substance used in a *śrāddha*, and thus the primary scriptural sense must be restricted to avoid rendering the text meaningless. (3) Therefore, others say it means "abounding in clarified butter. (4) That too is incorrect, because the instrumental case is not prescribed to denote abundance (*prācurya*), and it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). (5) Consequently, since the instrumental case conveys precisely the independence from other substances that act as rivals to the principal, the meaning is: "with clarified butter as the principal substance."
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rules,
the ancestors of men are satisfied for a month.
For two months with fish-meat, and for three months with the meat of the antelope. || 158 ||

(1) This is like the word "sesame seeds" (*tilaiḥ*) found in such statements of Manu and others as [Manu 3.267–268b]. (2) Even though there is a requirement for the spreading of gold fragments (*hiraṇyaśakala*) and the pouring over [of ghee],
they proceed with the omentum (*vapā*) at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), and with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) [at the midday pressing].
At the midday pressing with the limbs, and at the third pressing. || 159 ||

And so it has been said. (1) For this very reason, the authors of the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*, the *Madanapārijāta*, and others have explained it in exactly this way. (2) Therefore, on another day, the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should be performed with the remainder of the *śrāddha* using clarified butter alone, since that is the primary substance.

(3) Some maintain that "this *śrāddha* is exclusively of the *ābhyudayika* type. (4) That is not correct, because [the *pārvaṇa*] is established by its being the subject under discussion, which is more parsimonious. (5) Furthermore, since no specific distinction is stated regarding the *pārvaṇa* which is already applicable [by default].

(6) Some maintain that "one should perform the worship of only three Brahmins, according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya* (the maxim of the partridge). (7) Others hold that there is no fixed rule, because that maxim does not apply here due to the [number] being subordinate to the object (*uddeśya*), and because—in the verse "having worshipped the Brahmins according to one's ability" (*viprān śaktyā prapūjya cet*)—the capacity (*śakti*) applies to both the act of worship and the number, just as it does to the worship itself.

(8) Thus, the sequence of performance here is as follows: (9) On the day preceding the day of the journey, one should observe the restraints (*niyama*), such as eating only one meal consisting of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), because of the earlier statement that [the performer] must be "well-restrained" (*susaṃyata*). (10) On the following day, there is a fast (*upavāsa*). (11) And in some traditions, the shaving of the head (*muṇḍana*) also takes place. (12) On the subsequent day, having performed the daily obligatory rites (*naityaka*) such as bathing which produce purity, and having worshipped Gaṇeśa and one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) with devotion according to one’s capacity; having performed the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* using ghee as the primary substance; having honored the Brahmins according to one’s means with gifts such as clothing, ornaments, cows, land, and gold; and having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the journey, one should assume the attire of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭika*) consisting of saffron-colored garments and so forth. Departing from the village at the auspicious hour (*muhūrta*), one should circumambulate one’s own village of residence and proceed to another village within a distance of one *krośa*. There, one should break the fast (*pāraṇa*) with the ghee remaining from the *śrāddha*.
And on the road, [the recitation] extends for a full *krośa*. || 160 ||

Because of such statements as these, which prohibit traveling for a *krośa* after performing a *śrāddha*, one should therefore proceed on another day after performing the ritual bathing and other duties, remaining observant of the rules;
one should even go by circumambulating that village. || 161 ||
(1) Thus, in the Smṛtiratnāvalī.

(2) "And this procedure applies if the *muhūrta* occurs in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) on the day following the fast (*upavāsa*). (3) But when it occurs in the latter part of the night (*apararātra*), then some say: 'Being unable [to complete the fast] on that very day, one should perform the fast, the *śrāddha*, and so forth, and having undertaken the journey at the time of the *muhūrta*, go to another place and perform the *pārvaṇa* rite in the morning; for the fast is desired precisely so as not to conflict with the principal act. (4) That is to be considered: whether the *muhūrta* falls in the former or the latter part of the night, one should perform the fast on that day, and at the time of the *muhūrta*, having established the departure—consisting of fruits, garments, and so forth—in some location according to the method taught in the *jyotiḥśāstra*, and having performed the *śrāddha* and other rites in the morning, one should depart from the house, take that [prepared] departure-gift, circumambulate the village, and proceed to another village where the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) is possible. For it is improper to set aside the time of the day following the fast for the *śrāddha*, and (5) because it is impossible to perform a fast after having performed a *śrāddha* without scriptural authority. (6) Indeed, it is for the sake of such a situation alone that the method of departure is described in the *jyotiḥśāstra*.
(7) In this regard, one who is ill or otherwise incapable of fasting should perform some substitute for the fast according to his ability. And the substitutes are as follows:
"A night-meal, sacrificial food, boiled rice, or grain; fruit, sesame seeds, milk, water, or clarified butter;
the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or even air—each subsequent one among these is more highly praised. (162) Thus it is said.

(1) Wearing the dress of a *kārpaṭika* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the pilgrimage, and thus it applies only at the time of departure, not even during daily meals and so forth, because of the prohibition against wearing saffron robes (*kāṣāyavāsas*) at the time of ritual action, as in the rule: "At the time of work, one should be naked or wear saffron robes. (2) This is because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*māna*) to contradict that [restriction]. (3) Since the injunction regarding the dress is satisfied by its prescription for the mere act of departing, the dress of a *kārpaṭika* is likewise maintained at the sacred site (*tīrtha*) when following various holy places and the like. (4) However, some say: "But it does not apply even at the time of bathing, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and so forth, because there is no authoritative basis for it. (5) Others, however, maintain: "From the commencement until the conclusion of the pilgrimage, just as there is a prohibition against accepting gifts and the like, the dress is prescribed as an auxiliary; therefore, one must always wear that dress. (6) Otherwise, what would be the status of other observances (*niyama*)? Thus they say.

(7) Even one who has returned from a pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), having observed a fast near his own village in another village, should on the following day worship the planets and his chosen deities (*iṣṭadevatā*), perform the *pārvaṇa* rite with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honor the Brahmins, and upon reaching his own village, circumambulate it as before. Having discarded his travel attire at the designated spot and entered his own home, he should break his fast with the clarified butter remaining from the *śrāddha*. Regarding this, some say: "Because of the word 'likewise' (*tathā*) in the scriptural statement, 'And having returned, one should likewise again worship the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins,' there is an extension (*atideśa*) of all the duties pertaining to the departure. (8) That is not correct; for the word 'likewise' is justified simply by the extension of the duty of worshipping the gods and so forth. (9) For this very reason, it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Having arrived and worshipped the ancestors... (10) The conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is also exactly like this.

(11) Here, someone [objects]: "In the resolve for the journey (*yātrā-saṅkalpa*), there should be no mention of the fruit (*phala-ullekha*); for, from both the introduction and the conclusion—namely, 'if one is prepared to go to Gayā' and 'the fruit shall accrue to him going to Gayā'—it is understood that the purpose is that alone, according to the maxim: 'For the purpose [of an action] is distinguished by the objective (*uddeśa*)'. Thus, as he goes, whatever fruit has been stated for that sacred site (*tīrtha*) shall belong to him; there is no doubt about this. || 163 || (= 153)

(1) And because of such statements as these; otherwise, if the fruit of the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices were obtained at every single step, it would follow that visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) would be useless. (2) Furthermore, as for the scriptural reports heard here and there regarding the attainment of fruits such as heaven or the Rājasūya sacrifice during a pilgrimage (*yātrā*), those too are merely commendatory declarations (*arthavāda*), according to the principle that the fruit of the primary rite is mentioned in reference to its subsidiary parts.
[Objection: "But one obtains the fruit born of bathing, yet not the fruit of the pilgrimage itself—" (= 106) [Verse 164]

(1) If it is argued that there is a separate fruit for the pilgrimage itself based on such statements as these, (2) we say no; for the meaning is established as follows: "By means of a pilgrimage, one does not obtain the full fruit of the sacred site (*tīrtha*), but rather only that which arises from the mere act of bathing. (3) Furthermore, from statements such as, "Half the fruit of the sacred site belongs to him who goes there incidentally," it is the sacred site alone that possesses the fruit. (4) From statements such as, "Having performed that very [pilgrimage] by means of a vehicle, one would obtain only the fruit of the mere bath," it follows that for one using a vehicle, the sacred site itself is either fruitless or yields a diminished fruit. (5) Even regarding the performance of religious duties (*dharma*) and so forth during the journey, the fruitfulness belongs to the sacred site alone, not to the pilgrimage. (6) Moreover, the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) should not be "desiring to obtain the full fruit of the sacred site," because the pilgrimage is not enjoined as the means for attaining the fruit of the sacred site. (7) Therefore, the mention of a fruit in that context is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), like the statement regarding the overcoming of rivals.

(8) However, in the case of a pilgrimage (*yātrā*) consisting of penance (*prāyaścitta*), since there is no purpose for another (*pārārthya*), its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is not understood; therefore, it possesses an independent fruit. (9) Consequently, although one makes a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at the outset, there is no further resolve upon reaching the sacred site (*tīrtha*); for bathing and other acts at the *tīrtha* are included within that very [pilgrimage] by virtue of being the means of accomplishing it. (10) This should be considered: because of the hearing of the words "to go" and "goes," there is a contradiction between the opening and the conclusion, and thus no purpose for another is understood; (11) rather, it is the act of going itself that is perceived as possessing the fruit.

(12) Since a sacred site (*tīrtha*) that is not entered through action cannot possibly be a means for achieving a result, there must be an expectation of action. In this context, rather than abandoning the act of "going" (*gamana*) which is presented within the same sentence as "going thus," it is illogical to assume the entry of the verbal roots of bathing and so forth. Therefore, since it is understood that "going" itself is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), and the meaning is understood as "the result which has been stated [accrues] from the sacred site, i.e., from going to the sacred site," the second reason [adduced by the opponent] is also contradictory. (13) Furthermore, if the purpose [of the pilgrimage] is not understood in this way, then to claim that the results such as heaven heard of in various places fall under the principle of [results] belonging to auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is a great rashness. (14) Moreover, by reflecting on the previously cited injunctive statements (*adhikāra-vākya*) such as "Visiting a sacred site is meritorious" [38] and "Whatever pilgrimages there may be, O Lord of Sages... [77], it is understood that the pilgrimage (*yātrā*) itself is the primary element. For a presentation of independent eligibility (*svatantra-adhikāra*) does not apply to an auxiliary part. (15) Thus, an interpretation of the passage beginning with "But not the fruit of the pilgrimage to sacred sites" [79] that involves a strained construction is indeed unauthoritative. (16) Even in passages such as "Half of the fruit of the sacred site belongs to him" [107], when there is a requirement for a delimiting verbal root, it is the very act of "going" presented in the same sentence as "he goes" that serves as the delimiting factor. (17) Furthermore, what is the restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) that establishes primacy for a pilgrimage intended as penance (*prāyaścitta*) and not elsewhere—other than the drinking of water from a vessel (*kośapāna*)? [This implies no such rule exists.]
(19) Therefore, in all cases, the journey is fruitful. (20) Nor does it follow that sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are useless;

for regarding actions—whether small or great—and their fruits within their own respective domains, a distinction is prescribed based on the commonality of the location, even though there is no [intrinsic] distinction. 165.

(1) Because, according to the principle stated in *TV* 1.2.1.7, p. 130, one may postulate a distinct intermediate genus (*avāntara-vaijātya*). (2) Or, because in such cases [the passage] is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

(3) Therefore, even a journey that does not have expiation as its purpose is fruitful. (4) This applies to bathing, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and so forth as well. (5) However, this much is the distinction: bathing, ancestral rites, and the like are [to be performed] just like the *agnihotra*.
But when one [thing] has both [qualities], there is the principle of the distinctness of conjunction (saṃyogapr̥thaktva). || 166 ||

(1) Thus, by this principle, it possesses a dual nature as both optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*), because there are scriptural injunctions for both forms. (2) Consequently, if one who has reached a sacred site (*tīrtha*)—possessing that occasion—does not perform the rite, then even if he obtains the fruit of the journey, he incurs sin and is censured by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). (3) For this very reason, even in a pilgrimage for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the procedure ends with the performance of the rites at the sacred site, so that the principle of "the failure of the latter while seeking to join the former" does not apply. (4) And thus, if one who has reached a sacred site dies by chance without having performed the bath and other rites, or is forcibly led elsewhere by barbarians (*mlecchas*) and the like, then, due to the absence of personal fault (*puruṣāparādha*), there is neither sin nor is the pilgrimage fruitless. (5) Therefore, enough with this dispute with those who assert the fruitlessness of pilgrimage, which contradicts the world.
(6) Others, however, say: "Granted that the pilgrimage has its fruitfulness; nevertheless—'For one traveling to Gayā, there shall be the fruit of an Aśvamedha at every step. (167)

(1) Thus, this very fruit which was heard regarding the pilgrimage to Gayā also applies to all pilgrimages to sacred fords; for a scriptural principle established in one instance applies elsewhere as well. || 168 ||

(1) Furthermore, when there is a desire for a fruit, since this very act is heard of as having going [to a holy place] as its fruit, it is appropriate as the fruit due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*); whereas, by the *viśvajit-nyāya*, [assuming] heaven as the fruit would involve the extraneousness (*bahiraṅgatva*) and the burden of postulation (*upasthiti-gaurava*). (2) That too is extremely weak, because in various places, both generally and specifically, other fruits are heard of in connection with pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*). Generally, first of all, in the *Bhārata*, within the *Dānadharma* section, concerning *Goloka*: [The text continues: "By visiting the holy places of the Gaṅgā, one attains the world of Brahmā; by visiting Prayāga, one attains the world of Śakra; by visiting Kurukṣetra, one attains the world of Viṣṇu; and by visiting Gayā, one attains the world of the Pitṛs. Those wise men, devoted to pilgrimages,
rejoice there in that abode of cows.
Thus [it is said] in MBh 13.105.44cd. Likewise, having enumerated Prabhāsa and other sites, [it says]: "And those who follow the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, and the Yamunā..."
There, those auspicious ones possess divine forms and wear divine garlands.
They depart, rich with the fragrance of merit. || 170 ||
Thus, in the *Vāyavīya* [section] as well, it says: “O hero, wandering among the sacred fords (*tīrtha*s),” and so forth;

[47] Thus, in this manner, one should observe the presentation of results in all the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, and so forth, after introducing each respective sacred site (*tīrtha*). However, it is not written here for fear of prolixity. And thus, when the result is obtained from either the syntactical connection (*vākya*) or the context (*prakaraṇa*) as appropriate, there is no further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) because of its being satisfied by that alone; for where is there expectancy, and where indeed is the rule of the "more internal" (*antaraṅga*), or where is the rule of the "most internal" (*antaraṅgatama*)? Furthermore, the state of being more internal may even be the reverse, since it is precisely that which is heard as a specific [injunction] that is more internal. Moreover, because there is no assumption of heaven (*svarga*), there is no burden of mental presence (*upasthiti-gaurava*) either. Therefore, enough with this dispute with those who look too far into the Purāṇas.

Thus ends the procedure for going on pilgrimage, within the section on general matters, in the *Tristhalīsetu* composed by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvarasūri. [p. 48] Now, the observances (*niyama*) regarding pilgrimage.
In the *Bhārata*:
"He who enters a sacred ford after having conquered lust, anger, and greed—
for him there shall be nothing unattainable through that pilgrimage."
Those wise men who wander through sacred fords according to the prescribed rule, enduring all pairs of opposites, go to heaven. (MBh 13.26.60 = 655)
(1) Those who endure dualities such as cold and heat;
Śaṅkha and Pulastya say:
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
He who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is content with whatever he may have,
and who is free from egoism, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
He who is free from guile, free from worldly undertakings, moderate in diet, has conquered his senses,
and is liberated from all attachments— he enjoys the fruit of pilgrimage.
O king of kings, he who is free from anger, truthful in character, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords.

(1) Restraint of the hands consists in desisting from striking others and seizing the property of others; (2) restraint of the feet consists in desisting from trampling others with the feet and going to places that should not be visited; (3) restraint of the mind consists in the absence of covetousness toward the possessions of others and the non-contemplation of what is undesirable by the mind.
And false adherence is known as the threefold mental [defilement]. || 174 ||
Thus ends the cessation of the threefold evil. (1) ‘Vidyā’ is the knowledge of the greatness of sacred fords (*tīrtha*). As for the statement:
“Vidyā is the knowledge of the true scriptures,” [that refers to a different sense]. || 175 ||

(1) Thus it is stated in the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*; that is not correct, because it is irrelevant to the context. (2) "Austerity" (*tapas*) refers to fasting, eating only once a day, and so forth. (3) "Fame" (*kīrti*) is renown for one's virtuous conduct; by means of this, one's being accused [of sin] is dispelled. (4) The cessation of accepting gifts occurs immediately after the commencement of the journey. (5) As for the statement:
"For him, pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrtha*) is in vain as long as he consumes that wealth. (176)

Thus, some say: (1) "In that case, the failure of the undertaking (*prayoga*) for which the acceptance of gifts was made applies only to that specific undertaking; (2) the cessation of accepting gifts does not apply to other undertakings because of the absence of auxiliary factors (*upāṅga*). (3) However, it is more reasonable [to hold] that this refers to wealth acquired through improper acceptance of gifts even prior to the commencement of the pilgrimage. (4) Furthermore, this cessation of accepting gifts refers to one who maintains the body without accepting gifts. (5) But it does not refer to ascetics (*yati*), celibates (*brahmacārin*), and so forth, because it is impossible for them to maintain the body without accepting alms-food, clothing, and the like. (6) Since their accumulation [of possessions] is forbidden, and since the pilgrimage cannot be sustained without accepting those [necessities], such acceptance is necessary for them. (7) "Content with whatever comes" means being free from greed for delicious foods and the like. (8) "Free from guile" (*akalkaka*) means being without deceit. (9) "Free from worldly undertakings" (*nirārambha*) means being devoid of activities such as buying, selling, and the acquisition of wealth. (10) "Moderate in diet" (*laghvāhāra*) means not eating excessively. (11) "One who has conquered the senses" (*jitendriya*) means being free from attachment to the objects of the eleven senses. (12) "Free from attachment" means being devoid of that [attachment] which is not sanctioned by scripture. (13) "Firm in his vows" (*dṛḍhavrata*) means being without violation of the vows he has undertaken, such as fasting. (14) The sense is that only those vows which can actually be sustained during the pilgrimage should be undertaken. (15) "Devoted to the welfare of all beings" means regarding all beings as equal to oneself.
Likewise:

"The one lacking faith, the evil-minded, the nihilist, the one whose doubts are not severed, and the one who relies solely on reasoning—these five do not partake in the fruit of the sacred fords. (177)
KāKh 6.54:

(1) ‘One of sinful nature’ means one who possesses much evil. (2) For such a person, the pilgrimage serves only for the destruction of sin; it does not yield the fruit of sacred sites, such as heaven and so forth.
For men who have committed sins, a sacred site becomes the pacifier of their sin.
"A holy place (tīrtha) bestows the aforementioned fruit upon men of pure soul," according to the statement in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"He whose banner of dharma is always raised high like the banner of the gods... [p.50]
And when evil deeds are concealed, that is called the "cat-vow. (179)

Regarding this, some say that according to Manu 4.195, the "one who acts like a cat" (*baiḍālavratika*) is a person of sinful soul; (2) the "atheist" (*nāstika*) is a heretic (*pākhaṇḍa*); (3) the "one whose doubts are not severed" (*achinnasaṃśaya*) is one who lacks certainty in all matters. Others hold that he is one who is devoid of certainty regarding the results, the means, and the procedure [of dharma].
[As Manu says: "For one whose soul is full of doubt, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. (180)
As stated in the Gītā (MBh 6.27.40c-d): “One who is intent on [fallacious] causes is a *haituka*, one who subverts the meaning of the Dharma-śāstras by means of fallacious arguments.
In the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa:
He by whom the eleven sense-faculties are indeed restrained obtains the fruit of the sacred ford; any other man shall be a partaker of evil.

In this regard, the restraint of the senses in the form of celibacy [is required] except during the fertile period; for one who goes to sacred bathing places, there is always untruth toward the celibate student. 182.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"The mind, when corrupted within, is not purified by bathing at sacred fords."
But that which has been washed a hundred times with water is as impure as a vessel for liquor.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* (V 23.4 = 69):
"Even one who is corrupt in heart, though he has properly and constantly bathed in all the waters of the Gaṅgā..."
We say that even one who is constantly devoted to bathing from birth onwards does not truly become pure.
O King, fish dwell in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, and flocks of birds reside in temples;
yet, being devoid of pure intention (*bhāva*), they do not obtain the fruit of those sacred fords or those divine abodes.
Then, having fixed one's being within the lotus of the heart, one should serve the sacred fords with a concentrated mind.
Elsewhere it is also said:
"In respect of a mantra, a sacred ford, a brahmin, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, or a guru—whatever one's conception is, such will be the accomplishment. (185)
(1) The sense is that one should perform the pilgrimage (*tīrtha*) while keeping devotion and pure intent within the mind.

(2) Furthermore, these observances (*niyamas*), such as the restraint of the hands and so forth, constitute auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) for all rites including pilgrimages and ritual bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha-snāna*), because of the general statement: "He enjoys the fruit of the sacred site."
*Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"O woman of excellent complexion, those men who undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords with hypocrisy and deceit do not attain perfection even when they die at a sacred ford. (186)
In Bhārata—

those holy places are reached by the virtuous, those who see the goal of the disciplined, through their purified faculties, by virtue of their prior faith and their study of the revealed scriptures. (187)
Likewise: "He who sets out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) while showing contempt for Brahmins..."
He shall not turn back; his life ends there.
Likewise:
A man going to a sacred ford (tīrtha) should perform the three twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) in one place;
he should not go there while un-bathed, nor while impure, nor after eating, nor while under the ritual impurity of birth or death (sūtaka). || 189 ||

(1) By the statement, “One should perform the three *sandhyās* in one place,” it is meant that one should not depart at night after having performed the midday rites, nor in the morning without having performed the daily obligatory duties (*nityakriyā*). (2) Regarding “not un-bathed,” the meaning is that if one is capable, one should go only after having bathed. (3) “Impure” means one who has voided urine or feces and has not yet performed the purification (*śauca*). (4) It also refers to one who, upon contact with a *caṇḍāla*, a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or others—which necessitates bathing, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth—has not yet performed such bathing or sipping. As for that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
During divine processions, weddings, when sacrifices have been commenced, and at all festive celebrations, contact with those who are untouchable does not cause impurity. || 190 ||
And Bṛhaspati says:

"At a sacred ford, at a wedding, on a journey, in battle, during a national calamity, and in the event of a fire in a city or village, contact with those who are untouchable does not cause impurity. (191) Thus it is said.
Regarding *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.27: "This [is that] where I was touched by this," there is no perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) whose object is that [past contact];
for the statement would be purposeful only if there were a denial of that very [perception]. || 192 ||

Thus says the author of the *Madanapārijāta* on page 261. (1) Others, however, say: "There is no fault in cases where touch is unavoidable, such as for the specific purposes of worshipping a deity or going on a pilgrimage; but regarding eating and other such acts, one is certainly not purified without bathing.
(2) The phrase "and not one who has undergone birth-impurity" (*na ca sūtakī*) means one who is not subject to ritual impurity (*āśauca*). As for that which [was stated]:
There is no impurity (sūtaka) regarding what has already been commenced. || 193 ||
Thus, (1) that [impurity] refers only to those vows and so forth that have been specifically enumerated:

"In the case of vows, sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), fire-offerings (*homa*), worship, and recitation (*japa*), there shall be no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) once they have commenced; however, if they have not commenced, there is impurity. (194)

Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the first half [of the verse] being purposeless. For this very reason, it is said: "In a sacrifice, the commencement is the formal invitation (*varaṇa*); in the two cases of a vow (*vrata*) and a fast (*sattra*), it is the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*);
at the Nāndīmukha rite, marriage, and so forth, it is the preparation of the sacrificial food (*pākaparikriyā*). (Verse 195)

(1) Viṣṇu has stated in the following verse that the undertaking [of the vow] concerns only that specific measure. (2) Others, however, hold that this [rule] should apply to cases such as month-long fasts where continuous performance is enjoined. (3) And it is not...

[Page 53] It is understood that in the case of a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), the performance must be continuous. Therefore, the absence of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) applies only when the journey has already commenced; this does not apply to other cases. For this very reason, they say that in rites such as feeding a thousand people (*sahasrabhojana*), *sūtaka* certainly occurs. Thus, it is established that whether [the journey is considered a single act or a series], if *sūtaka* should occur during the course of the pilgrimage, one should calculate the period of impurity right there and proceed only after purification has been attained. As for the following verse: "In marriage, in times of distress, at sacrifices, on a pilgrimage, and in rites at sacred sites (*tīrtha*), there is no *sūtaka* in those instances; likewise, one should cause the performance of ritual sacrifices and the like. (196 = 315, 385)

(1) Thus, the statement of Paiṭhīnasi is intended to mean that there is no impurity during a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) when there is no other alternative due to the unevenness of the path or similar circumstances.
(2) Following this same principle, a woman in her menses should spend four days right there and depart on the fifth day;
she becomes pure for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors on the fifth day. || 197 ||
Because of this statement, and because sustenance is a matter of destiny.

(2) If, while traveling according to this fixed rule, another sacred site (*tīrtha*) happens to come into view along the way, then bathing, *śrāddha*, and other rites must certainly be performed there; for it was stated previously [in verse 107]: "Half the fruit of the sacred site belongs to him who goes there incidentally. (3) Furthermore, because there would be the risk of transgression (*pratyavāya*) if one fails to perform the occasional rites such as bathing when the occasion of reaching a sacred site has arisen. (4) Some maintain that fasting and shaving, however, should be done specifically at the very sacred site intended for the visit. (5) Thus, if one who has set out on a pilgrimage to a sacred site should turn back due to fate, there is a specific rule regarding this in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
Whoever, having set out for a sacred ford (tīrtha), returns home again, should perform an expiation after being authorized by auspicious Brahmins. || 198 ||
(1) The meaning is that the expiation for the obstruction caused by one's resolve should be undertaken with the permission of Brāhmaṇas.
(2) However, if he has set out toward a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) but dies before reaching it, there is a specific rule regarding this case in the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
If one who has set out facing toward a sacred ford (tīrtha) should die in the interval while fasting has been undertaken, he shall go to the assembly of the ṛṣis. || 199 ||

(1) Regarding “*anaśane*” (in fasting), the word “*ca*” (and) is to be supplied [from the previous verse], meaning “and in the vow of fasting consisting of month-long fasts (*māsopavāsa*) and so forth.
(2) The meaning is that even for one who dies during the interval of such a type of practice, there is the attainment of the world of the *ṛṣis*.

(3) However, when the river named Karmanāśā falls across the path of those from the west on their pilgrimage to Gayā and those from the east on their pilgrimage to Kāśī and other sites, one must cross it by some means so as not to touch its water;

for by touching the waters of the Karmanāśā, by crossing the Karatoyā, or by swimming across the Gaṇḍakī with one's arms, one becomes liable to undergo the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). || 200 ||

Because of this statement. (1) However, the Easterners, having read the text as "By touching the waters of the Karatoyā and by crossing over the Karmanāśā," say that one should travel by boat via the route of the confluence of the Gaṅgā or by the route further upstream. (2) That is not correct, because they themselves accept that even touching the waters of the Karmanāśā is undesirable; thus, there would be the fallacy of having to postulate another unrecorded scriptural passage prohibiting such contact [with the Karmanāśā], [whereas the following verse exists]:
"A man who has fasted for three nights, being self-controlled and pure, obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice upon bathing in the Karatoyā and the Kuraṅgā. (201)
Thus, in the *Mahābhārata*, in the section on the duties of giving (*dānadharmas*), it is said:
"Having reached the Karatoyā river, a man who has fasted for three nights [attains merit]."
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world. || 202 ||
And because this contradicts the account in the Āraṇyaka-parvan (MBh 3.83.3) regarding the hearing of [the sound] from bathing in the Karatoyā:
"O Karatoyā, of ever-flowing waters, most excellent of rivers, highly renowned..."
O Hara, you cause the sin of the wicked to be washed away in this world.
(1) This is also because it contradicts the mantra for bathing with water from the hands cited in the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*. (2) Therefore, the reading [we have] provided is indeed the correct one.
(3) In this manner, other duties pertaining to the journey (*yātrā*) that are established by the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) should also be understood.
Thus end the rules for the journey.

[55] Now, regarding the arrival at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) and the daily duties (*dinakṛtya*): if one should travel there mounted on a vehicle or wearing shoes, then on the day of reaching the sacred site, one should abandon the vehicle, shoes, and so forth for as much of the path as can be traversed on foot, and proceed on foot. Once the sacred site has come into view, one should prostrate with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*), discard head-coverings, weapons, garlands, bodices, and the like, and then enter the sacred site. As it has been said:
Having abandoned all vehicles, men should travel on foot;
having rolled upon the rolling-ground there, they should assume the appearance of mendicant pilgrims.
(1) Having rolled about on the ground, saying "I roll about," one should prostrate with the eight limbs. (2) As for the prostration with the eight limbs:
with the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the head, and likewise the chest.
Prostration with the mind, speech, and sight is said to be eight-limbed. || 205 ||

(1) By the phrase "having assumed the form of a pilgrim" (*kārpaṭika*), the abandonment of perfumes, garlands, weapons, armor, and so forth is indicated. (2) Alternatively, the meaning is that if the form of a pilgrim was not assumed at the commencement of the journey, then it must be done on the day of entry. (3) Then, having reached the sacred site (*tīrtha*), one should offer a handful (*añjali*) containing flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), fruits, and other items, saying: "Salutation to the unconquered sacred site" (*amuktatīrthāya namaḥ*). (4) Furthermore, it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) that one should present offerings (*upādhaukanika*) such as fruits, garments, gold, and the like according to one's capacity.
Immediately after that—
First, one should touch the pure water at the sacred ford with the syllable *praṇava*;
then, having entered it, one should bathe properly according to the application of mantras.

PraKh 1.28.123 (1): Having touched the *tīrtha* with the syllable *praṇava*, one should then plunge into the pure water; the meaning is that one should bathe along with one's clothes. As stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, in the narrative of Śivaśarman:
"Having arrived and seen [the site] at Maṇikarṇikā..."
Having bathed with his clothes on in the pure water of the celestial river, he [ascended] the boat that carries one to heaven.

(1) From this indicative mark (*liṅga*); (2) therefore, having recited the mantra-less [formula] "by means of the application of the mantra" (*mantrayogataḥ*), one should bathe "properly" (*yathāvat*) according to the path prescribed by the rules. And the mantra is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Oṃ, salutation to the God of gods, the blue-throated one, the bearer of the staff."
Salutation to Rudra, who holds a bow in his hand, who wields a discus, and who is the creator.
May Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and the most venerable Mother of the Vedas,
the destroyer of the sins of this sacred ford, be present here.
"This mantra is declared for all sacred bathing sites (tīrtha). Having recited this and paid homage, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rule. (208)

(1) Here, because it is stated, "having uttered [the word] 'iti' and having paid homage," this mantra is not an instrument for the ritual bath (*snāna*), but rather serves merely as a prayer. (2) Furthermore, if it were an instrument for the bath, there would also have to be an understanding of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) within the mantra itself. That mantra is as follows:
"O you whose roar is like the sound of the ocean, who hold a staff in hand, the destroyer of the Asuras!"
O Creator of the world, O Destroyer of the world, I bow to you, O Lord of the gods.
O sharp-fanged one, great-bodied one, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon!
Homage to you, Bhairava; you should grant me permission.
Having recited this mantra, one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford;
otherwise, the Lord of the Ford certainly takes away half of the fruit thereof. (209)
(1) Furthermore, there is an option between two mantras because they share the same purpose, namely the act of petitioning.
(2) And this ritual bathing is to be performed after the shaving of the head;
first comes the invocation at the sacred ford, and immediately after that, the tonsure.
Then one should perform the bath and other rites, and afterwards one should carry out the śrāddha ceremony.
Because of this statement:
"Having gone [to the water], one should perform a bath; immediately after that, a shaving. (211 = 282)
(1) This statement refers to the subject of bathing with one's clothes on.
[p.58] Now, regarding fasting at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*):
following that, there is the statement, “One should perform the bath according to the rules” [208].
Then, on that day, one of firm vows should observe a fast;
O Goddess of gods, there is nothing whatsoever superior to fasting at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Fasting is prescribed as the pacifier of the sins of the wicked and the fulfiller of the desires of the virtuous, especially when undertaken for the sake of a deity.
Therefore, O fair-faced one,
one who observes vows, a pilgrim, and especially a widow, should perform a fast at that sacred ford.
O Goddess, regarding the eating of another's food, the fruit belongs to the one whose food it is.
In the Kāśīkhaṇḍa (PraKh 1.28.126c–d, 64–65b, 78c–79):
"A fast at the sacred ford must be observed, as well as the shaving of the head. [213]
In the *Nāradīya*: "Having reached a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a man, being pure, should observe a fast. (KāKh 6.65ab = 229, 249)
Having purified your soul through fasting, you ought to perform what is to be done.
In this *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* it is said:
"On the day preceding that day on which the arrival at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) occurs, one should observe a fast;
when that day has arrived, one should perform the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*). (215)

(1) Thus, fasting on the day prior to reaching the sacred site (*tīrtha*) is prescribed. (2) Consequently, there is an option between this and the rule stating, "Then one should observe a fast on that very day, O observer of good vows," which refers to the day of actually reaching the sacred site. (3) Furthermore, the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* does not have as its sole subject matter Kāśī alone, because it speaks after introducing a procedure that is common to all sacred sites.

[59] (4) Here, someone says: "In the *Pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice, when the *Subrahmaṇyā* litany is to be employed according to the *tantra* method, on the first day—which is the *agniṣṭut*—an *Āgneyī* (verse addressed to Agni) is obtained for the purpose of summoning the *Subrahmaṇyā* during the *upasat* period through the extended application (*atideśa*) by name from the one-day *agniṣṭut*. However, just as that is set aside for the sake of favoring the many days by means of the *Aindryā* (verse addressed to Indra) obtained according to its own archetype (*prakṛti*) on the second through fourteenth days, so too in the present case, because there are many scriptural statements enjoining fasting on the day of arrival (*prāptidina*), the single statement from the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* enjoining fasting on the previous day is set aside. Since they do not possess equal force, fasting on the previous day is for the purpose of purifying the body by way of destroying sin, like the fasting associated with lunar eclipses and the like. (5) For it is only for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified that the aforementioned fruit of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is possible. (6) It is not, however, caused by the mere act of reaching the sacred ford. Thus he says.

(7) That is not so. If fasting on the preceding day were a mandatory auxiliary (*aṅga*), then since fasting on the day of reaching the sacred site (*tīrtha*) is also mandatory as an occasion-specific (*naimittika*) rite, it would follow that two fasts must be observed, which contradicts the practice of all learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*). (8) If, on the other hand, it were not mandatory, then there would be a contradiction with the scriptural injunction (*śravaṇa*) that treats it as obligatory (*nitya*). (9) Furthermore, if this were optional for the sake of a desired result (*kāmya*), it would entail the undesirable consequence of postulating a different unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its fruit. (10) Moreover, in the case of enjoining a different fast qualified by the specific time consisting of the day prior to arrival, there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*). (11) In our position, however, since the fast itself is already established, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) because we merely enjoin the alternative time consisting of the preceding day, and there is no need to postulate a different unseen merit.

(12) Furthermore, there is no acquisition here of the fast (*upavāsa*) as qualified by the specific day, such that a quality taught in a subsequent passage (*utpannaśiṣṭa*) would fail to apply—just as in the case of the *vājina* offering—because it is already occupied by a quality taught in the original injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*). (13) This is because, through statements such as "shaving and fasting," when the essential nature of the rite is enjoined, the two periods of time consisting of that day and the preceding day are equally authoritative since they are both taught in subsequent passages (*utpannaśiṣṭa*) by other sentences; thus, an option between them is appropriate, just as in the case of milk, curd, and so forth in the *agnihotra* sacrifice.

(14) Nor should it be argued that "by the statement immediately following [the rule for] shaving on the day of attainment (*prāpti*), it is understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) that the fast is indeed a duty of that very day. (15) For that would be based merely on the order of recitation (*pāṭha*). (16) Furthermore, in the face of the contradiction with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) consisting of the word *pūrvadina* ("previous day") found in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, the order of recitation—even though read in the third place—cannot determine the sequence according to the fifth book's principle (*pañcamikanyāya*), just as the word *daśama* ("tenth") contradicts the reading "the tenth day of Āśvina is taken" regarding the month of Āśvina. (17) Moreover, since the sentence prescribing fasting on the previous day would otherwise result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) due to the aforementioned reasons, there arises the possibility of its being set aside by even many sentences prescribing fasting on that [attainment] day, according to the maxim: "The relative strength and weakness of those [rules] obstructed by meaninglessness is reversed. (18) For in the case of the *Pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice, although the *Āgneyī* verse is not obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) because of the predominance of many other elements, the *codaka* still fulfills its purpose by providing the remaining subsidiary parts. (19) Here, however, there would be the contingency of rendering meaningless a scriptural statement that is heard as if it were mandatory; thus, there is a difference between the two cases.

(20) Furthermore, in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, after first stating, "A fast at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) must be observed, and likewise the shaving of the head" [213], the immediately following sentence, "On which day... [215], prescribes the time consisting of the preceding day. Therefore, even by virtue of conforming to the introductory context (*upakrama*), it is understood that the position of fasting on the preceding day is indeed intended. (21) By this, the argument that "since the term 'fast at the sacred ford' is not heard [in that specific sentence], the statement regarding the preceding day does not concern the fast at the sacred ford, but rather prescribes a fast for the purpose of bodily purification" is refuted; (22) because since the term 'fast at the sacred ford' is heard in the introductory sentence, this [subsequent] passage is also understood to have that same purpose.

(23) However, if some one who considers himself a Mīmāṃsaka were to say: "If the fast prescribed after the tonsure is moved forward to the preceding day, the tonsure itself must also be moved forward, just as when the *prayāja* offerings mentioned in the scriptural injunction ‘they sacrifice the animal while it stands’ are moved forward, the parts that precede the *prayājas* are also moved forward"—(24) even that is not correct. For in that case [of the animal sacrifice], the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) whose sequence is already determined in the archetype (*prakṛti*) are extended to the animal sacrifice by the rule of transfer (*codaka*); thus, when the subsequent *prayāja* is moved forward, the earlier ones are also moved forward in accordance with that established sequence. (25) Here, however, since the sequence is not yet determined at the time when the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) provides knowledge of the mere nature of the rite and there is a need for a sequence, it has been stated that the injunctions indicating the day to be performed on the preceding day and the day itself operate simultaneously. Therefore, just as in the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), the altar (*vedi*) enjoined for the previous day in the rule ‘on the previous day, on the new moon, he prepares the altar’ does not cause the movement forward of the ritual items ending with the covering of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśābhivāsanānta*), so too the fast would not cause the movement forward of the tonsure. (26) By this, the argument that “if the fast is to be performed on the previous day, it follows that the tonsure must also be performed on that same day” is refuted. And thus—
Having first performed the shaving of the head in the vicinity of Someśvara, || 216 ||
"Thus says the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
'On that day, one should then observe a fast. (PraKh 1.29.4a-b = 250) || 217 ||

(1) Furthermore, statements regarding fasting on specific days of attainment, such as those beginning with *tyādi*, are all established as being optional (*pākṣika*); thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
(2) And as for that which is found in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, in the narrative of Śivaśarman, beginning with "Then he reached Māyāpurī"—
Having observed a fast at the sacred ford and likewise kept a vigil during the night,
he should bathe in the Gaṅgā in the morning and diligently offer libations to those who are to be propitiated.
[61] Just as that best of brahmins desired to take his meal, he was seized by a cold fever and trembled violently, being deeply afflicted. 218.

KāKh 7.117–118 (1): This is the statement regarding fasting on the day when [the lunar day] arrives; likewise, in that same work, in the *Mālyavat-upākhyāna*, after describing King Mālyavat’s vigil and other rites on the day of arrival, it says, “Then, having risen in the morning,” and thereafter he performed the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa). 219.
Such is the statement in Kākh 34.113b; and in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, in the narrative of Kāmakalā, it is said:
"Having come to Maṇikarṇikā, having bathed, and having given much wealth..."
Regarding the statement, "Having caused the shaving of the head, she remains pure while observing a milk-vow" (verse 220),
all of that— because it is in the form of a narrative and because it is applicable to one alternative view— does not sublate the injunction for fasting on the preceding day.

(2) As for the claim that "just as in the case of a *śrāddha*, it is appropriate that even a fast occasioned by reaching a sacred site (*tīrtha*) should be performed on that very day and not on the preceding day, because the occasion has not yet arisen; otherwise, it would contradict the logical principle that 'the occasional rite (*naimittika*) exists only when the occasion (*nimitta*) is present,'" (3–4) that is based on a failure to properly perceive the principles of Mīmāṃsā. (5) For in common worldly practice, even future rain is seen to serve as an occasion for building a house, and in the Veda, even future possession of the *Rathantara* melody and so forth is seen to serve as an occasion for the precedence of the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavyāgratā*) and other rites.
It is for this very reason that the Commentator stated:

Now, as for what was said—that "there must be a preceding sign (nimitta) for a subsequent signified effect (naimittika)"—this is not an absolute rule. For even that which is yet to come can be a sign, such as the performance of agricultural work when it is thought, "It will rain. || 221 ||
Thus [it is stated] at Śabara-bhāṣya 2.3.1.2, p. 577.
The venerable Bhaṭṭa-pāda also says:

"In both worldly and Vedic usage, it is observed that past, future, and present times function as causal conditions without restriction; therefore, the fact that the *rathantara* [sāman] is future is not to be questioned. (Verse 222)
Thus [it is stated] in *TV* 2.3.1.2, p. 577. This passage from the *Vārtika-nyāyasudhā* should also be consulted regarding this matter;
however, even if one maintains the insistence that it must be based solely on an actual past event (*bhūta*), nevertheless...
Since it has been determined that "it will come to be," its status as a cause is indeed possible because it has already become [an established fact]. || 223 ||
Regarding this, the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda also said:
"That which is determined with absolute certainty is indeed already established. (NS 2.3.1.2, p. 896 [p. 62]) || 224 ||

(1) Therefore, fasting on the day preceding [the pilgrimage] is not solely for the purpose of destroying sin, but rather has the attainment of the sacred site (*tīrtha*) as its specific cause. (2) Consequently, regarding fasting at a sacred site, it is established that there is an option (*kālavikalpa*) as to whether the time is the day of arrival or the day prior to it. (3) In the first of these two positions, one performs the fast after smelling the remnants of the *śrāddha* performed at the sacred site, just as in the case of Ekādaśī and other such observances.
(4) Furthermore, this fasting at a sacred site is intended only for the sake of obtaining a specific fruit; it is not mandatory.

Having reached the sacred ford (tīrtha), one who is devoted to vows, fasts, and observances, bathing for three days and staying there for three nights, is liberated from all sins and becomes possessed of well-being. || 225 || (= 668)

(1) "Because the statement of Devala declares that fasting for three nights and immersion for three days have as their fruit liberation from all sins and the attainment of well-being"—so it is said in the *Kalpataru*. (2) That is not so, because [the practice] is enjoined as mandatory by the previously cited statements of Nārada and others. (3) The statement of Devala, however, concerns fasting for three days as an optional rite (*kāmya*) performed in addition to [the regular visit], rather than being the primary rule for the holy site (*tīrtha*). (4) This is because in the injunctions prescribing fasting at a holy site, the singular number is heard, and thus it consists of a single night's fast. (5) Furthermore, in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, in the narrative of Śivaśarman and the narrative of Kalāvatī, it is heard that the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) occurs precisely in the morning during fasting at a holy site; therefore, it is accomplished in a single day. (6) Consequently, the fast is mandatory.
[63] Now, regarding the tonsure at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), Devala states:
"Tonsure and fasting— this is the rule for all sacred fords."
Except for Kurukṣetra, Viśālā, Virajā, and Gayā. || 226 ||
‘Viraja’ is in the region of Utkala, where the Mountain Viraja was established by Dharmarāja upon the navel of the demon Gayāsura. As it is said in the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa]:
“The belly of the Daitya was stepped upon by Dharmarāja with the Mountain Viraja.”
"The goddess Virajā resides near the navel-cavity.

(227) Furthermore, the sacred site of Loṇāra in the Deccan is also Viraja, because its status as Viraja is declared in the Āditya Purāṇa: "When this rite has been performed in Viraja, one becomes free from passion (viraja). (228)
And so forth.
In some places, however, the reading is “Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gayā,” or alternatively, “Viśāla, Puṣkara, Gayā.”

Others, however, read the text as "having avoided Gayā and the Gaṅgā. That is not correct, because it is not seen in many authoritative works and because it contradicts the many statements to be cited below which enjoin the shaving of the head at the Gaṅgā. In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa:
"A fast at the holy ford must be observed, and likewise the shaving of the head."
For the sins residing in the head depart through shaving. || 229 ||
Likewise (Kākh 6.65 = 213, 249):
One should offer water as blood and offer the funeral cake as if it were impure.
All that does not accrue to one who is without a shaven head.
(230) [p.64] In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Shaving of the head and fasting... (231)
Thus, it is indeed like the speech of a god.

(1) Here, the Easterners say: "Because the word *sarvatīrtha*—by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound [meaning] 'all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are in this'—refers exclusively to Prayāga, the fasting and shaving of the head are to be performed there alone. (2) That is incorrect; for if the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with the singular number, since the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*), namely Prayāga, is a single entity, the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) lacks plurality. Consequently, the plural suffix would not arise, leading to the undesirable conclusion that the word *sarvatīrtheṣu* would be ungrammatical. (3) Thus, the claim that "plurality is unintended, just like the singularity of the cup (*graha-ekatva*)" has already dissolved through miscarriage; for if the plural suffix itself does not arise, there is no occasion to consider whether its intended meaning is expressed or not. (4) In the case of "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), since singularity resides in each individual cup, the singularity is said to be unintended in order to include all cups while maintaining the grammatical correctness of the singular ending. (5) This is simply not the case here.

(6) Now, if in order to avoid this fault, the analysis (*vigraha*) is made using the plural form, namely, "those in which all holy places (*tīrthas*) exist," (7) even so, because there is an absence of the many [places] characterized as Prayāga that are denoted by the word *sarvatīrtha*, the plural suffix would not arise, and the grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutā*) remains as it was. (8) If it were argued that "there are many Prayāgas, such as Devaprayāga and others," (9) even so, since the meaning of the constituent parts—namely, the existence of all holy places—is absent in those [other Prayāgas], and thus the plurality required for a *bahuvrīhi* compound is lacking, that same [grammatical defect] would persist.
However, if...
All sacred fords and all the gods dwell here in Avimuktaka.
The Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords.

(1) If, by considering such statements as "all" (*sarva*) and so forth, one were to justify the use of the plural number because there exist many various *tīrthas*, and then establish the intended meaning by disregarding the plurality—just as in the case of the singular number in the word "cup" (*graha*)—then: (2) since there would still be many referents for the term "all *tīrthas*," a doubt would certainly arise as to which single location among all those *tīrthas* constitutes the site for the ritual shaving (*vapana*) and other rites. (3) However, it will be stated later that there is no means of determination—such as context (*prakaraṇa*) or other indicators—to resolve this in favor of the specific Prayāga known as the confluence of the white and black waters (*sitāsita-sambheda*).

"One should perform the tonsure at Prayāga; one should cast off the body at Vārāṇasī"—by such other definitive statements as these, the word "all holy places" (*sarvatīrtha*) is restricted to Prayāga alone. This is not so, because there are many Prayāgas, such as Devaprayāga and others, and thus the specific one intended must be determined.

(3) If it is argued that this is determined by the fact that "the word *prayāga* without an accompanying suffix does not exist among them," (4) [we reply: no. For in that case, this would be a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*)—like the fourfold division—of the injunction "in all sacred fords" (*sarvatīrtheṣu*), and that is not possible. (5) For in that instance, since the general injunction "he divides the sacrificial cake into four" (*puroḍāśaṃ caturdhā karoti*) is indistinct because its scope is limited to sacrificial cakes in general, it is appropriate that there be a restrictive application to the specific scope of "he divides the cake dedicated to Agni into four" (*āgneyaṃ caturdhā karoti*). (6) But here, since the general injunction "this rule applies in all sacred fords" is distinct because its scope includes every single ford by virtue of the force of the word "all" and the plural number, a restrictive application is impossible. As it has been said:
A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by a specific one.
(1) Even though there is a concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*), this is because a summary is also possible in other systems (*tīrthāntara*) by means of the statements that are about to be mentioned.

(2) Nor can the sentence regarding Prayāga function as a sublater of the sentence regarding all holy places (*sarvatīrtha*), in the same manner as a word or a sentence [sublates another]. (3) For in that case, although the sentence concerning the *āhavanīya* fire is sublated by the word or sentence in a specific context, there remains the possibility of other oblations (*homāntara*) as its object; thus, since there is no absolute sublation, the charge of futility does not arise, and its status as something to be sublated is logical. (4) Here, however, if the sentence regarding Prayāga were to sublate the sentence regarding all holy places, there would be no other object remaining for the latter, and it would consequently result in mere futility.

(5) Furthermore, there occurs a sublation of the general by the particular, and the statement regarding all holy fords (*sarvatīrtha*) cannot be considered general, because you yourself have accepted that it has the specific holy ford of Prayāga as its object. (6) Moreover, if either a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) or a sublation (*bādha*) were asserted [of the general], it would follow that the statement regarding all holy fords would possess a general form. (7) How is it not contradictory to assert that the word "all holy fords" refers exclusively to Prayāga alone?

(8) As for the claim that the injunction “one should perform shaving at Prayāga” is not an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction), because the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* prescribes shaving at Prabhāsa—stating first, “Having performed shaving in the vicinity of Someśvara,” and then providing the statement “shaving and fasting”—which serves as an injunction for shaving at other sacred sites (*tīrtha*s); and because the *Devalasmṛti* contains an injunction for shaving without reference to a specific context; (9) Nor is it a *niyama-vidhi* (a restrictive injunction), because since the requirement is already fulfilled by the general statement regarding all sacred sites, there is no unobtained portion to be supplied; (10) Nor is it a *parisaṃkhyā-vidhi* (an exclusive injunction); for in that case, the syntactical interpretation would have to be either “at Prayāga one should shave only, and nothing else,” or “shaving is to be done only at Prayāga. (11) Not the first, because it would entail the cessation of bathing and other such acts; (12) not the second, because it would incur the three defects of sublation (*bādha*) and so forth of what is already established. (14) Therefore, this has been refuted by some as being merely a “separated restatement” (*vayutyānuvāda*) and not an injunction. (15) That, however, is merely the specter of an unwarranted dilemma (*vikalpa*), since the status of an *apūrva-vidhi* is impossible to deny. (16) Nor is its novelty (*apūrvatva*) lacking simply because it is already established by the words of Devala and others; for when there is a difference in texts or authors, the injunctive force (*vidhitva*) of even identical matters remains intact. (17) Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of treating the injunctions for the *Agnihotra* found in various Vedic branches, and the injunctions for the *Sandhyāvandana* found in various *Smṛti*s, as mere restatements. (19) Furthermore, there is a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the restativeness belongs to the Prayāga statement because it is established by that, or to this statement because it is established by that. (20) Moreover, if this were a restatement, then the statements regarding shaving at other sacred sites mentioned below would likewise become restatements by the same logic. (21) And it is not proper for many statements to be mere restatements. (22) Furthermore, a restatement would be purposeless. (23) On the contrary, it would follow that the general statement regarding all sacred sites would itself be a collective restatement of matters already established by the specific injunctions for shaving and fasting at each individual site. Enough of this internal dispute; let us return to the subject at hand.

(24) Since this statement is found in the sections on Gayā in the *Agnipurāṇa* and the *Vāyupurāṇa*, and in the section on Prabhāsa in the *Skandapurāṇa*, what doubt could there be regarding its reference to Prayāga? (25) Furthermore: “O Lord of the Earth, all holy places are present here”; [as stated in the verse: “O descendant of Kuru, ten thousand crores of holy places are indeed present in Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day. (236)
From the statement in the Āraṇyaka-parvan (MBh 3.80.42): "O Puṣkara, all sacred fords and the gods dwell here in Avimuktaka. (237) (= 232)
(1) Furthermore, because Kāśī is also a "tīrtha of all tīrthas" according to the statement in the *Brahmavaivarta*, the same [objection] applies there as well.

(2) Likewise, there exist various statements intended to praise specific tīrthas or to establish the presence of all tīrthas within them. (3) However, these are not stated here for fear of prolixity. For example:
"And Prayāga, the lord of tīrthas, [removes] the impurity deposited by all tīrthas."
One should forcibly take away the great wealth of those from the land of the Five Rivers. || 238 ||

(1) Furthermore, statements such as these in the *Pañcanada-prakaraṇa* and other texts would be contradicted if all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) were present there. (2) Now, if it is argued that the word "all sacred fords" is used at Prayāga by convention, regardless of its etymological derivation (*yoga*), (3) that is not so, because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for that.
“Act thus, O Kaunteya, by bathing in all the sacred fords;
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment. (239)

If it is argued that “the statement recited in the Prayāga section of the *Matsyapurāṇa* (MaPu 108.33) is the authority on this matter,” (2) that is not so; for in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, after beginning with “It is known as Agnitīrtha” (MaPu 108.27a) and enumerating many sacred sites (*tīrthas*), [it continues:]...
And there are many other auspicious sacred fords that remove all sins;
having bathed in them, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
Act thus, O Kaunteya, performing ablutions at all sacred fords;
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant. || 240 ||

(1) Since it is designated [as such] up to the end of verse 108.33, the word "all" (*sarva*) is understood to refer to all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) under discussion. (2) How then can this word "all sacred fords" be forcibly interpreted as referring specifically to Prayāga?
Furthermore—
"All holy places dwell there where there is discourse concerning the noble stories of Acyuta.
Thus, all holy places as well as the Agnihotra—
"We say they are certainly not equal.
(242) "Whatever merit is in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is in all sacred fords," (243) "Thus, O Gaṅgā, you embody all sacred fords. (244) (= 233)
(1) In such passages, the term *sarvatīrtha* is seen to refer to many sacred fords (*anekatīrtha*), but not specifically to Prayāga.
"O Lord, they declare Prayāga to be superior to all sacred fords. (245)
(1) Furthermore, this statement from the *Mahābhārata* would be contradicted if Prayāga were considered the locus of all tīrthas;
(2) moreover, in the *Agni Purāṇa*:
I shall describe the majesty of all sacred fords, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(1) Having begun thus and having described numerous sacred sites such as Gaṅgā, Kāśī, and Prayāga over many chapters, the *Agni Purāṇa* concludes by stating at the end: “Shaving the head and fasting—this is the rule for all sacred sites” (AgPu 115.7cd). (2) Therefore, this refers to the subject matter of various sacred sites in general, and not exclusively to Prayāga alone. (3) Furthermore, whenever the word *sarvatīrtha* is seen in the Purāṇas referring to a single specific site, it is employed in the singular number; for example, in the *Sahyādrikhaṇḍa*, in the section concerning the *Mātṛtīrtha*.
The supreme sacred site of the Sahya mountain is known as Mātṛtīrtha;
O lords of sages, Mātṛtīrtha should be understood as the highest of all sacred sites.

In that place are all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), where Rāma [dwells], O Reṇukā. By bathing at this *Sarvatīrtha*, men obtain the merit of bathing at every sacred ford. There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford superior to *Sarvatīrtha*.
In such passages as these, (1) the singular number is not employed.

(2) Furthermore, injunctions prescribing tonsure at various sacred sites (*tīrtha*) are indeed found in the Purāṇas. (3) In that regard, after mentioning many sacred sites in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* with the passage beginning “First, the king of sacred sites,” and having described the manner of pilgrimage in between, [on p. 69] it says: “A fast at the sacred site must be observed, and likewise the shaving of the head.”
"Since the sins residing in the head depart through shaving," (249).
Thus, shaving has been described in general terms regarding all sacred sites (*tīrtha*).
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
There, having plunged into the treasure-house of waters, one should perform a bath;
first, however, having undergone a shaving near Someśvara,
one should cast off the hair there while meditating upon Śaṅkara in the mind.
There, having discarded all the hair, one should perform the bath once again.
Whatever sin a man oppressed by the struggle for livelihood commits,
O Daughter of the Mountain, all of that remains in his hair.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cast off one's hair there;
for he who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices [does not equal him].
O fair-faced one, he does not obtain that fruit which is gained from sowing;
moreover, the shaving of hair is not recommended for women.
Now hear from me the rule for those women who have husbands:
having gathered up all their hair, she should cut off two finger-breadths. (250)

Having thus prescribed the tonsure for the *prabhāsīya* [pilgrimage] up to this point, at the conclusion, as a relevant digression, the tonsure and fasting are ordained for all sacred bathing sites (*tīrtha*):
"This rule applies to all sacred bathing sites: both the tonsure and the fasting. (PraKh 1.29.3c–6b, 12, 8–9b) [250]
In the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*, within the narrative of Kāmakalā, there is also seen the shaving of the head and fasting at Kāśī for other purposes:
"Having arrived at Maṇikarṇikā, having bathed and given much wealth..."
Having caused her hair to be shaved, she remained pure, observing the *payovrata* vow.
(251) [p.70] The term *payovratā* means one whose food consists of water alone.
It is stated elsewhere as well:
Having first performed the bath and other rites, one should carry out the tonsure at the sacred site;
having observed the vow of fasting at the sacred site, one should then perform the śrāddha ceremony.
Likewise:
"One should offer water and blood; one should offer the funeral cake as if it were impure. All that does not reach [the ancestors] for one who is without a shaven head. (253) (= 230)
Likewise:
"Shaving the head and fasting [are required] at the Gomatī when Jupiter is in Leo;
but when it has entered Virgo, these are for those on the dark fortnight, yet not for the inhabitants of its banks. (254)
Likewise, regarding the Gaṅgā: "However many nails and hairs, driven by the wind,
fall into the waters of the Jāhnavī, [they destroy] the sins of men who have committed evil."
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the heavenly world.
Likewise:
"He who, having reached the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, does not have the tonsure performed, shall go to the Raurava hell for an eon, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage. (256)
(1) Or there is the reading: “In the Gaṅgā, in the field of Bhāskara.
Likewise:
“When one’s mother, father, or guru has died in the Gaṅgā, in the field of Bhāskara...”
"Shaving of the head is prescribed in seven cases: at the establishment of the sacred fires and at the drinking of Soma.
Likewise—
Indeed, for as many thousands of years as there are nails and hairs that fall into the waters of the Ganges, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Likewise:
"Upon reaching the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, the accumulations of sin tremble;
they remain clinging to the hair, therefore one should have it shaved."
If a wise man, having reached the Gaṅgā, does not have his head shaved, all his ritual acts become as if unperformed; such a man becomes a traitor to the sacred ford.

(1) Thus, even though the rule for shaving the head is heard of in various sacred sites (*tīrtha*), it would be a great act of temerity for those who claim that shaving is prescribed elsewhere than at Prayāga.

(2) Furthermore, as for the claim that the statements prescribing the shaving of the head at the Ganges are rootless (*nirmūlatva*) because they were not recorded by the author of the *Kalpataru*, (3) that is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that the injunctions regarding the casting of bones and so forth are likewise rootless. (4) If it is argued that "the non-observation of the *Kalpataru* author is the proof of rootlessness, rather than his failure to record them," (5) then what is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that non-observation?
