(6) It cannot be his failure to record them alone, as that would result in the same fault mentioned previously; (7) and because it would lead to the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). (8) Nor is there any other [proof], since none can be defined. (9) Or, even if he were not observed, how could there be rootlessness? (10) For the author of the *Kalpataru* is not some other omniscient Lord; enough of this.

(11) As for the claim that the statement, “In the Gaṅgā at Bhāskarakṣetra,” does not refer to the Gaṅgā in general, but rather to the Gaṅgā as delimited by Prayāga—due to the prohibition, “Having avoided Gayā and the broad Gaṅgā”—and that the prohibitive statement refers instead to the Gaṅgā as undelimited; (13) this too has already been refuted by stating that such a reading in the prohibitive text is itself improper. (14) Furthermore, you maintain that the general form of many scriptural statements is restricted to a specific sense “in accordance with the practice of authoritative persons (*śiṣṭa*) whose conduct is beyond reproach. (15) But that [general sense] is sublated by the practice of the many learned Vedic *śiṣṭas* residing in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), (16) because the practice of non-Vedic persons, however learned, is of little authority. As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭa:

Therefore, the opinion of those who are devoted to the scriptures and dwell in Āryāvarta is held to be the authoritative means of determining the meaning of words as they function within the context of ritual action. (TV 1.3.4.9, p.
(1) Furthermore, if the term *sarvatīrtha* were intended to refer exclusively to Prayāga, the use of the plural number would be unjustified.

(2) Nor can it be argued that, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the reference is restricted solely to Prayāga while the plural sense is not intended—as in the case of the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*).

(3) This is because the possibility of such an intention or non-intention has already been shown previously to have no scope here, as it would result in the compound being grammatically incorrect (*asādhutā*) if it were a *bahuvrīhi*.

(4) Furthermore, the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the plural number does not contradict our position, but rather supports it; indeed, it contradicts yours alone. (5) For instance, just as in the cases of "whose two *puroḍāśa* cakes are burnt," "whose all the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) should be lost or defiled," and "he sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," the non-intentionality of the number residing in the object of reference (*uddeśya*) establishes that shaving is to be performed at every crossing-point (*pratitīrtha*). (6) If, however, there were intentionality (*vivakṣā*), it would apply only to the collection as a whole, and not to each individual instance.

(8) However, someone offers this objection: "In the case of the singular number [of the ladle], there is no lack of intentionality (*avivakṣā*) because it is not a qualifier of the object to be designated (*uddeśya*) as something to be processed (*saṃskārya*); and (9) in the case of the dual number [of the oblation], there is no such lack of intentionality because it is not a qualifier of the object to be designated as a causal factor (*nimitta*). (10) That is not correct; for in those two cases, being "that which is to be processed" and being "the causal factor" are not included within the body of the logical principle (*nyāyaśarīra*), (11) since in both instances, the lack of intentionality is established solely by virtue of being qualifiers of the object to be designated.

(12) As for the objection regarding redundancy in the section on the destruction of both (*ubhayārti*), it must be resolved by refuting the additional doubt that "the state of being both (*ubhayatva*) is included within the very nature of the cause (*nimitta-svarūpa*), and not a qualification of the cause. It is not [resolved] by means of a distinction in the objects, such as the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) and the form of the cause. (14) Otherwise, the examples of causes provided by the Vārttikakāra—namely, "for whom the two *puroḍāśa* cakes are burnt" and "for whom all the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) should perish"—as well as the example of the plural number of the oblation to be refined in the rule "he sprinkles the oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," would be inconsistent. For this very reason, Pārthasārathi Miśra states in the section on the destruction of both: [text follows].
By the principle of the *grahādhikaraṇa*, it is already established that "the qualification of the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant" (*avivakṣita*),

but it is not the case that the nature of the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) itself is not intended to be significant. Here, however, just as neither mere distress nor mere sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is the occasioning cause, but rather their combination is the occasioning cause— so too, because both terms are recited in the text, all three together constitute the occasioning cause.
"Let there be a sign," [he said]. || 261 ||
In the *Tantraratna* (p.
554), Bhaṭṭa Someśvara also [states that] when there is an intention to express a qualification of the subject (*uddeśya*), there arises the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*).

Even though the logic proving the lack of intention [to express] is equal, this is not cited as an example here because, in order to avoid the meaninglessness of both terms, there is an excess of suspicion regarding the intention to express "bothness" as being included within the subject matter (uddeśya). || 262 ||
Thus they say, and so forth.

(1) Furthermore, even if there were no status as a *nimitta* (condition) or as something to be refined (*saṃskāryatva*), why would there not be a lack of intentionality (*avivakṣā*) simply because it is a qualificand (*uddeśyatva*), as in the case of the injunction: "One should sprinkle the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings upon the oblations"? (2) In reality, however, because the word "in all holy places" (*sarvatīrtheṣu*) functions as a qualifier of the specific *tīrtha*s which serve as the *nimitta*, a lack of intentionality regarding the plurality (*bahutva*) is indeed possible, just as it is with the term "both" (*ubhaya*). (3) Moreover, the lack of intentionality regarding the plural number is actually consistent—even contrary to what might be thought—with the view that shaving occurs at each individual *tīrtha* by resorting to a *karmadhāraya* compound; it is not contradictory. Otherwise, as has been stated, the shaving would apply to the entire collection of *tīrtha*s as a whole, rather than to each individual *tīrtha*. (4) Therefore, since a lack of intentionality regarding plurality is necessary—as in the cases of "whose two cakes," "whose all oblations," and "the oblations with the remnants of the *prayāja*"—where they function as qualifiers of the qualificand, and since the two cases share the same logical status (*tulyayogakṣema*), the claim that the principle of non-intentionality does not apply to one who maintains that shaving occurs at *Prayāga* alone is utterly improper. This is because such a claim, by necessitating an intentionality [of the plural], results in the defeat of one's own position.

(6) Therefore, the application of the principle from the section on the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*) should be refuted precisely by means of the lack of scope and the conformity [to our position] according to the method we have stated; (7) thus, enough with this dispute over one's own side.

(8) Furthermore, because in a *bahuvrīhi* there would follow the consequence that the meanings of the two constituent words are not primary, and because there would follow the consequence of a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the meaning of another word—as in the case of the term *niṣādasthapati*—the *karmadhāraya* compound is indeed superior to the *bahuvrīhi* when compared with a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), (9) since [in the *karmadhāraya*] both word-meanings are primary and there is no figurative indication. (10) By this [argument], in the case of the passage "The king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should perform the sacrifice," a *dvandva* compound was accepted by setting aside the *karmadhāraya*, because a Kṣatriya is prohibited from serving as a domestic priest and because, as established in the *Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa*, the status of being a domestic priest is impossible for those denoted by the word "king" which refers to a Kṣatriya. (11) But here, in the case of the *karmadhāraya*, there is no such subverting factor.

(12) Now, if it is argued that "by relying solely on a *karmadhāraya* [compound], because it takes the form of many sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the word 'all sacred fords' (*sarvatīrtha*) actually refers to Prayāga alone," (13) even that is not correct. For in that case, is plurality intended (*vivakṣita*) or unintended (*avivakṣita*)? (14) Not the first, because intentionality is impossible when [plurality] serves as a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*). (15) Nor the other, because apart from intentionality, one would fail to obtain Prayāga as a collection of many sacred fords, and there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to shave one's head at every individual ford. (16) Therefore, neither a *bahuvrīhi* nor a *karmadhāraya* is tenable.

(17) Now, if it is argued that—even though a *bahuvrīhi* compound has but a single referent—the plural number is used either as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) with the intention of referring to the multiplicity of its constituent parts, as in the case of "Aditi shall release these bonds" (*aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktv etān*), or for the sake of honor, as in the expression "the teachers" (*ācāryās tu*) and so forth. (18) That too is incorrect; for when a straightforward interpretation is possible, it is improper to resort to a Vedic anomaly or other such interpretations which have no other recourse. (19) Furthermore, regarding the mantra containing the plural number that is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, there arises a doubt: is the plural number to be accepted as applying to a single object—on the grounds that it is a Vedic anomaly within that very context, just like the word "Vāyavas" (*vāyavaḥ stha*)—and thus inserted into the ritual, or is it to be displaced (*utkarṣa*) to apply to groups of animals having many bonds? Having raised this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that the plural number must be displaced because it lacks the capacity to apply to a single bond mentioned in the context. (20) However, since the meaning of the base noun (*prakṛtyartha*)—the "bond"—and the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*)—the objective case (*karmakāraka*)—both exist in the original ritual context, it is impossible to displace the base noun, the second-case ending denoting the objective, or the mantra itself merely to conform to the subordinate plural suffix. Therefore, the plural number is intended solely for the purpose of reference (*nirdeśamātrārtha*). (21) [The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states: Since the singular bond is present in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and since the primary elements—the nominal stem, the objective case, and the mantra—cannot be displaced for the sake of the subordinate plural suffix alone, the plural is used merely to indicate the plurality of instances. Thus, the mantra is applied to each individual bond.

Just as in the ritual application involving two wives, it is appropriate—according to the ninth-lecture principle—to say that the singular number in the mantra "I gird the wife" refers to each individual part; however, in this case, since the possibility of referring to the [entirety of] Prayāga is precluded by the force of the many stated objections, on what basis could one assert either its Vedic irregularity or its reference to individual parts?

(24) Moreover, the fact that the statement regarding all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) refers exclusively to Prayāga cannot be established except through *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). (25) In that case, what kind of *parisaṃkhyā* is it? (26) Is it "shaving of the head (*muṇḍana*) only at Prayāga," or "shaving of the head only at Prayāga"? (27) It cannot be the latter, because it would entail the cessation of bathing and other such acts [at Prayāga]. (28) Nor can it be the former, because it would entail the absence of shaving when there is a death of a parent or other relative. (29) Now, if it is argued that "shaving with a sacred ford as its locus occurs only at Prayāga and not elsewhere"—
(30) Because it would follow that [the rule] would not apply when one's father or others die at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as Kāśī.

(31) Now, if you argue: "Shaving caused by a sacred ford occurs only at Prayāga," (32) then, since shaving caused by that [specific reason] is not obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*), its acquisition must be through scripture (*śāstra*); thus, it would have to be admitted that the acquisition [of the rule] applies generally to all sacred fords. (33) Therefore, how is there no contradiction with your own statement for you who claim, "There is no injunction for shaving at other sacred fords"?
(34) Furthermore, in either of these two alternatives, the three faults—such as the sublation of what has been established (*prāptabādha*)—would result.

(35) Furthermore, if this injunction for tonsure were restricted solely to Prayāga, its inclusion in the sections concerning Gayā in the *Agnipurāṇa* and the *Vāyupurāṇa* would be untenable. (36) Moreover, by the natural force of the word "all" (*sarva*) in the injunction for tonsure, tonsure must take place at all sacred sites (*tīrtha*).
(37) Nor does the lack of restriction on the word "all" lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [as it is limited by the context of the relevant passages].
The sanctity of sacred fords is traditionally held to arise from their marvelous power, from the earth, from water, and from fire, as well as from the acceptance [of them] by sages. (263) (= 75)

(1) It should not be argued that because the *Bhārata* passage stating Bhīṣma’s words—“A place and water that yield extraordinary fruits are called *tīrthas*” —implies that tonsure and fasting must apply everywhere, even to springs and such within one’s own country; for (2) the word “all *tīrthas*” (*sarvatīrtha*) refers specifically to those well-known great *tīrthas* enumerated in the *Purāṇas* as *tīrtha*-locations; and (3) because it refers specifically to those *tīrthas* in which tonsure is prescribed by particular injunctions, the term “all” (*sarva*) is used in a qualified or restricted sense (*ādhikārika*). || 264 ||
This is according to the maxim [found] in MS 1.2.1.16.

(1) Nor should it be said that "there is an absence of the injunction for shaving at any place other than Prayāga," because (2) statements enjoining such [shaving] at Prabhāsa, Kāśī, and other locations have already been cited previously.

(3) Furthermore, regarding the interpretation offered by some of the sentence “*gaṅgāyāṃ bhāskarakṣetre*” [256.1, 257], which—accepting the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by identifying *bhāskarakṣetra* with Prayāga—states that it means “in the Gaṅgā as delimited by Prayāga,” (4) that too is incorrect; for it will be stated later that Prayāga is the field of Prajāpati, and thus it cannot be the field of Bhāskara. In this regard: “The man who gives up his life-breaths there in the field of Savitṛ, having ascended to the world of the Sun, rejoices in heaven like a god. (265)
(1) For, from the greatness of Koṇāditya and the others [mentioned] thus, it is understood that they alone constitute the *bhāskarakṣetra*.

(2) Furthermore, if one were to explain [the compound] by means of the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), there would be the consequence of [the number] being six, and thus the numerical designation "in seven" (*saptasu*) would be untenable. (3) Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of the term "in the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyām*) being redundant.

(4) Furthermore, if the rule regarding sowing were intended to apply solely to Prayāga, then since there would be no possibility of its occurrence at other sacred sites (*tīrtha*), the specific prohibition "excepting" (*varjayitvā*) would be logically untenable.

(5) As for what is said: "Just as when it is stated, 'There shall be an offering of mung beans (*maudga-caru*),' the exclusion of black gram (*māṣa*) and other such grains is already established by that specific injunction itself; yet the subsequent statement, 'Black gram is indeed unfit for sacrifice,' is intended to show that 'black gram should not be accepted even as a substitute, because it is utterly unfit for sacrifice'; (6) likewise, the prohibition against sowing [seeds] at Gayā and other such places is also intended to express extreme lack of merit. (7) To this, someone objects: "Since the statement 'unfit for sacrifice' is supplementary to the injunction regarding mung beans and serves to praise them, it cannot have the meaning that 'black gram should not be taken even as a substitute. (8) For the purpose of a censure lies solely in the glorification of that which is enjoined. (9) Therefore, according to the maxim—'Indeed, a censure does not proceed to censure the censured object, but rather to praise the enjoined object'—the intent here is precisely the praise of the mung bean, just like the passage, 'Jartila seeds and gavīdhuka seeds are indeed no oblation.'"
(10) But this does not mean that *māṣa* beans are absolutely unfit for sacrifice.

(11) Furthermore, in such passages as “others are indeed non-animals,” “this is indeed no sacrifice,” and “*māṣa* beans are indeed unfit for sacrifice,” the excellence (*prāśastya*) indicated by words such as “animal” is negated by the particle *nañ*; thus, the purpose is to convey a lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*). As it has been said:
“Having first taken up the excellence residing in cows, horses, and so forth...”
"The absence of that [excellence] in other animals and so forth is expressed by a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). (TV 1.4.12.23, p.
362) (1) However, in the phrase "having excluded," because there is no negative particle (*nañ*), it does not have the sense of "lack of excellence."
A śrāddha ceremony should be performed there, however, excluding the offering of the arghya water and the invocation.
Just as in that [case], one should avoid [these] at śrāddhas performed at sacred fords (tīrtha). || 268 ||
And so it is said:

(1) Furthermore, since there is no scriptural injunction for the employment of a substitute in the Vedic ritual, the non-employment of *māṣa* beans as a substitute will follow simply from the absence of such an injunction; (2) what, then, is the purpose of the prohibition, "The *māṣa* beans are unfit for sacrifice"?
(3) Likewise, a second prohibition of that which has already been prohibited serves to indicate an extreme fault.
Thus it has been said:

"Even when the sixth [lunar day] and others are avoided, as well as the beginning of the month, on the new moon, during meat-eating, and on the full moon and the oil-bath day, the fourteenth day is mentioned for the sake of the greater severity of the fault. (269) Thus.

(1) "And since there is no other prohibition in the context under discussion, the prohibition against sowing at Gayā and other such places does not have the purpose of declaring them absolutely unfit. (2) That is extremely superficial; for in the sixth section of the third quarter of the *Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra* [p. 77], it is stated:
"And that which is prohibited without qualification, for that is what the Vedic text declares. (JS. 3.4.27).

In the sūtra MS 6.3.6.20(1), having accepted that the statement “beans are indeed unfit for sacrifice” is intended as a prohibition, and since that which is prohibited must not be substituted, [beans cannot serve as a substitute]. || 271 ||

By stating this, both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Bhāṣya accept that the intent is the prohibition of a substitute; for that which is prohibited leads to demerit (pratyavāya). || 272 ||

Since even the teacher Karka, in his commentary on this sūtra (KātŚrSū 1.129), accepts that its purpose is prohibitory, (1) how then can it be a subordinate element of the injunction regarding mung beans? (2) How much less can it have the intention of being a mere praise, as in the case of the statement "jartila seeds are indeed not an oblation"? (3) And how much less can it serve to demonstrate a difference from something else—such as the comparison "they are not cattle"—given that there is no negative particle (*nañ*) to trigger the application of such a comparison?

(3) As for the claim that "in the Vedic tradition there is no taking of a substitute without an explicit scriptural statement," this may hold true for those who are not Mīmāṃsakas; (4) because in that very same fourth section it has been stated that the substitute is established by logical necessity (*nyāya*), as there is no scriptural basis (*vācanikatva*) anywhere for it—[the scripture stating only]:
"If one does not find Soma, one should press substitutes. || 273 ||
Even in cases such as this, a rule [of exclusion] may in some instances function as a positive injunction. // 274 //
(1) This is because that very sūtra [MS 6.3.4.16] itself accepts that [the statement] serves merely as a restrictive rule (*niyamamātrārthatva*).

(2) As for the claim that "the prohibition of what is already prohibited is for the purpose of making known an extreme fault," (3) even that is easily resolved by the proponent of the theory of non-praise (*aprāśastya*) through the acceptance of the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), namely: since the injunction regarding all sacred sites (*sarvatīrtha*) has the purpose of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), there is a prohibition against shaving elsewhere; therefore, the subsequent prohibition regarding Gayā and other such places is for the purpose of indicating an extreme fault.

(4) Therefore, the statement “they are unfit for sacrifice” (*ayajñiya*) should be refuted as being equal to the statement “except at Gayā. (5) For in that case, when a sacrificial pap (*caru*) made of mung beans and the like is prescribed, the principle that “if the primary substance is unavailable, a substitute similar to it should be used” applies; thus, since black gram (*māṣa*) would attain the status of a substitute for mung beans due to their similarity in the absence of mung beans, it is appropriate to state their unfitness for sacrifice in order to prohibit that. (6) But here, since the shaving of the head at Gayā and other such places is accepted as a mandatory requirement (*aṅga*), a prohibition is impossible; for what purpose, then, is the declaration of their absolute lack of merit (*atyantāprāśastya*) made?

(7) Furthermore, is the statement of lack of excellence—“Indeed, *jartila* [sesame seeds] are not an oblation”—intended for the praise of the prescribed sowing at Prayāga, in the same manner that the statement “milk is an oblation” is intended for the praise of the milk to be prescribed? (8) Or is it intended for the prohibition of sowing at Gayā and other such places, as in the case of “Beans are unfit for sacrifice”? (9) It cannot be the latter, because since there is no authority for you to perform sowing at Gayā and so forth, a prohibition would be inappropriate, and it would result in the acceptance of our own position. (10) Nor can it be the former, because unlike the phrase “not an oblation,” there is no negative particle (*nañ*) here; thus, there is no perception of praise by way of a lack of excellence. “One should avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating. (275)

This is because, as in the case of the expression *ityavad*, and as in the expression *‘arghyāvāhanavarjitam’* [267], the verb *varjayati* conveys only a prohibition; and furthermore, if it were intended to convey a lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

(3) Alternatively, even though the rule for shaving the head applies specifically at Prayāga, the prohibition against Gayā and other sites might be intended to indicate that the fault is greater elsewhere. Or else—
Eating in the evening and in the morning is prescribed by the Vedas for the twice-born. (276)

(1) In this regard, for the sake of explaining the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) according to those who maintain the doctrine of restrictive enumeration, [it is said]: "One should not eat in between; the rule is equal to that of the *agnihotra*. (277)
In the second chapter of the *Smṛticandrikā*, on page 609, regarding the statement of Manu:

"(1) [The prohibition of Gaya and other such places] would also have the purpose of explaining that [prohibition]. (2) This is not so; for in either case, it would result in a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), and that has already been refuted previously. (3) Furthermore, if its purpose were to explain an exclusive specification, the enumeration of Gaya and other places would be redundant. (4) For it would suffice to state merely "not at any other holy site" (*nānyatīrthe*).

(5) If it is argued: "Could this not be a restatement of the permanent (nityānuvāda), like the statement 'fire is not to be piled in the intermediate space nor in heaven'? (6) No, because of the disparity; for in that case, it is indeed a restatement of the permanent because piling [the fire-altar] is simply impossible in the intermediate space and so forth. (7) Here, however, since shaving is possible elsewhere than at Prayāga, it cannot be a restatement of the permanent. (8) Furthermore, it would result in meaninglessness through the introduction of a different name.

(9) Enough, then, of this excessive parching of the throat. (10) Although this meaning—that "in all holy places other than Gayā and the like, there shall be tonsure and fasting"—is indeed understood from the very natural sense of the statement itself, nevertheless, this extensive effort at refutation has been made so that those of small intellect might not fall into error through the arguments propounded by the wicked-minded. (11) Thus it is established: in all well-known great holy places other than Kurukṣetra and the like, there shall be tonsure and fasting.
(12) And this tonsure must be performed again upon reaching a sacred ford after ten months;
if one should go to a sacred ford again within a year minus two months, then one should diligently perform both the tonsure and the fast. || 278 || (= 551)

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. (1) It must necessarily be performed only upon reaching the completion of ten months. (2) However, it may occur earlier through a desire for the fruit, but this is not a mandatory rule; such is the meaning of the phrase "with effort. (3) We shall, however, state the specific rule regarding Prayāga later.

(4) Here, this must be considered regarding the shaving: (5) is the resolve "I shall perform the shaving" (*vapanaṃ kariṣye*), or "I shall have it performed" (*kārayiṣye*)? (6) On this point, some say: since the shaving occasioned by reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is understood to be enjoined by injunctions such as "One should perform the shaving at Prayāga" [234], and (7) because shaving is performed for the sake of livelihood even by a barber who lacks any such occasion, an occasional injunction (*naimittika-vidhi*) would be inapplicable; (8) furthermore, from the natural sense of statements such as "Having reached the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, he who does not have the shaving performed" [256]; (9) or because the word *kuryāt* is used with the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "he should have it performed," thereby enjoining the shaving itself; (10) and because that which is enjoined is connected to a fruit, and only that which possesses a fruit is to be performed; (11) therefore, the resolve is "Desiring the aforementioned fruit, I shall have the shaving performed. (12) Nor should it be argued that, because of the injunction "one should perform the shaving," the rule "only the injunctive verb-form should be employed" applies, and thus the resolve should be "I shall do it" (*kariṣye*). (13) For that rule concerns words whose purport lies in the nature of the sound of the word for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), such as mantras and deities; (14) here, however, the purport lies in the mere meaning, just like the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Therefore...
If a word of injunction were to function as a mantra, its efficacy would consist in that [injunction] being the impelling force. || 279 ||

In the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* 10.4.12.23, Jaimini states that [the word *vapana*] possesses the status of a *mantra*. And thus, since the injunction has the shaving (*vāpana*) as its intended meaning, according to the maxim: "When the employment of words lies within our own control, why should we employ a non-expressive term?", the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) should be either "I shall cause the shaving to be performed" (*vapanaṃ kārayiṣye*) or "I shall perform the shaving" (*vāpanaṃ kariṣye*), but not "I shall do the shaving" (*vapanaṃ kariṣye*).

(3) This is not tenable; for although injunctions such as “one who does not have [the hair] shaved,” “therefore one should have them shaved,” and “one should perform shaving at Prayāga” possess both forms [of being both descriptive and prescriptive], there are also statements such as: “Whatever sins there may be, even those equal to the murder of a Brahmin, reside in dependence upon the hair; therefore, I shave my hair. (280)

(1) Thus, because of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall perform the shaving" alone is appropriate. (2) Nor is there a contradiction (*bādha*), for no connection [of the term with other body parts] is perceived; since the word "shaving" (*vapana*) is used specifically for the act of separating the hair, there is no contradiction, as seen in the passage: "When shaving the hair and beard, he clips the nails... (ĀpDhS 1.31.20). || 281 ||

It is like the following cases: (1) Just as, because of the scriptural injunction “one offers in the *āhavanīya*,” the act of throwing a substance into the *āhavanīya* constitutes a *homa*, and since that [act] has the *adhvaryu* as its agent, even though the *yajamāna* is not its agent, in the case of optional *homas* (*kāmyahomas*) and the *agnihotra-homa*, when the *adhvaryu* is the agent, the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is simply: “I shall perform such-and-such a *homa*”; (2) or just as, although the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*) has the *adhvaryu* as its agent according to its name (*samākhyā*), there is nevertheless a resolve based on injunctions such as “one desiring offspring should pile [the altar] knee-high,” namely: “I, desiring such-and-such, shall perform the piling”; (3) so too is it here. (4) And thus, the elders’ etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *agnicit* as “one who has piled the fire” (*agniṃ citavān*) becomes logical.

(5) And thus, even when there is a causal factor consisting in the arrival at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), the meaning of the word *vapana* as a formal ritual act (*saṃvidhāna*) certainly persists. (6) As for those statements containing the causative suffix (*ṇic*), such as “he who does not have the shaving performed” [256], they are also appropriate when taking the final, completed sense of the action.

(7) As for the claim that "because [the word] has as its purport merely the object, there is an absence of purport regarding the injunctive word"; (8) let it be so. Nevertheless, because the performance preceded by the recollection of the injunction resides in the intellect, and for the sake of parsimony, it is logical that the injunctive word itself should be employed in the *saṅkalpa* (formal resolve). (9) For this very reason, those who are well-versed in Mīmāṃsā have stated that the purpose of a name is also the practical usage of the *saṅkalpa* and so forth, just like the connection of a quality with a fruit.

(10) Furthermore, the principle that [the Veda] "depends upon us" and so forth is not applicable here; (11) because, as established by the reasoning already stated, its capacity to convey meaning is proven and thus there is no lack of denotative power, and because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra itself—namely, "I offer"—acts as the regulator, there is no dependence upon us.

(12) Alternatively, the word *vapana* has multiple meanings. In this context, it sometimes denotes the causal agent’s activity (*prayojakavyāpāra*), consisting of the act of arranging for the removal of hair; (13) and at other times it denotes the activity of the person being prompted (*prayojyavyāpāra*), because it is used in both ways—as in “the shaving was done by me” (*mayā vapanam kṛtam*) and “the shaving was caused to be done” (*vapanam kāritam*). (15) In that regard, just as contextual factors (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth serve as indicators of intended meaning (*tātparya*), so too does the co-occurrence with another word. (16) When there is co-occurrence with the word *kuryāt*, it refers to the causal agent’s activity; (17) but when there is co-occurrence with the word *kārayet*, it refers to the activity of the person being prompted. (18) This being the case, since by the force of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra only the causal agent’s activity is to be manifested, the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is simply: “I shall perform the shaving. (19) Enough of this prolixity.

(20) "And this shaving should be performed according to the sequence of hair and beard; having gone [to the water], one should perform a bath, and immediately thereafter the shaving. One should shave the hair and the beard, and have the nails clipped. (282) (= 211)
According to this statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa*, one should have the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails shaved, arranged toward the north. || 283 ||
(1) Thus, according to the sequence of the well-known reading in the statement recorded by Aparārka: "He has his hair and beard shaved"— || 284 ||

Some say, "Because it is seen in such scriptural passages [as *tyādiśruti*]. Others, however, maintain: "(1) These statements merely enjoin the shaving of the hair and so forth, but do not prescribe their sequence either, due to the resulting burden and the consequence of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). (2) Therefore, the shaving must begin with the beard.

(3) Accordingly, among the Āpastambas, there is heard a praise of shaving the beard and so forth, preceded by a censure of shaving the hair first: 'The gods did what they did at the sacrifice; the Asuras did the same. Those Asuras [shaved] above the backs...'"

They did not see [him]. They shaved their hair first, then their beards, then the armpits; thereupon they went downward and were defeated. He for whom they shave in this manner goes downward and is indeed defeated. Then the gods saw him above the backs; they shaved their armpits first, then their beards, then...

[He cuts] the hair; from that they came into being. They went to the heavenly world. For him who has his hair cut in this manner, he prospers in his own person and goes to the heavenly world. Now, Manu saw this pair for the barber: first he shaved his beard, then the armpits, then the hair. From that, indeed, he was propagated with offspring.
"With cattle; he for whom they thus shave [the hair] is procreated with offspring, cattle, and pairs. (TaiBr 1.5.6.1–3).
Thus, by shaving the beard and the tuft first, one avoids even the momentary state of being loathed by the world due to the appearance of a barbarian (*mleccha*); this is the view favored by many.

(2) Even there, for the sake of following the clockwise direction (*udaksaṃsthatā*), the shaving of the beard on the right side comes first. (3) However, in the event of the death of a parent or similar relative, for the sake of following the counter-clockwise direction (*dakṣiṇasaṃsthatva*), the shaving of the beard on the left side comes first. Regarding the method of shaving, it is stated in the *Aparārka*:
"The wise man should have the shaving performed while facing either north or east."
One should have the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails shaved, arranged from left to right.
Starting from the right ear for the sake of dharma or when there is an accumulation of sin,
one should shave the head beginning with the top-knot (śikhā) during the nine purificatory rites (saṃskāra), shaving from the top-knot to the end.

(1) For the sake of dharma, such as when shaving at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the like, one should shave in an upward direction starting from the right ear. (2) When the shaving is necessitated by an accumulation of sin, one should shave starting from the top of the head and proceeding downwards on all sides, not in an upward direction. (3) Regarding the "new consecration" (*navasaṃskāra*), namely the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*): the meaning of the subsequent verse is that one should shave starting from the right ear up to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), or starting from the crest-lock down to the left ear.

(4) This shaving must be performed by ascetics (*yati*) and others without preserving the crest-lock; however, an ascetic, a *śūdra*, and a widow should perform the shaving while keeping the crest-lock intact. 287.
According to this statement, there the ascetics should have their hair shaved during the seasonal transitions, with the exception of the armpits, the private parts, and the topknot. || 288 ||

(1) Thus, because of this restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*) regarding the junctions of the seasons (*ṛtusandhi*) alone, there should be no shaving even when reaching a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) at a time other than the seasonal junctions.
(2) The practice (*ācāra*) of those remaining among the ascetics (*yati*) is likewise.

(3) However, by those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), shaving occasioned by a sacred bathing place must be performed even at times other than the festival days (*parvan*). (4) This is because, being occasional (*naimittika*), it lacks the restriction of the festival days—just like shaving occasioned by the death of a son or similar event—and (5) because of traditional practice (*ācāra*).
(6) Even one whose father is living must have his head shaved at a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*);
for, except at a *tīrtha*, except for a sacrifice, or upon the death of one's mother or father, he who shaves his hair is a slayer of his father. 289.

Because of this statement: (1) here, due to the mention of the word "son," the scope is restricted to those whose father is living; (2) otherwise, he would have simply said, "he is a patricide. (3) Furthermore, because the injunctions regarding shaving apply equally to those whose fathers are living; (4) even in that case, they say: "At other holy sites (*tīrtha*), it is only at the first pilgrimage; but at Prayāga, however, it is on every pilgrimage. (6) And at a holy site, shaving must be performed even during a prohibited time; for the prohibition is stated by Vriddha-Gārgya:

One should avoid shaving on Sundays, Tuesdays, and Saturdays; at night; during an eclipse; on the day of a vow; on the day of a Śrāddha; on the day of the new moon (pratipad); and on the Bhadrā days. 290.
(1) Āra is Mars; (2) Saura is Saturn; (3) Pāta is Vyatīpāta; (4) Riktās are the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days; (5) Bhadrās are the second, seventh, and twelfth lunar days. Gārgya states:
"The sixth, the new moon, the full moon, the day of Pāta, the fourteenth, and likewise the eighth [are inauspicious]."
Sin is present in these three: in oil, in sexual intercourse, and in the razor.
Vyāsa said:
One should not perform [the rite] under the lunar mansion in which a man was born;
nor, O Bhārata, should it be done under the two Proṣṭhapadas (Bhādrapadās), nor under the Āgneya (Kṛttikā).
However, among all those [deeds] that are cruel, one should avoid those with malefic stars. || 292 ||
Likewise:
"When the sun is in Aquarius, Cancer, Virgo, or Sagittarius..."
Yama causes the hair from the householder's body to be consumed by the ancestors. || 293 ||
Likewise:

"In the case of marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread, and the tonsure ceremony, shaving the hair is not permitted for one year, half a year, and half of that [respectively]; nor is it desired when the wife is pregnant. (294)
(1) and so forth. An exception to all this applies upon reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*):

"Even when a prohibition exists, one must certainly perform occasional shaving (*naimittika-kṣaura*) on the occasion of the death of a parent or similar relative, during initiation (*dīkṣā*), for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and at a sacred ford. (295)
According to this Smṛti:

"At a sacrifice, at the command of a king or a Brahmin, upon death, at the release from bondage, and at a marriage—on all days, weekdays, lunar mansions, and lunar dates—shaving bestows the desired fruit. (296)
(1) This is because, in the statement of Nārada, the enumeration of the causes is intended as an illustration;
for it is said here: "As many hairs as there are of those cut off in the waters of the Jāhnavī..."
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the heavenly world.

(1) Because of this statement, some say that one should have the hair shaved while seated on dry land in such a way that the hairs fall into the Gaṅgā and other waters by themselves. Others, however, [cite]:
"One should not throw husks, hair, excrement, ashes, bones, phlegm, nails, or body hair into the water. (298)

(1) Based on these prose statements from the *Śaṅkha-smṛti*, some say: "It is not to be thrown into the water, but rather, having dug a pit on the bank, one should throw hair, nails, and so forth into it. (2) Others, however, say:
"As many hairs and body hairs as are indeed driven away by the wind..."
They fall into the waters of the Jāhnavī for men of meritorious deeds. || 299 ||

(1) On account of this statement, they say that one should have the tonsure performed at such a site on the riverbank where hair and other things, driven by the wind, fall into the water, but no specific ritual action need be undertaken by oneself. (2) In this matter, the determination is according to local custom. (3) A detailed discussion regarding the tonsure of women whose husbands are living and of children will be made in the section on Prayāga.
Thus ends the consideration of tonsure in the *Tristhalīsetu*.
[86] Now, therefore, regarding bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Neither one who has not undertaken a vow, nor one who has not disciplined his self, nor one who is impure, nor a thief [should bathe]."
O descendant of Kuru, a man of crooked mind does not bathe in sacred fords.
Likewise:
"Neither one who is crooked, nor one whose self is undisciplined, nor one who is ignorant, nor one who commits evil [attains this]."
O Kauravya, a man of crooked mind does not bathe in sacred fords.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"In rivers, streams, natural excavations, pits, and springs..."
It is recommended in lakes that are not man-made, and especially at sacred bathing places (tīrtha). || 302 ||
(1) "Bathing" is the understood remainder. As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Even after bathing in all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) on earth that are meritorious, O twice-born one..."
A person is liberated from all sins, even from every single one of them. || 303 ||
Likewise, concerning sacred fords (tīrthas), [it is said]: "Where bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, ancestral rites, giving, and so forth are performed... (KūP 2.33.144).
O best of sages, each one individually purifies the seventh generation of his lineage.
(304) Furthermore, this should not be performed at a specific location where the current flows in the opposite direction and so forth.
As it has been said:
Bathing in a river where the water has receded is forbidden for the twice-born;
however, in that same river, one should avoid bathing at the washerman’s landing-place for a distance of ten cubits.
Likewise:
"For waters that have just arrived from a river, produced by the first surge, and which have been disturbed by someone and emerged from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), are indeed ungraspable. (306)
(1) An exception regarding this [rule] concerns the Gaṅgā:
"Flowing against the current, contact with dust, and the depositing of street water—these do not defile the Gaṅgā, for she is herself the very flow of dharma. (307)
There is another prohibition as well:
the *śālmali*, *tintiṇī*, *nimba*, and *karañja* trees; the *harītakī*, *kovidāra*, *kapittha*, *arka*, *badarī*, *eraṇḍa*, and *śigru* plants.
One should avoid bathing in the shade of the śelu and the khadira trees. || 308 ||
(1) And so forth; alternatively, the reading is “*badarī ca vibhītakī*.

(2) Furthermore, the prohibition against bathing during the night, at the twilights (*saṃdhyā*), and so on, does not apply when one has unexpectedly reached a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), because that is an occasion-specific (*naimittika*) requirement. For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
“One should not perform a bath at night, nor [perform] a fire-oblation (*homa*) or a gift-giving (*dāna*) during the nights.”
And one should perform occasional ritual bathing and giving of gifts during the nights. || 309 ||
Vṛddhayājñavalkya also says:
"At the times of an eclipse, a wedding, a saṅkrānti, a journey, and the birth of a child, bathing is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is prescribed even at night. (310)
(1) “And this bathing at a sacred ford at night pertains to the first and last two watches;
however, the ‘great midnight’ should be known as the middle two watches. One should perform the bath during the first and last watches of the night just as one does during the day. [p.88] 311 ||

"Thus, according to the statement of Parāśara," say some. (1) Furthermore, this absence of prohibition refers to the case of arriving at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) by chance. (2) However, if one arrives at a *tīrtha* intentionally, it must certainly not be done during the night or other such times. (3) Likewise, if the arrival occurs incidentally, it may be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
Bathing at sacred fords, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings with barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth.
Having begun thus,
Yama declares that ritual duties (kāryāṇi) are to be performed even during an intercalary month (malamāsa). In this regard:
The bathing at sacred fords (tīrthasnāna) has been previously introduced. || 313 ||
Thus, in the Madanapārijāta, [it is stated] regarding the second [day] and so forth, on page 547. || 314 ||

(1) [This is] elsewhere, because there is a prohibition against visiting a sacred site (*tīrtha*) for the first time. (2) However, the elders say it is "caused by the accidental arrival at a sacred site.
(3) Even during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), bathing at a sacred site that occurs by chance should be performed. As it was stated by Paiṭhīnasi:
"At weddings, in times of distress, at sacrifices, on journeys, and at rites at sacred sites..."
In that case, there is no *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth); likewise, one should not perform rites such as ritual sacrifices (*karmayajña*) and the like.

(1) ‘*Sūtaka*’ is also indicative of *mṛtaka* (impurity due to death). (2) ‘Rites at a sacred ford (*tīrthakarma*)’ refers to bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and so forth.
(3) Regarding the specific rule for bathing for the sake of others, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
If one should drown oneself on behalf of a mother, a father, a wife, a brother, a friend, or a teacher, that person shall receive an eighth part of the merit. || 316 ||
But in the Smṛtidarpaṇa, however: "He shall receive a tenth part. (317)
The reading is *PraKh* 1.28.41. However, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated:
"for the sake of one's grandfather, brother, maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, father-in-law, supporter, teacher (*ācārya*), preceptor (*guru*), or sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*)."

Having bathed for the sake of their wives, maternal aunts, and paternal aunts, one obtains an eighth part [of the merit]; performing it for the sake of one's mother and father, one obtains a fourth part. || 318 ||
SAS, p. 154: (1) Husband and wife obtain half [of the estate] for each other’s sake.
(2) Paiṭhīnasi states another distinction:
One should immerse an image made of kuśa grass in the waters of a sacred ford;
and whoever one intends for that immersion, he shall obtain an eighth part of the merit.
Atri (50): The mantra for that occasion is:
"You are Kuśa; you are the son of Kuśa; you were created by Brahmā himself."
When you have bathed, he for whom this binding of the book exists has also bathed.

(1) Thus: "A 'representation of kuśa grass' (*kuśapratikṛti*) must be made as an image of kuśa grass itself," say some. (2) Others, however, on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "the tying of a knot" (*granthibandhana*), say that the representation is merely the tying of a knot with each respective name.

(3) A certain [author] says: "This bathing for the sake of others (*parārthasnāna*) and the establishment of the representation should be performed with reference to those who are living or those who are deceased, because of the general injunction. (4) That is not correct; since the deceased partake in the fruits of libations (*tarpaṇa*), ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and so forth, it is more appropriate to intend the fruit for those who are living alone.
(5) Furthermore, another distinction has been stated by Śaṅkha:
"Having reached a sacred site (tīrtha), one should perform a bath there as a secondary act;
one obtains the fruit arising from the bath, but not that which results from the pilgrimage itself. (321)
Śaṃkha 8.12 (= 106) [p.90] (1) “By way of attachment” (*anuṣaṅgeṇa*) means through the occasion of trade, service to a king, and so forth.
(2) Jābāli states another distinction:
One should immerse oneself facing the current where the waters flow;
likewise, among all stationary waters, one should face the sun.
(1) Other matters, such as bathing with clay and so forth, should be understood from other texts.
Thus ends the procedure for bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) in the general section of the *Tīrthasetu*.
[p. 91] Now, the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

(2) Having first performed the ritual bath according to one’s own Vedic school (*sva-śākhā*), and having subsequently performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods and sages in the same manner, the rite for the ancestors must also be performed. As it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:

"Whether at the improper time or the proper time, the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) must be performed without delay; one should never allow an obstacle to arise. (323) Thus it is said.

Kākh 6.60 (= 386) (1) Furthermore, the libation to the ancestors (*pitr̥tarpaṇa*) is also stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*, beginning with the word "sacred ford" (*tīrtha*): "The libation to the ancestors must indeed be performed by those who have actually arrived [at the sacred site]. (= 381)
Likewise, it is said elsewhere:
"But that man who, having bathed at a sacred ford, does not perform the libation for the ancestors, his ancestors, seeking water, drink instead the discharge from his body. (325)
Likewise:
"In mountains, in famous sacred fords, and especially in rivers, the ancestors always remain full of longing, seeking water. (326)

(1) And here, having satiated all the ancestors who are to be mentioned, one should offer a single handful of sesame seeds to all of them. Regarding this, the mantras in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* are as follows:
"The gods, asuras, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūṣmāṇḍas, trees, and birds; [may they all be satisfied]."
May all creatures— those that move in water, those that dwell on land, and those that depend on the air—
quickly attain satisfaction by this water given by me.
To nourish those who dwell in all the hells and amidst the various torments, this water is offered by me.
May those who are not kinsmen, or those who were kinsmen in another birth,
and whoever else has expectations from us, all attain complete satisfaction.
"May this water with sesame seeds, offered by me, be truly inexhaustible for those situated anywhere, whose selves are afflicted by hunger and thirst. (327)
In the Vāyavīya [Purāṇa] as well (ViPu 3.11.32–36): "From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans..."
May all the ancestors—the mothers, maternal grandfathers, and the rest—be satisfied.
May this water mixed with sesame seeds be for the sake of the millions of ancestors of past generations who dwelt in the seven continents, and for all the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā.
"And this is the fruit in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition]: 'O King, I have thus described to you this offering of water for the sake of desire.'"
By giving this, a person delights the entire world.
O sinless one, by giving water for the fulfillment of desires to these [ancestors] properly, endowed with faith, one obtains the merit arising from the nourishment of the world. (ViP 3.11.37–38)
In this context,
at the ancestral rite (śrāddha) for the fortnight and also regarding gold, one should follow [the recipient] while offering water with sesame seeds.

(1) Thus, based on the statement of Sumantu, some perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the sake of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) after the dismissal of the Brahmins at the Hiraṇyaśrāddha performed at a holy site, but not before it. (2) That is incorrect, because many scriptural passages enjoin that very rite immediately following the ritual bath at the sacred ford. (3) As for the statement of Sumantu, it prescribes that [libation] after the Hiraṇyaśrāddha only for those followers of a Vedic school (*śākhin*) for whom the libation is an integral part (*aṅga*) of the Śrāddha. (4) For this very reason, in the *Prayogapārijāta*, this was stated specifically with reference to the libation that is an integral part of the Śrāddha:
Therefore, it is established that the libation at a sacred ford (tīrtha-tarpaṇa) must be performed immediately after the ritual bath. || 331 ||

(1) Another specific rule regarding libations is stated elsewhere: "If a man crosses a river without having offered libations to his ancestors, they, becoming intensely distressed, become desirous of drinking his blood. (332) (= 670)
(1) Herein, regarding this libation, the sequence of those to be gratified is as follows: first the father, then the mother, and likewise the stepmother;
then the maternal grandfathers along with their wives, and after that, one's own wives.
A son-in-law, brothers, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles along with their wives;
a daughter, a sister, a daughter’s son, and a sister’s son are thus declared.
The father's sister, the mother's sister, the father-in-law, and the preceptor are likewise [to be honored]. (333)
(1) ‘Riktha’ means wealth.
These [ancestors] are the ones to be honored as fathers at a sacred ford, during the libation ceremony, and in the Mahālaya rite.
(2) ‘Pite’ means the triad beginning with the father; (3) the same applies here to ‘māte’.
Furthermore elsewhere:
“The triad of father and mother, the stepmother, and the triad beginning with the maternal grandfather.”

In the Mahālaya rite, as well as in the libation at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the following are the recipients: the teacher, the wife, the son and so forth, the father, the mother, one’s own brothers, their wives, the father’s mother, one’s own sister, her offspring, her husband, the wife’s father, the true guru, the disciples, and the paternal ancestors. (334)

(1) Thus: the word *tritaya* (triad) is connected with both “father” (*tāta*) and “mother” (*ambā*) respectively. (2) The term *sastrī* (with their wives) is an adjective qualifying the triad beginning with the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). (3) Others, however, desire that the offering (*tarpaṇa*) for the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*) and the others be performed separately, as in the case of the *śrāddha* rite. (4) The phrase *strītanayādi* (wives, sons, etc. is used in relation to the person performing the libation (*tarpayitṛ*). (5) Regarding *tātajananīsvabhrātaraḥ*: the father’s brothers are paternal uncles (*pitṛvya*), the mother’s brothers are maternal uncles (*mātula*), and one’s own brothers are the brothers of the performer of the libation. (6) *Tatstriyaḥ* refers to the wives of the paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and one’s own brothers. (7) Alternatively, there is the reading *sastriya*. (8) In that case, it refers to the father’s brothers and so forth.
[94] The meaning is "together with his wife. (9) The term *tātā* refers to paternal aunts, maternal aunts, and sisters who are accompanied by their offspring and husbands.

(10) Consequently, one should understand that the formula for application regarding a paternal aunt is of such a nature as "to her who is appropriately accompanied by her husband and her offspring," and so forth. (11) *Jāyāpitā* means father-in-law. (12) The rest is clear. (13) In this context, there is an option (*vikalpa*) with respect to brothers, paternal uncles, and others, according to the sequence previously stated.

(14) Thus, when one is unable to perform all the aforementioned libations, a concise libation (*saṃkṣepatarpaṇa*) should be performed, while saying: "May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied.
One should offer three handfuls of water, performing this concise libation. || 335 ||
According to this statement:
(1) "May this entire world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, including all that is stationary and moving, attain the supreme goal, being satisfied by the water offered by me. (336)
With this mantra, or alternatively: "May the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, down to the very foundation of the universe (Brahmā-stamba),
and all the ancestors— mothers, maternal grandfathers, and the rest— be satisfied."

“May this water with sesame seeds be for the millions of ancestors of the past who dwell in the seven continents, and for all the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā. (337) With this mantra, one should offer three handfuls of water along with sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass. (2) Here, the mantra is to be repeated for each handful of water. (3) [Objection: But surely, since the mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the act of giving the handfuls of water is a single action, [the mantra should not be repeated]?
The conjunction of the ritual action and so forth should occur at the end of the mantra. || 338 ||
Śābarabhāṣya 11.4.19.53

(1) According to this principle, just as in the case of the injunction, “One threshes while reciting, ‘May I strike down the enemy from heaven’,” and as in the case of, “One sprinkles the altar three times while reciting, ‘Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, thee’,” there would be only a single recitation of the mantra. (2) It is not so, for with each handful (*añjali*), different water is offered. (3) Consequently, since a mantra is employed for a specific purpose, it should apply only to that object and not to all; thus, because of the apprehension of this distinction, the ritual purification (*saṃskāra*) is not accomplished for the whole. To achieve that accomplishment, just as in the cases of pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) or cutting (*lavana*), the mantra is applied to each individual handful as a distinct substance. (4) In the cases of threshing and sprinkling, however, those same rice grains are threshed again, and that same altar is sprinkled again; therefore, because the substance is one and the purification is obtained, there is no repetition of the mantra. (5) Therefore, like the offering of *arghya* at the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), there is a repetition of the mantra with each handful.

(6) However, some say: "Because the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the phrase *‘iti bruvan’* [335] indicates simultaneity, as in the case of *‘yuvā suvāsā’*, the mantra functions as a descriptive reference (*kriyamāṇānuvādin*) and thus lacks the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Therefore, one should offer three handfuls of joined palms while reciting the mantra only once.
(7) Furthermore, regarding the prohibition of sesame seeds (*tila*) in the libation (*tarpaṇa*), Gārgya states:

"On Sunday, Tuesday, and the thirteenth lunar day; on the Nandā tithis, on a Friday, and under the Maghā nakṣatra—one should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), bathing with clay, or the libation with sesame seeds.
Thus says Marīci. (394) [= 394] Marīci:—
On the seventh lunar day, on Sundays, at home, and likewise on one's birthday,
one who desires servants, sons, and a wife should not perform the libation with sesame seeds.
O King, on both fortnights, on the seventh day, at night, and during the two twilights,
one who desires knowledge, sons, or a wife should avoid sesame seeds for seven [days].
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "Upon marriage, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and the tonsure (*caula*), according to their respective order,
some say there is no sesame libation for one year, half a year, and half of that [quarter-year]."
And they say that when [the anniversary] has already occurred, one should not perform the libation with sesame seeds in that month.

"Thus, this [rule] does not apply to the libation at a sacred site (*tīrtha*); for it is said: 'At a sacred site, on a specific lunar day (*tithi*), at Gayā, and during the fortnight of the departed (*pretapakṣa*')."
Even on a forbidden day, one should perform the libation mixed with sesame seeds.
Because of this statement,
[the rite] should be performed on specific lunar days and at specific sacred sites, as well as for one who has died, at all times—
SAS, p. 30.
And because of the statement cited from the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"[p.96] (1) All other general rules regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*) are to be understood from other texts. (2) Even a widow must perform the libation at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)."

Every day, one should perform the libation for the husband with water mixed with kusa grass and sesame seeds, preceded by the mention of his name and lineage; and likewise for his father and his grandfather.

(1) Because this is stated daily even among the duties of widows in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, Brahmakhaṇḍa 2.7.69; (2) because at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one has an even greater entitlement to it by virtue of the occasion; (3) and because this refers to a case where there is an absence of sons and grandsons; (4) likewise in the *Madanapārijāta*;
(5) however, an ascetic (*saṃnyāsin*) should not perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
"A monk shall not perform the *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth), nor the *śrāddha*, the *piṇḍa*, or the water-libation rites," according to this *smṛti*.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Tristhalīsetu* composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara Sūri.
In the section on general matters, the libation for the *tīrthas* [p.
97]: Now, concerning the impurity caused by the menses (*rajodoṣa*) of rivers in connection with bathing at and offering libations at *tīrthas*, Devala states:
Between the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not perform ritual bathing in them, nor offer libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Atri says:
Between the signs of Leo and Cancer, all rivers are in their menstrual period;
a person should not perform ritual acts such as bathing in them.
(1) And this refers to waters other than those of the great rivers:
all rivers between the [rivers] Siṃhaka and Karkaṭa are in their menstrual flow;
one should not bathe in them, with the exception of those that flow into the ocean. 348.
Thus it is stated by Vyāghrapāda. (1) Regarding a further distinction concerning great rivers, the *Bhaviṣyottara* states:
"O Goddess, at the beginning of the month of Karkaṭaka, the great rivers are in their menstrual flow;
for three days they remain so, but on the fourth day they become pure, just like the Gaṅgā. || 349 ||
Thus [it is said]. (1) And regarding the great rivers, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Veṇikā, Tāpī, and Payoṣṇī are proclaimed to be on the south of the Vindhya. (350). (= 55)
The Bhāgīrathī, Narmadā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī,
Viśokā, and Vihastā are situated to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
"These twelve great rivers originate from the fields of the divine sages.

(1) Regarding small rivers, however, it is stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa* that they remain in their menstrual state until the rising of Agastya: "As long as the Blessed One, the ornament of the southern quarter, does not rise..."
"Until then, the rivers carrying dust are proclaimed as *karatoyā*s.
(1) *Karatīyā*s are those with very little water.
(2) Another distinction has also been stated by Kātyāyana:
One should not bathe in those small streams on earth that dry up in the summer, until ten days have passed since they were filled again in the rainy season. (353)
(1) Regarding the regions of the Gaṅgā and others, Devala states:
"The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī born from the Plakṣa tree. (The Sarasvatī that flows through Kurukṣetra is the one born from the Plakṣa tree.)
And those others who are designated as the nine are not overcome by passion.
The Śoṇa, Sindhu, Hiraṇyā, Kokā, Lohita, Ghargharā, and Śatadru—these seven rivers are proclaimed to be purifying. || 354 ||
In the Smṛtisaṃgraha:
"The Gaṅgā, the Gautamī, the Sarasvatī, the Veṇā, and those known as the nine [rivers] are not overcome by the quality of passion (rajas). (355)
(1) ‘The daughter of Tapaṇa’ is Yamunā. The Veda states: “The Gaṅgā is the flow of dharma, as are the holy Yamunā and the Sarasvatī.”
Though possessing internal stains of passion, they remain pure in all circumstances. || 356 ||
And thus,
O Goddess, during the first three days when the Gaṅgā is in her menses in the month of Karkaṭa— || 357 ||
(1) Statements such as these regarding the impurity of dust (*rajas*) in the Gaṅgā and other rivers refer to internal dust (*antar-gata-rajas*).
Likewise:
"In the [month of] Karkaṭaka and others, the Gomatī is defiled by dust for three days."
The Candrabhāgā, the Satī, the Sindhu, the Śarayū, and likewise the Narmadā. || 358 ||

(1) Furthermore, this defect of dust belongs to the rivers, not to those who dwell on their banks. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nigama*: "[... but not for those who dwell on their banks" (359; = 254).

(1) Even water defiled by dust becomes naturally pure when joined with the waters of the Gaṅgā and other such rivers, and it does not corrupt the waters of the Gaṅgā and so forth. As it is said in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"By union with meritorious water, even defiled water becomes purifying. And in the *Mahābhārata*: [as follows].
"Even having reached that which is impure, the Gaṅgā attains purity.
(361) There is also another distinction mentioned in the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*: "But for those [rivers] whose course does not extend for eight thousand bows..."
Those are not proclaimed to be rivers carrying the sound of flowing water; they are merely hollows.
"In the rainy season, fresh water may be impure for three nights;
but out of season, it remains so for ten days. Having drunk it, one should not eat for a day and a night.
(1) There is also another specific rule in the *Bhaviṣya*:
Even if a great quantity of old water were to remain, the wise maintain that it is not defiled when mixed with fresh water. (363)
Yogayājñavalkya:
Twice-born men should avoid bathing in rivers and other waters that are defiled by menstrual impurity;
for them, the twilight worship and the libations are rendered useless. 364.
(1) ‘Kadarthitaṃ’ means contemptible.
Likewise:
“A goat, a cow, a buffalo, and a Brāhmaṇa woman who has recently given birth,” and so forth.
And the earth, as well as fresh water, becomes pure after ten nights. || 365 ||
(1) Water from wells and other sources recently dug is called "new water" (*navodaka*).

(2) However, in certain rites, there is no defect caused by menstrual impurity (*rajas*). Regarding this, Vyāghrapāda says: "In the absence of wells and tanks that contain inexhaustible water... [p. 100]
"Even when the water is defiled by dust, the enjoyment of the village is not defiled"—
so says Vasiṣṭha:
"At the Upākarma ceremony, at the Utsarga, and likewise at the ritual bath for the deceased..."
And during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, there is no impurity caused by the menstrual flow. || 367 ||
"Gomila 1.143," and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the impurity of riverine menstrual blood in the *Tristhalīsetu*.
Now, regarding the *tīrtha-śrāddha*,
it is stated in the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Padma Purāṇa*: "At sacred fords (*tīrtha*), shrines, cow-pens, islands, gardens, and houses..."
A wise person should offer the ancestral oblation (śrāddha) in secluded places that have been well-smeared with cow dung.
In the *Padma* and *Matsya Purāṇas*, after enumerating sacred fords (*tīrthas*) beginning with “The sacred ford named Puṣkaraka,” it is stated [in *Matsya Purāṇa* 22.65a]:
“A śrāddha performed at these sacred fords is held to yield ten million-fold merit.”
Therefore, one should perform the śrāddha rite with great effort at a sacred ford (tīrtha). || 369 ||
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "In particular, for these regions, the merit shall be infinite. (MaPu 22.81a; PadPu, Sṛkha 11.84a–b, 85a–b).
The śrāddha at Gayā is inexhaustible, as is that at Amarakaṇṭaka in Prayāga.
On Mount Varāha and especially on the Gaṅgā,
and particularly at Vārāṇasī, where the Lord Hara himself resides.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prabhāsa, at Bilvaka, on Mount Nīla,
at Kurukṣetra, at Kubjāmra, on Bhr̥gutuṅga, and on the Himālaya.
At Kedāra, at Phalgutīrtha, and indeed at Naimiṣāraṇya;
especially at the Sarasvatī, and most particularly at the Puṣkaras.
At Kuśāvarta on the Narmadā, at Śrīśaila and Bhadrakarṇaka,
especially on the Vetravatī, and particularly on the Godāvarī.
In these and other such sacred fords, on sandy banks,
and on the shores of rivers, the ancestors are always satisfied.
Viṣṇu: At Puṣkara, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible, as are recitations, fire-oblations, and ascetic penances. [KūP 2.20.28c–29b, 32–36] [p.102]
Merely by bathing at Puṣkara, one is liberated from all sins.
Having spoken thus [in Viṣṇusmṛti 85.1–3],
[one should likewise bathe] in other sacred fords (tīrtha), in the best of rivers, at confluences, and at sources.
"On the sandbanks, in groves, at springs, in forests, and in pleasure-gardens," and so forth.

Regarding the term *prabhavāḥ*, it refers to the sources where rivers originate, as indicated by the expression "at the confluences of the best of rivers" (*saridvarāsu saṅgameṣu*). This is stated according to the original context.
Devala said:
The places honored for the performance of śrāddha are Gayā, the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī,
Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
The ancestors are gratified by what is given here on riverbanks, at sacred fords, on mountains, on sandbanks, and in secluded places. (372)
Śaṅkha says: At Vārāṇasī, at Kurukṣetra, on Bhr̥gutuṅga, in the Himalayas,
and on the banks of the Narmadā and Bāhudā, one enjoys everything as infinite.
At Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and likewise at Puṣkara,
as well as at Saṃnihitī and Gayā, everything becomes inexhaustible.

(1) Here, although the performance of *śrāddha* is established everywhere by the force of the general injunctions prescribing *tīrtha-śrāddha*, the specific mention [of particular places] is for the purpose of enjoining a connection between specific qualities and results (*guṇaphala*), just as in the case of "for one desiring sensory power, [one should sacrifice] with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*). (2) It is not, however, an injunction for a distinct and different *śrāddha*, because that would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because there is no lack of an alternative recourse (*agatikābhāva*), as in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*).
After enumerating the sacred sites (*tīrthas*) in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
Those who indeed perform the śrāddha ceremony at these and other such sacred fords (tīrthas) become purified after bathing and giving gifts according to the prescribed rule. (374)
‘Having given’ means having offered water with sesame seeds according to the procedure prescribed for the rite of libation (tarpaṇa). || 375 ||
Thus it is stated in the Smṛtiratnāvalī.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"In a region sloping toward the south, or at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or even in one's own home..."
One should perform the śrāddha rite with great care, provided it is accompanied by the purification of the ground and other such preparations. || 376 ||
As for that which Yama said:
"If one should perform the offering for the ancestors on lands belonging to others, the śrāddha rite is obstructed by the ancestors of the owners of that land. (377)
Likewise, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If a fool offers libations to his own ancestors in the house of another,
the ancestors of the owner of that land forcibly seize them."
Then one should give them the foremost portion, as well as the price for their lives. || 378 ||

(1) One's own property should be given away, having been relinquished "to them," that is, to the fathers who are the owners of that land. (2) "To those living" means the price should be paid to the current owners. (3) In this context, the lands of others, such as their houses and so forth, are prohibited; however, sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like are not, because they have no single owner. As it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Forests are meritorious in every respect, as are the banks of rivers;
all these are said to be without ownership, for there is no private possession over them. (379)
Likewise:
"Forests, mountains, rivers, sacred fords, shrines, natural ponds, and pits—no owner exists over these. (380)
(1) ‘Gartā’ refers to natural, non-artificial specific sites such as the *brahmayoni* and others.
(2) Furthermore, this *śrāddha* must be performed immediately after bathing and the offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*), without delay. As it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:

“The *śrāddha* should be performed there, omitting the offering of water (*arghya*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*). It should not be that which is defiled by the sight of dogs, crows, vultures, or ravens. (406)
That is declared to be the *śrāddha* of the non-Buddhists which brings satisfaction to the ancestors;
likewise, men should perform the *śrāddha* at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), whether at the proper time or even at an improper time.
And once [the guests] have arrived, one must perform the libation for the ancestors;
likewise, the offering of rice balls is prescribed, for it is exceedingly dear to the ancestors.

“Nor should delay be made, nor should one create an obstacle. (381) Regarding this: (1) “By those who have arrived” means immediately after the obligatory bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and so forth; for such a degree of delay is permitted by the rules governing bathing, libations, and the like. (2) Furthermore, there is no avoidance of prohibited times even in the case of a *śrāddha* at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); thus Śaṅkha says:
When at a sacred site (tīrtha) or when the necessary materials are available, one need not wait for the proper time;
having found a worthy Brahmin recipient, one should perform the Śrāddha immediately. || 382 ||
Likewise, in the Ādi-parvan of the Mahābhārata, Arjuna says to Aṅgāraparṇa:
"O sky-traveler, whether one has eaten or not, by day or by night, there is indeed no restriction of time once one has reached Gaṅgā, the best of rivers. (383)
In the *Citrapathāmāhātmya*:
"Whether having eaten or not having eaten, whether by night or by day."
Whether during a festival or at an improper time, whether pure or even impure.
O beloved, whenever the river Citrapathā is seen there, its very appearance is the authority; time is not the determining factor in that case.
(1) "Impure" (*aśuci*) means also by reason of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"At weddings, during times of distress, at sacrifices, on journeys, and at rites performed at sacred fords..."
In that case, there is no impurity (*sūtaka*); likewise, one should perform rites such as the sacrifice of action (*karmayajña*).
As stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"Whether at an improper time or otherwise, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one should perform the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*). [p.105]

It must be performed without delay; one should certainly not create an obstacle. (386) (1) "At the proper time" (*kāle*) refers to the afternoon and so forth, as well as when there is an absence of food and the like. (2) "At an improper time" (*akāle*) refers to the night and so forth, even for one who has already eaten. (3) Since reaching a sacred site (*tīrtha*) is itself a qualification for the performer, the intention is that the *śrāddha* must be performed in all circumstances, just like the ritual of formal reception (*grahaṇa*). (4) The term "time" (*kāla*), however, is mentioned by way of illustration. (5) In that context, the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood in the same manner as in the expression "the ocean or a great being."

(6) However, some [interpret] "at an improper time" (*akāle*) as meaning even at times other than those prescribed for *śrāddha*, such as the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), yet not including the night and so forth, because that would contradict prohibitions. (7) For this very reason, regarding the statement of Devala—"And when a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or the requisite materials are available, one need not wait for a specific time"—the phrase "one need not wait for a specific time" means that one should not look forward to the new moon day or the afternoon; however, one must certainly avoid the night and other such prohibited times.

[The opponent] says: "It has been stated [in the *Śrāddhaviveka*] by Śūlapāṇi. This is not correct. (1) Because there is no prohibition of performing a *śrāddha* on any day of the week or lunar date (*tithi*), this occasional (*naimittika*) *śrāddha*, which occurs immediately following the specific occasion (*nimitta*), is already established [as required]; therefore, a formal injunction (*vidhāna*) would be redundant.

(2) Alternatively, it might be argued: "Since a *śrāddha* is not mandatory on every day or lunar date, even at a time such as the first lunar day (*pratipad*) when a *śrāddha* is not obligatory, if one arrives at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the *śrāddha* must certainly be performed."

(3) "Thus, the term 'unseasonable' (*akāla*) was stated for the purpose of indicating its obligatory nature.
