(4) That too is not correct; for the necessity of performing an act when a specific occasion arises is established by the rule regarding occasional rites (*naimittika-vidhi*) itself, as in the case of the *gṛhadāheṣṭi* sacrifice and others. (5) Therefore, to give the term 'unseasonable' its proper significance, it is more logical that it serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition of [performing rites] at night and so forth. (6) For this very reason, Śaṅkha stated in general terms: "One should not restrict the time. (7) And in the *Citrapathāmāhātmya*, he states quite explicitly: "Whether by night or by day. Viṣṇu also says:

For that which is given in the evening is indeed plundered by Rākṣasas, except for [rites performed on] lunar eclipses, solar eclipses, transits of the sun (saṃkrānti), and śrāddhas at sacred fords (tīrtha). Therefore, it is established that when one has unexpectedly reached a sacred ford, a śrāddha and other rites should be performed either after having eaten or at the beginning of the night.
(2) However, when on the day the rite is due there should be an obstacle—whether divine or human—then the *śrāddha* should be performed on another day.

(3) [Objection: But surely, because it is stated that "it must be performed only when [the time] has arrived," implying it is to be done immediately after the arrival [of the time], and since that [arrival] does not exist on another day, there should be an omission here as well—just as there is an omission of the *śrāddha* when an obstacle such as birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
(4) On the other hand, in the case of the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) and so forth, performance even after an obstacle such as birth-impurity is appropriate.
If that day should be defiled by something such as birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should perform it again on that very same day after the impurity has ceased. || 389 ||

Because of such statements [elsewhere], however, since there is no such statement here, elision alone is appropriate. Likewise, when reaching a sacred ford (tīrtha) at night or during twilight, let there be elision; for there is a prohibition against performing śrāddha at night or at twilight, and on the following day, there is no time remaining immediately after [the arrival] that would permit its performance.

(3) This would indeed be so if there were a prescription of time, as in the case of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions. (4) But here, the mere fact that reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) serves as the occasion (*nimitta*) is stated. (5) And thus, the time is obtained through the principle that "when an occasion arises, the performance of the rite contingent upon it must be carried out immediately, provided no obstacle exists. (6) Therefore, if an obstacle occurs, its performance at another time is not contradictory, just like the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice. (7) For instance, regarding the rule "one should offer the *vaiśvānara* cake on twelve potsherds when a son is born," the *jāteṣṭi*—though prescribed—is not to be performed immediately after birth; since it would conflict with the prohibition against nursing before the *jātakarman* rite, and because performing the sacrifice and the *jātakarman* consecutively would lead to the child's death and thus contradict the very purpose of the rite, it was established in the fourth book (*Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra*) that it should be performed after the *jātakarman*. Furthermore, in the subsequent section, it was proven that although the immediate sequence following the *jātakarman* is set aside due to the impurity caused by the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), and since the occasion itself has already arisen, it cannot be entirely omitted, the sacrifice must instead be performed on a lunar festival (*parvan*) immediately after the period of impurity, in accordance with the requirement for purification. (8) Likewise, in this case as well, its performance at another time is not contradictory.
(9) However, this is the distinction: (10) in that case, an obstacle in the interim is inevitable, whereas here it is only occasional.

(11) But when one goes outside while still unperformed in the śrāddha due to an obstacle, then—because of the absence of the location that constitutes a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)—the śrāddha occasioned by that [location] is indeed lost, just as the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice is not performed when a son has died, because there is no locus for the fruit such as purification (*pūtatva*).
(12) If, however, one should go outside by one's own volition while the śrāddha remains unperformed, then one would incur sin due to personal transgression.
(13) However, in the case of an unforeseen obstacle, one does not incur a lapse; this is the extent of the distinction.

(14) Regarding the arrival at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) during the night or at the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), it has already been stated that, by virtue of the previously cited scriptural statement, the prohibition is set aside and the *śrāddha* must be performed at that very time. (15) This same entire determination applies to bathing, shaving, fasting, and so forth as well, because they are equal in being occasional (*naimittika*) duties. Likewise, in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
Neither the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor the time is the cause there;
whenever a sacred ford (tīrtha) is seen, that moment is equal to a thousand auspicious festival days (parvan).

(1) Therefore, the intended meaning is that the prohibition regarding the lunar day (*tithi*), day of the week (*vāsara*), asterism (*nakṣatra*), and so forth, which has been stated [elsewhere], does not apply to a *śrāddha* performed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). (2) And that prohibition was stated by Gārgya:
"On the Nandā [lunar days], on Friday, on the thirteenth [lunar day], and during the three births [of the moon]."
A householder should not perform a śrāddha for these, due to the depletion of his sons and wealth. || 391 ||
(1) Regarding "in the three births" (*trijanmani*): it refers to the birth-day, the birth-nakṣatra, and the birth-star. Vṛddhagārgya states:
"In the Prajāpatya, the Pauṣṇa, the Pitrya, and likewise the Bhārgava [nakṣatras]..."
But for him who performs a Śrāddha [at that time], his son perishes. || 392 ||
(1) Rohiṇī belongs to Prajāpati; (2) Revatī belongs to Pūṣan; (3) Maghā is the asterism of the ancestors.
As stated in the Bhārata:
"One should not perform [rites] under the asterism in which a man was born."
O Bhārata, one should not perform [the rite] under the two Proṣṭhapadas nor under the Āgneya (Kṛttikā);
one should avoid all the Dāruṇa nakṣatras and the Pratyari nakṣatra as well.

(1) Kṛttikā belongs to Agni. (2) Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla are cruel [nakṣatras]. (3) The fifth, fourteenth, and twenty-third asterisms from the birth star are *pratyara*. (4) Although these statements have been accepted by Hemādri and others as being intended for the prohibition of *śrāddha* for the deceased (*preta-śrāddha*), they are nevertheless cited here because some authorities accept them as prohibiting *śrāddha* in general. (5) Likewise, there is a prohibition regarding the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).

On Sundays, on Tuesdays, on the thirteenth lunar day, and during the Nandā, Bhṛgu, and Maghā constellations, one should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), bathing with clay, or the libation of sesame seeds (tilatarpaṇa). — From the Rāmakautuka. (= 339) [p.108]

During the Nanda, Aśva, Kāmara, Vyāra, Bhṛgu, Agni, Pitṛ, and Kāla yogas, as well as during the Gañja, Vaidhṛti, and Pāta yogas, those desiring sons should avoid offering the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa).

(1) Nandās are the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days; (2) Aśva is the seventh; (3) Kāma is the thirteenth; (4) Ravyārau refers to Sundays and Tuesdays; (5) Bhṛgu is Friday; (6) Agni, Pitṛ, and Kāla-bhāni refer to the asterisms Kṛttikā, Maghā, and Bharaṇī;
(7) Gañja and Vaidhṛti are two *yogas*; (8) Pāta is Vyatīpāta. Thus says Kārṣṇājini.
During the years following marriage, the initiation of vows, and the tonsure ceremony— one year, half a year, and half of that respectively—
one should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), bathing with clay, or the libation of sesame seeds (tila-tarpaṇa).

Likewise, in other cases of mere growth [of the fetus], the eminent sages such as Garga and others have prescribed the exclusion of the offering of funeral cakes for ritual performers for one month. (396)
Manu says:
One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen. (397)
In the Vāyupurāṇa, Manu (3.280) states:
"The evening [time] lasts for three muhūrtas; one should avoid performing a śrāddha during that period."
One should never perform the worship of the ancestors during the period of twilight.
That time is declared to belong to the Asuras; one should avoid performing a śrāddha there.
And so forth. (1) Even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the *tīrtha-śrāddha* must be performed;
one should perform both the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*) *śrāddha* even in an intercalary month. [399]
Thus, from the words of Jābāli:

"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with self-restraint during the intercalary month (malimluca), as well as the Śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha-śrāddha), the Gaja-chāyā rite, and likewise the Śrāddha for the deceased. (400)
And because of the statement of Bṛhaspati [in *Br̥hatsrāddha* 149]:

"This injunction for bathing, Śrāddha, and so forth, during the twilight, at night, in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), or when one is impure due to ritual pollution (*āśauca*)—even after having already eaten—is intended for the case of arriving unexpectedly at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); it does not, however, apply to a case where one has done so intentionally."

(2) Because the occasion consisting in the arrival at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is to be accomplished through human effort, it differs from [the arrival at a sacred site] by way of its being something that must be grasped [as an opportunity].

(3) Consequently, one should mentally effect the arrival at the *tīrtha* precisely at a time when it is not prohibited. (4) However, in the case of an accidental arrival—even at a prohibited time—one should perform ritual bathing, ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and so forth, just as in the cases of seizing [an omen] or the birth of a son; such is the intended meaning.
(5) And this refers specifically to the *śrāddha* performed with non-golden [coins]. (6) For by that much alone, the purpose of the previously cited scriptural statement is fulfilled.

(7) However, the *annaśrāddha* [should be performed] at night or during the two twilights, or for one who has already eaten upon reaching a sacred site (*tīrtha*) on the second day. (8) But in the case of impurity (*āśauca*) upon reaching a sacred site, it should be performed when the impurity has ceased; (9) because the connection to the sacred site still exists even then, it differs from [the case of] the initial arrival. (10) In the case of reaching a sacred site during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), since delay is prohibited, one should perform the *śrāddha* at that time and then perform it again in the pure month; (11) because the arrival at the sacred site persists even then, the fruit is greater due to the purity of the time.
One should perform the *yaugādika*, the monthly (*māsika*), the fortnightly (*aparapakṣika*), the *manvādika*, and the *tairthika* śrāddhas during both months as well. || 401 ||

And because of the statement recorded in the *Smṛticandrikā*: (1) Here, "belonging to the dark fortnight" (*aparapakṣika*) refers to the monthly *śrāddha* performed during the dark fortnight, and not to the *mahālaya-śrāddha*, since that is prohibited in that context. (2) Nor does this statement refer to the occasion of reaching a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), for in the absence of this [monthly rule], the *śrāddha* would already be accomplished by that [general rule]; thus, it would follow that the mention of "pertaining to a *tīrtha*" (*tairthika*) would be redundant. This is the general direction. (3) A specific rule regarding the Brahmin invited to the *śrāddha* is found in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"At sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), one should never examine a Brahmin at all."
Manu declared that food should be given to one who has arrived seeking food. (402)
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "One should not examine a Brāhmaṇa [for his lineage] at a sacred site, nor should one consider the time;
when a wise man has reached a sacred site, he should perform the *śrāddha* at that very moment. (403)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"A twice-born man who comes to a sacred ford seeking food should certainly not be examined; he is simply to be fed. (404)
And this [statement] at Kākh 6.58ab is for the purpose of granting permission in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa worthy of the Śrāddha;
even in that case, one should not examine [the guest] solely on the basis of his qualities.
But one who is possessed of extreme faults, such as causing a loss of caste and so forth, must certainly be avoided. || 405 ||
Thus it has been explained in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī* [p.
110]. Now, regarding what is prohibited at a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, the *Devīpurāṇa* states:
"And the *śrāddha* should be performed there, omitting the water-offering (*arghya*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*).
(406) Likewise:
"The water-offering, the invocation, and the placing of the thumb upon the twice-born [brāhmaṇa]..."
And one should avoid the question regarding satiety and the scattering of food at a śrāddha performed at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha). || 407 ||
In some cases, however: "There is no invocation, no binding of the directions, and no fault arising from [impure] sight;
the wise should perform the Śrāddha at a sacred site (tīrtha) with compassion. (408)
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"Since both the gods and the ancestors are always present in the Gaṅgā, there is no need for their invocation or dismissal. (409)
Likewise:
"There should be no invocation at a sacred ford (tīrtha), nor should there be the offering of the arghya water;
for the ancestors are already invoked and have indeed received their arghya at the sacred ford. (410)
The rite of offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) is also not performed at a śrāddha at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Thus it is stated in the Smṛtiratnāvalī. Devala says: "And in this case, one should not prohibit birds such as hawks, vultures, and the like."
"The ancestors, being of that same nature, arrive there"—this is the Vedic teaching. (412)

(1) Furthermore, this prohibition regarding the summoning [of ancestors] applies specifically to a *śrāddha* occasioned by reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and not to every *śrāddha* performed at a sacred ford as its locus; (2) because the phrase "there" (*tatra*) [at 406] employs the locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*), the prohibition applies only to that *śrāddha* which is occasioned by that [arrival]; and (3) because in the concluding summary [at 381], "only by those who have arrived" (*prāptair eva*), the arrival itself is proclaimed to be the occasion.

(4) "But surely, since the locative of cause depends upon co-utterance with another word and since the state of being a cause is understood through a sentence, let this be simply the locative of locus; (5) for it is stronger as a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*) and as a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)."

(6) No, because since it is impossible for [the word *tīrthe*] to function as a case-ending denoting an agent (*kāraka*), it is the sentence itself that can serve as the determining factor. (7) To explain: first of all, it is not tenable to say that "this is a locative case in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), which makes known the locus-status of the sacred site (*tīrtha*) by way of being a subordinate element (*śeṣitā*), like [the examples] ‘the cows are to be kept in the house’ or ‘one should pour curds into heated milk’"; (8) because the sacred site does not produce any excellence of refinement (*saṃskāra*) or the like through the *śrāddha*. (9) Nor is it tenable [to take it] as the principal (*aṅgin*)—as in the case of ‘there one should offer the *jaya* oblations’—because the sacred site, not being something to be enjoined, has no requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and (10) because it lacks the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the fruit. (11) Nor is it the locus-status of the sacred site by way of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*), as in ‘but in the absence of fire, one should offer it in the hand of a Brahmin’ or ‘what one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire’; (12) because if the sacred site were a subordinate element with respect to the *śrāddha* in general, it would follow that the *darśa-śrāddha* and other rites performed at home would be defective.

(13) If it is argued that "in the case of a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, the sacred site (*tīrtha*) is a constituent part (*aṅga*) by virtue of being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," (14) we say no, because the relationship between the *tīrtha* and the *śrāddha* has not yet been determined; (15) because the very meaning of the term *tīrtha-śrāddha* is still being ascertained; and (16) because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the repetition of the word *tīrtha*.

(17) Therefore, as in the case of the injunction "one offers when [the butter] has not split," since this cannot be a case for an instrumental case-ending denoting a *kāraka*, this word "therein" (*tatra*) must be a locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*). (18) In that regard, because the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is permanent and lacks occasional occurrence, it cannot logically be the occasion; thus, its status as an occasion is derived from the fact of its being attained. Alternatively, the status of its attainment as the occasion is understood by considering such scriptural statements as, "It must be performed only when [the time] has arrived" [381].

(19) [Objection: "Even so, in the case of the statement, 'One should avoid the *arghya* and other offerings in that *śrāddha* which is occasioned by a sacred ford (*tīrtha*'), if one intends to specify the *nimitta* (occasioning factor) called 'sacred ford' as a qualifier of the *śrāddha*—the object of the injunction—then, according to the principle stated under the topic of the two-fold purpose (*ubhayārthādhikaraṇa*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). (20) Consequently, the prohibition of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites would apply to all *śrāddhas* whatsoever. (21) [Reply: It is not so. For a syntactical split occurs when one intends to specify a qualifier of the object of the injunction (*uddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*), but not when the object of the injunction is qualified [as a whole]. (22) This is just as in the case of the rule, "The *Maitrāvaruṇa* priest gives the directions (*preṣyati*) and recites the responses (*anu cāhe*"), where the object of the injunction is the giving of directions and the recitation of responses as qualified by the aforementioned conjunction (*sāhitya*).

(23) And in that case, because it is presented by a proximate means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in its specific form as the subject under discussion, its presence in the intellect alone is the cause of determination (*vinigama-hetu*), just as in the case of a mantra consisting of both a command (*praiṣa*) and a recitation (*anuvacana*) due to its textual recitation. (24) Therefore, there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). (25) This has been elaborated upon by Bhavadeva, so it will not be discussed further here.

(26) Consequently, the prohibition of the *arghya* offering and so forth applies only to the *śrāddha* performed on the occasion of reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha-prāpti-naimittika-śrāddha*), and not to every *śrāddha* having that as its locus, such as those performed on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) and the like; just as—
The Śrāddha ceremony, including the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa), should be performed during the two solstices, the two equinoxes, and at the transits of the sun (saṅkrānti).
(1) Thus, the prohibition of the *piṇḍa* offering applies only when occasioned by such events as the *saṅkrānti*, and not likewise during the annual rites (*vārṣika*) and so forth.
As it has been said:
"But in this case, there shall be no abandonment of the *piṇḍa* in the ancestral sacrifice (*pitr̥yajña*) when occasioned by other [specific] causes. (414)

(1) If it be argued: "Even so, since invocation has as its result the bringing about of proximity, and since the ancestors are always in proximity at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), the invocation must be set aside—just as the cutting [of wood] and the digging [of the altar] are set aside when one uses fuel and an altar already prepared by oneself—because it would be redundant for the *śrāddha* performed at a sacred site itself. (2) It is not so; for, as in the case of the statement "for by that food is [the sacrifice] performed," the demonstration of proximity is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) intended to provide a reason. (3) Furthermore, even when they are in proximity, invocation is possible in a figurative sense (*upacāra*), just like the awakening of one who is already awake. (4) However, there is a setting aside [of invocation] only when there is a prohibition based on the specific occasion of the sacred site.

(5) Likewise: "There is no corporeal presence of the deity, because in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning deities), the body was rejected. (6) Nor is it mental (*bauddha*), because since the deity is accepted as being the mere word, such [mental presence] is impossible due to its insentience. (7) For what purpose, then, is there an invocation (*āvāhana*) elsewhere? (8) Know that it is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). (9) For this very reason, they also say that there is no modification (*ūha*) of the invocation mantra. (10) On this point, some [object]: "In the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, it was not presence (*saṃnidhāna*) that was rejected, but rather primacy (*prādhānya*). As for presence, however..."
At the commencement of ritual actions, the deities of the mantras are to be known. || 415 ||
Having mentally offered the deity, the oblation is sacrificed.

(1) Since [the agent] is understood through such statements as these to be present in the mind of the agent by virtue of being the intended object (*uddeśya*), it is simply impossible to negate [that presence]. (2) Furthermore: because it is not preceded by verbal testimony (*aśabdapūrvatvāt*), the status of primacy (*prādhānya*) is excluded in those cases.
And here: "I am present there among those stone images and so forth. (417)
According to the statement of Śrī Rāma in the *Rāmottaratāpinīyopaniṣad*, fourth section, page 166: "Hari is eternally present within the śālagrāma stone. (418)
(1) Because of such statements as these, proximity is accepted by all; (2) likewise for the ancestors—as [stated in] RV 10.15.6:
"To the south, bending the knees... (419 = 428).
Seated in the lap of the ruddy ones.
"Yonder one, this is for you. (RV 10.15.7) [421] (= 431).
Gobhila Gṛhya Sūtra 4.2.35.
From such passages as these, proximity is understood. Likewise: "One should not lift up first the vessel that has been set down for the ancestors;
for there the ancestors remain, so Śaunaka has said. (422)
On the previous day, the Pitṛs indeed enter into the invited Brahmins; therefore, on that night, the sacrificer and they should remain there, self-restrained. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 4.7.14) 423.
(1) Its cognition [of the deity] occurs through such [passages] as these.

(2) Furthermore, in the ninth [book], the refutation of the fivefold attributes of the deity—such as its having a physical form and so forth—was not undertaken out of mere pedantry, but rather for the sake of establishing *ūha* (adaptation of mantras) and ensuring its status as a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*). (3) For instance, if the deity were the primary factor, then since the mantras for the offering (*nirvāpa*) and other rites would be prompted by the specific nature of Agni and the other deities, it would follow that in an oblation to Sūrya (*saurya*), where Agni and the other deities are absent, the mantras would not apply, and thus *ūha* would be impossible. (4) Consequently, the observation of *ūha* in passages such as "The mother does not increase, nor the father" would be untenable.

(5) However, when the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is primary, because the mantras are employed for its sake, the season (*ṛtu*)—as manifested by the mantras—accomplishes the *apūrva*. Thus, modification (*ūha*) is established in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) that possesses a different deity. (6) Therefore, just as the deity was manifested in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too in the modified sacrifice; thus, the status [of the mantra] is established as being like the archetype.

(7) Likewise—in the case of animals such as frogs, the leaves and roots of herbs and trees, and the sounds such as *hiṅkāra* produced by horses—all of which are insentient, since they cannot possibly be bestowers of fruit, the *apūrva* alone must be the primary factor.
But the deity is subordinate.
(8) "Is it not the case that even a householder who is faithful and truthful is liberated? || 424 ||
Women are to be treated with respect— || 425 ||
Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra, Śrāddha Sūtra 9 (1):

"Because, by such statements as 'tyādi', the śrāddha rite itself has its purpose in the fruit [of the action], since it is preceded by the Vedic word; and because even for the ancestors, [the entitlement] is preceded by the Vedic word. (426)

This is merely a matter of the scope of the logical rule [MS 9.1.4.9]. (1) Nor should it be argued that “the Śrāddha is for the sake of the ancestors because a fault is heard of only for one whose father is dead if he does not perform the Śrāddha,” (2) because there is no case-ending expressing that purpose (*tādarthya*), and the intent is rather toward the necessity of performing the Śrāddha;

(3) and because even for such a person, its status as a means to a result is established through the principle of the distinctness of conjunctions (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*). (4) To this we say: not so, because there is no evidence that a sacrifice is for the sake of a deity. (5) In the case of the Śrāddha, however, there is an abundance of evidence for its being for their sake. For instance:
Then the ancestors, wearing the sacred cord over the right shoulder, approached him with their left knees bent and said to him:
"Your food shall be [offered] month by month."
"Having bent [the knee] to the south, below the knee," so says the Śruti (ŚBr 2.4.2.2). || 428 || (= 419)
O Fathers, come to eat the oblation! 429.
O Fathers, rejoice here! 430.
And from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of such mantras as "asāv etat ta" (VS 2.31a), etc. [p.115].

Those situated in the world of the gods are satisfied by oblations poured into the fire; those situated among the ancestors by the gratification of the twice-born; and those situated in hell are satisfied by the three funeral cakes offered upon the earth.
"Br̥h" (Śrā) 110 refers to Bṛhaspati;
[as stated] in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
Through the ancestral rites (śrāddha), the ancestors obtain satisfaction lasting for that entire rainy season.
At that time, the śrāddha offered to the ancestors during the Brāhma [muhūrta] is said to be inexhaustible. || 3.14.7c-d || 434 ||
Yājñavalkya says:
"When they are satisfied, they satisfy him. (435)

Thus, from the statements of Kātyāyana, Manu, and others, as well as from the passages in the *Vāyu-purāṇa*, *Agni-purāṇa*, and so forth located within the section on Gayā and other sacred sites, it is understood that the *śrāddha* results solely in the satisfaction of the ancestors: "Longevity, progeny, wealth, and knowledge... (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.47a).
"In them being satisfied, they satisfy him" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.269a)—
in such passages as this, their status as bestowers of results is also understood.
When he crushed— || 438 ||
From such Vedic mantra-texts as Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 12.7.3.21 and others, it follows that the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice also has the ancestors as its purpose;
however, the head [of the sacrificial animal] is offered with the first rice-ball. || 439 ||

(1) By means of this and other passages, it is shown that even the *śrāddha* rites for pretas serve the purpose of the ancestors by way of accomplishing the body. (2) For this very reason, the accomplishment of the *vigraha* (the ritual form) is also established.
"One should deliver the seven lineages" (440).
Those dwelling in hell go to heaven. || 441 ||
Having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors.

(1) By such statements as these, the fruit of the *śrāddha* is also understood to belong to that [deity]. (2) Therefore, since it is understood from the *Śruti* and other sources that the *śrāddha* is for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*), there is no lack of being preceded by the word [of the Veda] in this case. (3) Nor are these merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), (4) because there is no contradiction with the fact that they are seen in the scriptures to be for the sake of another, and so forth. (5) Thus, in the *śrāddha*, the deity is the primary element, while the ritual act is subordinate. (6) In sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like, however, the reverse is the case.

(7) This [objection] is rooted in a lack of thorough investigation of the Mīmāṃsā. (8) For instance: as for the claim that "because the deity is present in the agent's cognition, it is impossible to deny its presence," (9) that is not so. By whom is this "presence in the agent's cognition" termed "objecthood" denied? (10) For what is denied is a presence brought about by invocation (*āvāhana*); and this [presence in the cognition] is not brought about by invocation. (11) Since invocation consists precisely in making [the deity] present in the cognition, there can be no absence of presence in the cognition subsequent to the invocation. (12) Furthermore, if presence in the cognition were brought about by invocation, then in the sacrifice to Viṣṇu of the wide strides (*urukrama*), which involves the sublation of invocation, and in the *śrāddha* at sacred sites (*tīrtha*), which involves the denial of it, there would follow the consequence of an absence of presence in the cognition. (13) As for that presence brought about by invocation, it has already been refuted by the rejection of [the deity's] having a physical body and so forth, just like coming and going.

(14) Furthermore, having stated that "the proximity of the agent's cognition cannot be negated," to then cite as evidence for such proximity the statements "I am present there" and "Hari is eternally present upon the Śālagrāma stone" is contradictory. (15) For by these [statements], the proximity of the agent's cognition is not being expressed. (16) And as for the citation intended to establish the presence of the Father, beginning with "up to the knees," that is exactly the same [in nature]: "Come, O Indra, by the paths invoked... (RV 2.18.7). 443.
O Agni, come hither for the feast! 444
O Vāyu, come hither, O beautiful one! 445
O Agni, come along with these [gods] on the same chariot. 446.
Be right here; do not depart. 447.
O Indra, come; O Lord of the Bay Horses, come. 448.
"O Maghavan, come tomorrow to the Soma-pressing. (ŚBr 3.3.4.18)

(1) Because the proximity of the deity of the sacrifice is also understood from such scriptural passages as these; and (2) because in rites such as the *tulāpuruṣa*, there is an extensive demonstration of the deity’s presence through phrases like “Come, come,” and in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, the presence of deities at sacrifices such as those of Saṃvarta and others is indeed established.

(3) As for the claim that “the refutation of the *vigraha* (embodiment) and so forth in the ninth [chapter] is for the sake of establishing the *ūha* (modification) of the deity, because it is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*),” etc., all of that is equally applicable to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). (4) For if the deity were the primary factor in the *śrāddha*, then in the case of a *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and others, there would be no application of the mantra from the Taittirīya recension—such as “May my mother, who was infatuated,” which contains the singular word *pitṛ*—nor of mantras such as “May the ancestors be purified,” since these are prompted by the specific nature of the [paternal] ancestors; consequently, the absence of those [mantras] would lead to the undesirable consequence of an absence of *ūha*. (5) And thus, the observation of *ūha* in the rule “according to the rule, by modification of the mantra” [Jaimini Sūtra 9.1.48] would be untenable.

(6) Nor should it be said that "this is a rule for modification (*ūha*), but not a rule for visualization (*darśana*)," (7) because in the case of the *śrāddha* rite for maternal grandfathers and in the rule for modification, this would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). (8) We shall clarify all of this immediately below.

(9) As for the argument beginning with "of animals" (*tiraścām*), that too is equal [in force], (10) because it is impossible for any sentient being to accept as the primary givers of the fruit [of the rite] either those dwelling in hell, or those born as animals such as worms and insects, or those in the form of trees and shrubs, or even liberated ancestors like one's father and so forth, by virtue of their respective individual karmas.

(11) Even that argument which, having stated that there is "no evidence for the sacrifice being for the sake of the deity," proceeds to present evidence for the *śrāddha* being for the sake of the ancestors, is likewise equal [to the previous case].
(12) Regarding that, as for the scriptural passage cited—“Then the ancestors approached him” [427]—this is its first part:
“The beings indeed approached Prajāpati; the beings are indeed the creatures. ‘Grant us prosperity so that... [and so on].
"May I live! Then the gods, having put on their sacrificial threads and having bent their right knees, sat down before him.
He said to them: "Sacrifice is your food; immortality is your strength; the sun is your light. (450)

(1) Immediately following that is the passage beginning with “Then he [makes him] a father,” and so forth. (2) In this regard, how is it that the former portion of this scriptural text does not establish that the sacrifice is for the sake of the deity? (3) And how is it that the latter portion establishes that the *śrāddha* is for the sake of the deity? Without drinking from the vessel [of evidence], this is nothing but a deception of the Vedic tradition.
Likewise—
"Come, O Indra; these oblations have been set forth"—with this [verse], *ekayā pratidhāpibat* (RV 10.116.8). || 452 ||
Thus [is] the state of being the enjoyer: "Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth. || 453 ||
The Lord of this world, who beholds the light of heaven. (RV 10.89.10) [454]
I have become the ancient lord of wealth. 455.
(1) Thus [he attains] lordship; Indra, being himself satisfied, satisfies him with offspring and cattle. || 456 ||
He alone leads him to prosperity. || 457 ||
I distribute food to the donor. 458.
He grants a son to the one who offers oblations. || 459 ||

(1) In passages such as RV 5.25.5d, the quality of being a bestower of fruits is understood; in passages such as “Indra is indeed satisfied with him” [456], satisfaction is perceived. (2) However, in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, there is no counting at all of such statements. (3) This being the case, if these [Vedic texts] find their interpretation through the form of praise and so forth, then let one’s vision be applied—even setting aside partiality—to those [texts] that establish the gratification of the ancestors and similar matters. (4) And therefore: “Or rather, because it is preceded by words, the sacrificial act should be primary, while the praise of the deity is subordinate. [JS 1.2.1] 460.
Thus, regarding the status of being an object of logical reasoning, there is no distinction whatsoever that can be established without divine vision.

(2) Furthermore, regarding the illustrative example cited to demonstrate the attainment of results for the ancestors and others—namely, "He shall uplift the seven lineages," and so forth—even there, nothing is contradicted by the fact that the *śrāddha* is not for the sake of the [actual] deities. (3) For it is not Yajñadatta, Janaka, and the like who are the deities of the *śrāddha*; rather, they are the Vasus and others. (4) The words "father" (*pitṛ*) and so forth are merely applied to them in common usage. (5) Yet, this much does not constitute identity. (6) Thus, the *śrāddha* is not for the sake of the Vasus and others; rather, they are merely subordinate factors (*guṇabhūta*) in the *śrāddha*. (7) And what is the *śrāddha* rite, characterized by those [deities], that brings about the satisfaction of Janaka and others, or their deliverance from hell—what is there that is illogical? As it has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors, the deities of the Śrāddha;
when satisfied by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of men.
(Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.268)

(1) And here, the quality of being gratifying inherent in the ancestral rite (*śrāddhakarma*) is metaphorically attributed (*upacaryate*) to the Vasus and others who are the means of accomplishing that rite, just as in the passage: “Indra, having been heated, gratifies him with offspring and cattle” [456]. (2) Likewise, in passages such as “Being themselves gratified, they gratify him” [435], the metaphorical attribution is exactly the same.

(3) Nor should it be argued: "How can the fruit, such as satisfaction and so forth, arising from a person of faith, accrue to ancestors like Janaka and others, given that the fruit must reside in the agent? (4) For, just as in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, where purity and other qualities accrue to the son, authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) demonstrate that the fruit belongs precisely to one who is not the agent. (5) This will be explained in detail in the section on Gayā, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

(6) Furthermore, since the presence of the ancestors is accepted as being perceptible, one should not postulate an imperceptible result; therefore, it must be admitted that the very result of the invocation (*āvāhana*) is their presence. (7) And thus, there would be a sublation of the invocation in every *śrāddha* performed at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), (8) because the result [of presence] is obtained from that very location due to its being eternally present.
Water, rice, and that which is mixed with them constitute the *prājāpatya* offering. || 462 ||
(1) In this case, just as the threshing [of grain] is set aside when the removal of the husk is accomplished by other means;

(2) nor should it be argued that "the invocation (*āvāhana*) there will serve the purpose of a restrictive unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*)," because (3) those things which have a visible purpose produce the unseen only through that visible medium, and thus, as in the case of the *kr̥ṣṇala* berry, when the visible purpose is absent, that [unseen merit] is also lost;

and (4) because the restrictive unseen merit, being produced as a byproduct, is not a motivator (*aprayojaka*), like the *vājina* curd-mixture. (5) Therefore, the presence of the ancestors is not possible.
(6) And if the fivefold attributes such as corporeality are accepted in the case of the ancestors, then:
"If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding their activity, we say no, because we observe multiple modes of perception. (463)

(1) Let it be accepted, even regarding deities, according to the first principle of the *Catur-lakṣaṇī* as stated by Vyāsa in the *Vedāntasūtra* 1.3.27; or let it not be accepted even regarding ancestors, according to the opinion of the sage Jaimini. However, a "half-old-woman" approach (*ardha-jaratīya*)—accepting one part while rejecting another—is not appropriate.

(2) The establishment of this point is that, based on the scriptural injunction, there is a sublation of the invocation (*āvāhana*) specifically in a *śrāddha* performed at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), but not in every *śrāddha* where a sacred site is the locus.

(3) As for the statement, “Why then is there invocation (*āvāhana*) elsewhere as well? Understand that it is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*); and following that, the claim, “For this very reason, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the invocation mantra either,” (4) that must be considered. Even if the invocation were for the sake of an unseen merit, the mantra has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by way of reminding one of the matter to be performed; and since that much suffices [for its validity], (5) it is not the case that because an action has an unseen purpose, there can be no modification of the mantra that accomplishes it. (6) Otherwise, it would follow that there could be no modification of the *svāhā*-utterance used as the means for the fifth *prayāja* offering. Furthermore—
To eat the oblation, [we invoke] the fathers. (464) (= 429, 478) May the Soma-loving fathers come to us. (465)

(1) Thus, because the word *pitṛ* (*father*) contained in the invocation mantra retains its original meaning even in the *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers and others, and because there is no other meaning [to be conveyed], no modification (*ūha*) occurs. (2) For this is so: this word *pitṛ* is used in two ways.
(3) In some cases, it is used by way of limiting conditions such as being a progenitor.
But if one's father should have passed away while the grandfather is still living, [he should offer the śrāddha to the grandfather].

In passages such as *Manu* 3.221a-b, [the term "father"] sometimes refers to the group of deities common to both men and women, conditioned by the status of being a *pitṛ* produced by the *śrāddha* rites ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; it is like the word "Marut" and so forth, and like the words "Agniṣvātta" and so forth, [which denote the class of ancestors] once the deceased has attained the state of a *pitṛ* through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. || 467 ||
According to the Viṣṇu-smṛti (ViPu 3.13.36a-b),
from that time forward, the deceased indeed attains equality with the ancestors. || 468 ||

And because of this statement by Hārīta: "(1) Thus, in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the prohibition of the word 'father' (*pitṛ*) mentioned in the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* is also logically justified.

(2) For this very reason, the word 'father' is seen used as a common term even for maternal grandfathers, paternal grandfathers, and so forth, as in: 'Thereafter, one should commence the *śrāddha* with devotion toward the six ancestors. (469)
One should pour the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors. || 470 ||
And as it is said in Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.252c-d:
"(1) Even though [the offering] is common to the mother and others, [one should say]:
'May all the ancestors—the mother, maternal grandfather, and so forth—be satisfied. (471)
(1) As for the statement: "Since the word *pitṛ* lacks a common denotation [for both], there are two for the gods (*daiva*) and three before for the ancestors (*pitrya*)... [472]...
In rites for the ancestors, the time of Kutapa should be adopted by the learned. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.228a) [Verse 473]
Silver should be given to the ancestors. || 474 ||
That vessel for the ancestors is turned face upwards. || 475 ||

(1) As for the objection that "the word *pitṛ* [father], having been prescribed by taking up the term *pitṛ* in [Yājñavalkya] 1.247c, does not apply in the *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) and others," (2) that is not correct; for even if it is not obtained through direct instruction (*upadeśa*), its application is possible through extension (*atideśa*). (3) Therefore, the word *pitṛ* is common [to all ancestors] precisely according to the path we have described.

(4) Thus, since the word *pitṛ*—remaining unaltered—is applicable even to the mother, the maternal grandfather, and so forth, because its denoted meaning is present there under the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being a "father" (*pitṛbhāva*), there is no occasion for modification (*ūha*); this is because the invocation (*āvāhana*) serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
What is to be avoided? And what is it? This syllable of the *ṛc* putrefies if one omits it; therefore, one should not omit a *ṛc*. 476.
(1) Because of the prohibition of *ūha* (modification) in the verse [cited] as ĀśŚrSū 5.4.8, there is no possibility of *ūha* here either.
(2) By this, the following is refuted, which someone has said:

“Modification according to the actual meaning is prescribed when [the rite] is enjoined; it does not apply to the archetype because of its unprecedented nature, but it does apply to the ectype because of a specific scriptural statement. || 477 ||

According to the statement of Kātyāyana in KātŚrSū 4.98–100, [the formula] "for the fathers to eat the sacrificial food" is used at the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather and others, which constitutes a modified form [of the rite]. (= 429, 464)
"May the ancestors come to us" (479).
With the mantra "Thou art sesame," [he offers] to the ancestors with the *svadhā* exclamation (480).
With the mantra “ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ,” he should satiate the ancestors. 481.
Here, O ancestors, rejoice! 482 (= 430).
Homage to you, O ancestors, for the sake of the essence! 483.
"O fathers, eat this honey. (VS 2.32a) || 484 ||
"O ancestors, this is your garment. (VS 2.31b) 485.

(1) Regarding the statement, "In mantras such as VS 2.32h, the word *mātāmaha* and others must be substituted in place of the word *pitṛ* for the sake of expressing the relevant meaning," (2) this is because the application of the word *pitṛ*—which functions on the basis of the condition of having attained the status of a father—is logically consistent even when applied to a maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others without modification; (3) and because there is a prohibition against its use in the case of verses (*ṛc*). (4) Furthermore, the statement of Kātyāyana is not recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Śrāddha ritual, but is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*). (5) Consequently, it is also logically consistent as referring to the Yajus-mantras that reveal the procedure for the offering (*nirvāpa*) and so forth.

(6) Nor should it be argued: "In this way, although there is no modification (*ūha*) because the nominal stem *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) in the mantra beginning with ‘*tilo ’si*’ is common [to both], nevertheless, since the plural number has a meaning not inherent (*asamaveta*) in a single maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and so forth, there should be a modification as if it were singular.

(7) For if the plural number has a meaning not inherent in the archetype (*prakṛti*), its application remains unmodified even in the ectype (*vikṛti*). Just as in the case of ‘*aditiḥ pāśān*’, the plural number is somehow justified even when there is only one, as in the case of the mantra for the *uparava* holes, or like ‘*vāyavaḥ stha*’.

(8) By this [it is shown that], although the word *pitṛ* ending in the plural number expresses the respective deities and thus possesses a meaning inherent in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the plural is used for each individual person; as it says: "Saying 'This garment is for you, O fathers,' [he offers] separately for each. (486)

This is due solely to the force of the scriptural statement. (1) However, in the case of a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), the [objection] that "because there is an absence of a scriptural statement, there is no modification (*ūha*) since the singular ending applies," is refuted by the principle that "only as much as is stated in the text is scripturally authoritative. (2) Furthermore, if one were to assume an intention (*tātparya*) for the scriptural statement to prescribe the plural number, then since there would be no distinction even when prescribing the use of the word *pitṛ* (father), it would follow that the same intention applies there as well; this would result in the absence of any modification (*ūha*) of the word *pitṛ*, which contradicts the stated necessity of modifying the word *pitṛ*.

(3) Furthermore, this being the case, since the plural number in the original statement has a meaning not inherent in the primary rite (*prakṛti*), then even in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), by virtue of the extension (*atideśa*) despite the absence of the plural word, there would be application only in its unmodified form according to the logic of the *pāśa* [singular rope], and thus no modification (*ūha*) would occur.
(4) Moreover, since the statement refers only to the specific mantra "etad va," what would be the status of other mantras?

(5) Therefore, having restated the mantra which contains a plural number as it occurs in the text, the injunction prescribes a repetition (*āvṛtti*) that constitutes a distinct word-meaning. (6) Alternatively, having restated everything, it prescribes only the giving of the garment; thus, the plural number is not based on the explicit wording (*vācanika*).
(7) [Objection: "Even so, in the *pārvaṇa* rite, let the very act of pouring sesame seeds into the vessels for the progenitor (*janaka-pātra*) and so forth be the archetype (*prakṛti*)."

(8) However, in the case of the rites related to the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), they will be modified (*vikṛti*). (9) Furthermore, the word *pitṛ* is capable [of denoting] the progenitor, whereas the mere utterance [of the word] is not so capable. (10) Therefore, in place of the word *pitṛ* in the two subsequent rites, the words *pitāmaha* and *prapitāmaha* should be substituted (*ūhya*), while the plural number remains exactly as it is. (11) And thus, there will be even more clearly a substitution in the case of the mother and others. (12) If it is argued that "the single word *pitṛ*, though having multiple meanings, need not be postulated," (13) [we reply: no, because within the same context (*samānaprakaraṇa*), there is an absence of the relationship between archetype and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*), according to the principle of the *aindrāna* and *aindrapradāna* offerings. (14) Thus, for the sake of the meaning being applicable to all three, the fact of having multiple meanings is accepted by the aforementioned arguments only as a last resort (*ananyagatikatayā*).

(15) Furthermore, if modification (*ūha*) were admitted for the latter two [verses] there, then the three utterances beginning with "May the fathers be purified" (*aśundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*) would become purposeless.

(16) Thus it is established: the word *pitṛ* does not undergo modification in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), because its meaning remains inherently applicable (*samavetārtha*), just as in the original ritual (*prakṛti*). (17) And the plural number [in the third verse] does not undergo modification because its meaning is not inherently applicable in the original ritual.
(18) As for the statement concerning Viṣṇu—

In this same manner, a wise man should perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers; he should do so according to the rule with the appropriate mantras, and for the remaining ancestors, it should be performed without mantras.

Thus, (1) that [statement] also does not serve as a modification (*ūha*) for the previously mentioned mantras, because of the expression “according to the rule” (*yathānyāyam*). (2) And this is the rule regarding modification: (3) a mantra employed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) with qualifiers such as “primary meaning” (*mukhyārtha*) and so forth, when extended by implication (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) through its function, would—if used with words whose meanings are not applicable to the new context—not have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) as it did in the archetype; therefore, it must be employed with words whose meanings are applicable (*samavetārtha*). As the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda said:
“By means of being primary, having a visible purpose, having its own meaning, and having an applicable meaning, etc.”
Mantras employed in the archetype (prakṛti) proceed [to the ectype] by means of the extension of the ritual function (kāryātideśa).
"In the case of modifications that have become functional, there are five kinds of unrestricted *ūha* (adaptation).
However, in the case of other meanings, they do not proceed to *ūha* by way of a previously unknown meaning. (TV 1.3.8.24, p.
(1) And the fivefold assumption of the function [of the original] has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Someśvara:

"By means of a direct injunction, in the absence [of a rule], by way of a specific prescription, through modification, from its own word, and from the restatement of a prohibition—in these cases, the function of that [original] is assumed. (489)

(1) Furthermore, in the previously mentioned mantras, because the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) retains its inherent meaning even in the modified form (*vikṛti*), and because it is not employed in any other sense, there is no modification (*ūha*). (2) [Objection: "In that case, what is the purpose of the statement, 'The mantra is modified according to the rule'? It is replied:
May the ancestors be purified. 490.

In this regard, the modification (*ūha*) follows from the logical principle stated at Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.6.14: (1) For here, if the term *pitṛ* were applied by virtue of the previously mentioned limiting condition (*upādhi*), then the recitation of the two mantras, “May the grandfathers be purified” and “May the great-grandfathers be purified,” would be purposeless. (2) Therefore, its application occurs solely by virtue of the limiting conditions such as being the progenitor (*janakatva*). (3) Consequently, in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), such as the *śrāddha* for the mother, maternal grandfather, and others, there must be a modification (*ūha*) because the referent is different.

(5) That [plural ending] also belongs only to the nominal stem itself. (6) However, even when there is only one father in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the plural number has a meaning that does not apply [to the individual]; therefore, it should not be modified. (7) Consequently, there is modification (*ūha*) in such cases as “May the mothers be purified” (*śundhantāṃ mātaraḥ*) and “May the maternal grandfathers be purified” (*śundhantāṃ mātāmahāḥ*). (8) The same applies to the paternal grandfather and others.

(9) For those followers of a Vedic branch (*śākhin*) for whom the formula “*pitṛbhyaḥ svadhocyatām*” and so forth is recited exactly like the *śundhana* mantra, there is likewise modification (*ūha*) in that case as well. (10) However, since Kātyāyana and Gobhila have specifically recited the mantra as “*mātāmahebhyaḥ svadhocyatām*” even in that context, there is no modification regarding that [specific version].
(11) But in the case of the mother and others, modification does occur; for instance, among the Hiraṇyakeśins, [the mantra] reads: “*yan me mātā pralulobhe*... [491]

In the mantras beginning with *HirGṛSū* 2.10.7(1), there occurs a modification (*ūha*) such as: “Whatever my maternal grandmother has corrupted, may my maternal grandfather remove that seed. (2) This is because words such as *pitṛ* (father) and so forth, being in the singular number, lack the capacity to denote [the plural] collectively. (3) Furthermore, if that were not the case, there would follow the absurdity of the uselessness of reciting mantra-readings such as “whatever my paternal grandmother has corrupted” (*yan me pitāmahī pralulobhe*). As it was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*:
“In the offering of food, likewise in touching, and in the giving of water-clods and so forth...”
‘“My maternal grandmother,” etc., would be an example therein. (492) Thus:
(1) ‘Example’ (*udāharaṇa*) means *ūha* (adaptation). (2) ‘In the case of contact’:
‘This honeyed [offering] is for you, O grandfather. (493)

[One should touch the food] for the purpose of feeding the Brāhmaṇas with the mantras beginning with HirGr̥Sū 2.13.1. (1) Likewise, in other instances as well, wherever a modification (*ūha*) is appropriate, it should be performed after due consideration.

(2) As for the claim made by some that "‘by means of *ūha*’ means by means of the recitation of the mantra, and not by means of a modification (*vikāra*) of its form," (3) that is incorrect, because the word *ūha* is not commonly established in the sense of "recitation. (4) Furthermore, since the recitation of the mantra would already be obtained by the very injunction "one should act thus" (*kuryāt*), like any other ritual duty (*dharma*), this [injunction regarding *ūha*] would become redundant. (5) Alternatively, it would result in a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) according to the principle of the *gr̥hamedhīyājyabhāga* offerings. (6) Moreover, it would lead to the meaninglessness of the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathānyāyam*). (7) Therefore, the scope of this [injunction] is exactly as we have stated.
(8) In such [formulas] as “O Father, this is your *arghya*,” there should not even be any consideration regarding *ūha* (modification) or *anūha* (non-modification);

(9) because, being a mere utterance (*abhilāpamātra*), it lacks the status of a *mantra*. (10) Or, if it were indeed a *mantra*, then by the statement “for the others, [the rite is] devoid of *mantras*,” it would follow that even the utterance itself must be excluded;
for this very rule has been declared: “For Śūdras, [the rite is] performed devoid of *mantras*. (494)

(1) Thus, by the statement in the *Varāha Purāṇa* (188.57a-b = 501), it follows that even a Śūdra must avoid uttering [mantras]. (2) Therefore, the word "mantra" applies primarily only to those that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), while elsewhere it is used figuratively. (3) For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that *ūha*, *pravara*, and names are not mantras. (4) This is the distinction between *ūha* and *anūha* regarding the *pārvaṇa* rite. (5) Now, it is said regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa*: therein, the *purāṇa-ekoddiṣṭa* is exactly like the *pārvaṇa*, because the status of being a *pitṛ* has already been attained through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. However, as for the *preta-ekoddiṣṭa*...
In the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, one should modify the mantras as if for a single person.

The modification (*ūha*) follows from this statement of Viṣṇu: (1) Since the status of being a *pitṛ* (ancestor) has not yet arisen due to the absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the word *preta* (deceased) in the singular should be employed in place of the word *pitṛ*. This is the meaning of Viṣṇu’s statement. (2) For this very reason, the cessation of the word *pitṛ* in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is stated in the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*. (3) However, the author of the *Smṛtiratnāvalī* states that "only the singular number should be modified for the plural [of ancestors], but there is no modification of the word *pitṛ* itself, because of the rule: 'In the case of the singular, two [words] are modified. (4) Otherwise, he would have simply said, 'One should modify according to the sense. (5) Therefore, in a *śrāddha* for a mother, a brother, a paternal uncle, and so forth, only the singular number is to be modified; the word *pitṛ*, however, remains exactly as it is. (6) This is because it denotes anyone who has died," thus explaining the meaning of Viṣṇu’s statement. (7) That is not correct, because it contradicts the cessation of the word *pitṛ* stated in the *Āśvalāyanapariśiṣṭa*. (8) Furthermore, if it were to denote anyone who has merely died, it would follow that there could be no modification in such [mantras] as "May the *pitṛ*s be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*), which was mentioned previously. (9) Moreover, even in the ritual formula (*abhilāpa*), the word *pitṛ* would necessarily apply everywhere.

(10) And because it contradicts the conduct of the learned. (11) Viṣṇu, however, having stated that "by the very principle of the *pitṛpada*, modification (*ūha*) would follow," did not enjoin that; rather, he enjoined only this much: "one modifies the mantras into the singular," on the grounds that "since the wording [of the original mantra] does not apply to the primary context (*prakṛti*), modification would not otherwise follow. (12) Therefore, it is established that the word *preta* ending in the singular number is to be modified as *pretaikoddiṣṭa*.
(13) "For the remaining [relatives], [the rite is] without mantras"—this is the remainder of the statement by Viṣṇu. (14) Śūlapāṇi explains its meaning:
in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others, the mantra containing the word *pitṛ* (father), which is subject to modification (*ūha*), must not be employed at all.

"But [the word] *tu* should not be used; nor, however, should it be employed even when devoid of the word *pitṛ*, because it is not the subject under discussion. (496) Thus, the meaning is that for paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others, the rite should be performed excluding the mantras for invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth. (497)

Thus it is stated in the *Kalpataru*. However, this is appropriate [only] for women who have not been married and whose wealth must be protected, as well as for the sons of Śūdra women, such as those born of a Pāraśava marriage:

"The Śrāddha for women is performed without mantras, and likewise for the son of a Śūdra woman; and before the instruction of the vows, the twice-born should perform that in the same manner. (MDh 2.66–67).
Thus, according to the recollection of Marīci: "In this context, the phrase 'of women' refers to women who have not yet married. (499)

Thus says Hemādri. (1) “Prāk” (before initiation) refers to the twice-born who have not yet been initiated. (2) They include women, Pāraśavas, and others; because they are uninitiated (*asaṃskṛta*), even when performing a Śrāddha for those who are initiated, they should perform it in the same manner, without mantras. (3) Alternatively, in the phrase “of the remaining ones” (*śeṣāṇām*), the genitive case denotes the agent. (4) Consequently, this refers to the remaining castes. (5) The meaning is that the Śrāddha which is to be performed by Śūdras, those equal to them, Pāraśavas, and uninitiated women, must be done by them without mantras. This has been stated in the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Pādmapurāṇa*, concerning the Śrāddha:
"Even a Śūdra may perform [the rite] without mantras according to this procedure, O King"—thus [it is stated].
Regarding the passage beginning with "First, the twice-born," etc., Marīci says: [Padma Purāṇa, Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa 9.193c–d (1)].
In the Varāha Purāṇa:

"This very same procedure is prescribed for Śūdras, excluding the mantras. However, for a Śūdra who is without a mantra, a Brāhmaṇa takes him [in initiation] with the mantra. (494) ... "Thus [it is said]. (501)
‘A Brahmin is seized by the mantra,’ meaning he is connected with it;
and this is a *paribhāṣā* (general rule). Furthermore, a *paribhāṣā* is not restricted by the immediate context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, for this—
Even during the recitation in the section on ancestral rites (śrāddha), as well as in bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, the Brāhmaṇa must recite the mantra for the Śūdra. || 502 ||
ŚrāVi, p. 231:
Thus says Śūlapāṇi.
(1) Here, the term "without mantras" is a prohibition of Vedic mantras. (2) By that, [the following] Paurāṇa...
Furthermore, the recitation of the name, lineage, and so forth must certainly be performed.
(3) Enough of this digression following upon a digression; let us return to the subject at hand. (4) Since the *tīrtha-śrāddha* has the *pārvaṇa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*),...
And Purūravas and Ārdrava are indeed cited in the context of the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha]. || 503 ||
Regarding *Br̥h* (Śrā) 93a-b (1):

although Purūravas and Ārdrava are included among the Viśvedevas according to the statement of Bṛhaspati, nevertheless, because that [inclusion] exists as an optional (*kāmya*) rite due to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), and because—by the logic of the "milk-pail" (*godohana-nyāya*)—the optional overrides the obligatory (*nitya*), and because even the occasional (*naimittika*) is considered obligatory (*nitya*) by virtue of its necessity, [one should instead employ] Dhuri and Locana in the optional rite. || 504 ||

By the statement of the *Br̥hadāraṇyaka* (9.2.1), those two [the *camasa* and the *godohana*] being set aside, the *dhuri* and *locana* [become the vessels]. And it should not be argued: "In that case, although the optional *godohana*—being the primary element—sets aside the obligatory *camasa*, how can there be a setting aside of the obligatory part by the optional part here, given the equality of their status as parts (*aṅgatva*)? For, by the same principle, the optional part also possesses the power to set aside the obligatory part;
just as in the *Jāteṣṭi*, the low-voicedness (*upāṃśutva*), which is a part of the optional sacrifice prescribed by the *Yajñātharvaṇa* passage [sets aside other requirements].
With the middle [portion], he offers the oblations up to the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

(1) Just as this [rule] sets aside the medium pitch (*madhyama-svara*) obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), which was itself established by a specific scriptural statement; (2) therefore,
when performing a *tīrtha-śrāddha* for the sake of a desired result (*kāmya*), [the deities are] Dhuri and Locana.
But when one performs [the rite] solely for the sake of permanence in the absence of desire, then [the deities are] Purūravas and Ārdrava. Also when—with sacrificial food for a month—506.

(1) The section on the fruits of qualities (*guṇaphala*) beginning with *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 1.257a is like the case of the *godohana* vessel; even so, since there is no optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* [in that context], the *dhūrilocana* [deities] are not obtained. Therefore, by relying on the obligatory (*nitya*) rite, those two [deities] are for the sake of the sixfold excellence of the ritual (*karmaṣāḍguṇya*) through the injunction of the fruit of the quality. (2) Nor should it be said: "By the rule of the eighth book (*aṣṭamika-nyāya*), the optional quality as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) does not apply at all to the *tīrtha-śrāddha*, which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇa*. (3) For that rule applies specifically to optional qualities occurring within the middle of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*). (4) However, items such as sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) are common to all *śrāddhas* by virtue of the statements of Manu and others; thus, enough of this.

Thus concludes the discussion regarding what is prescribed and what is prohibited for *tīrtha-śrāddha*, along with matters incidental thereto. Now follows the consideration of *anna-śrāddha*, *hema-śrāddha*, and so forth, as stated in the *Gāruḍa-purāṇa*:
Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform a śrāddha ceremony, providing uncooked grain-food for the twice-born.
Kātyāyana (GaPu 2.15.36a–b):
In times of distress, when there is no fire, at a sacred bathing place, while traveling abroad, or upon the birth of a son.
One should perform an Āmaśrāddha when the menstrual flow of one's wife has just begun.
O lord of men, Sumantu has declared that Brāhmaṇas and others have the right [to perform rites] even in the absence of cooked food,
O mighty-armed one, as well as for those who are without wives due to traveling abroad and other such circumstances.
The wise know that for Śūdras, the *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food) is always prescribed,
as well as when a crisis arises due to one's own circumstances of place or time.
In times of distress, when there is no fire, at a sacred bathing place, while traveling abroad, in the absence of a wife,
and especially during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should give raw food (āmapiṇḍa).
Likewise:
"One should perform a Śrāddha at a sacred ford (tīrtha), especially with cooked food;
it may also be performed with raw grain, gold, or even bulbs, roots, and fruits."
In the absence of these, one should perform [the rite] even with water, out of faith. || 510 ||
Likewise:

"In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born brahmins, during travel abroad, upon the birth of a son, or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform the Hema-śrāddha (the golden śrāddha). || 511 ||
Praśna-khaṇḍa 1. 206. 52

(1) "Thus, among these various forms of speech, the *pāka-śrāddha* (cooked-food śrāddha) is primary; in the absence of cooked food, or in the absence of Brāhmaṇas, the *āma-śrāddha* (uncooked-food śrāddha) is performed; in its absence, the *hema-śrāddha* (gold śrāddha); or else it should be performed according to the practice of the learned (*yathāśiṣṭācāra*). So say Madanapārijāta, Divodāsa, and others. (2) The Easterners also hold this view. (3) However, the authors of the *Smṛtiratnāvalī* and others state: "During an eclipse, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and so forth, the *āma-śrāddha* or the *hema-śrāddha* is primary, and the *pāka-śrāddha* does not take place at all. (4) We consider this latter view to be more reasonable: that near the waters of a sacred ford, one may perform it with uncooked food or gold.
For an *āmaśrāddha* performed always near bodies of water is highly praised;
one who offers a funeral oblation at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) obtains ten times the merit compared to doing so at home. (512)
Because of this statement: (1) however, in the case of the home and so forth, it is with cooked food alone;
(2) but the Southerners perform both, because of the previously mentioned statement, "especially with cooked food" [510];
(3) in this matter, the arrangement is according to local custom.
(4) However, a Śūdra must always perform [the rite] with raw food alone;
for the wise know that for Śūdras, the *śrāddha* is always one of raw offerings (*āma-śrāddha*).
Even a virtuous Śūdra should never feed cooked food to Brahmins.
If he feeds them, he would incur sin and would not obtain the fruit thereof. || 513 ||
Thus it is stated by Sumantu. (1) Regarding the specific rule for the *āma-śrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food), Vyāsa says:
But when giving raw grain, O son of Kuntī, one should give four times as much cooked food.
As for that which was said:
"O son of Kuntī, by giving raw grain, one indeed receives raw grain in double measure. (515)
(1) Thus, this should be understood as applying when one is unable to give with the fourfold qualities. For this very reason it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"O King, if they give raw grain, that should become double;
it may even be triple or quadruple, but one should not offer it with only a single quality."

"It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, provided with all necessary accessories. (1) Herein, each succeeding alternative is more principal than the preceding one. (2) One should give gold eightfold, fourfold, or twofold [the value of the food]. (3) In case of inability, one may give even an equal amount of raw grain or gold. (4) The doubling and so forth are calculated in relation to the man's daily sustenance.
Uśanas:
When one who knows the rules performs an *āmaśrāddha*, the giver of the *śrāddha* should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite for the Brahmin according to the prescribed injunction. (517)
Likewise:
"Whatever rite is prescribed for food that has been prepared, that same rite applies to a śrāddha with raw grain;
all [the rites], beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), as well as the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), should be performed, O Bhārata. (= 525)

Whatever one may give to the twice-born, whether it has been prescribed by the scriptures or not, with that one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite; with that very same substance one should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*). || 518 ||
Likewise:
"When one who knows the rules, endowed with faith, performs an *āmaśrāddha*... (519)

(1) The second half [of the verse] is as before. (2) Invoking the ancestors (*āvāhana*) and other such rites are performed in a *āmāśrāddha* (a śrāddha performed with raw food) on occasions such as the first reception of a child, but not in a *tīrthaśrāddha* (a śrāddha at a sacred bathing place), because its prohibition has been stated therein.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When one performs an *āmāśrāddha*, how should the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍadāna*) be conducted?"
Having taken [the portion] from the household cooking, [he should offer it] with parched grain flour or with milk-rice. || 520 ||

(1) The phrase "the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍadāna*) takes place" is the ellipsis to be supplied. (2) Regarding raw grain, cooked food, roasted barley flour (*saktu*), and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the arrangement is according to what is available.
As for the statement:
"If one should offer the rice-ball with raw [grain], one should feed the Brahmins with cooked [food]."
He who offers raw food prepares a ball of cooked food.
Both of these, declared by Manu, are worthy of hell; of this there is no doubt. || 512 ||
(1) Thus, that refers to the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*) and so forth.

(2) In the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food), the *apośāna* and other rites connected with eating cease because their purpose has been lost, just as the threshing (*avaghāta*) ceases in the case of *kṛṣṇala* berries. As it has been said:
"The inquiry regarding satisfaction (*tṛpti-praśna*), the immersion (*avagāha*), the inquiry regarding enjoyment (*juṣ-praśna*), and 'according to one's pleasure' (*yathāsukham*)."
In the case of an *āmaśrāddha*, this [offering] would not occur; the *apośāna* is the fifth.

(1) ‘Immersing’ refers to the placing of the thumb [into the water]. (2) Furthermore, these two do not occur in the case of an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food). (3) Nor do the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) occur, because it is a *tīrtha-śrāddha* (a śrāddha at a sacred site). (4) However, in the case of a *pāka-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with cooked food), the distinction is that only the rites beginning with the invocation are omitted.
In the case of a *hema-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with gold), there is also the cessation of the *piṇḍas* (rice balls). || 523 ||
Thus says Divodāsa. (1) However, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, there is an option.

(2) In the case of an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha performed with raw food), there is even the modification (*ūha*) of certain mantras. For this very reason, Marīci states: "The mantras are to be modified at the invocation (*āvāhana*), at the utterance of *svadhā*, and at the dismissal (*visarjana*)."
They are not to be modified for other rites; this is remembered as the rule for the *āmaśrāddha*.

(1) In the invocation (*āvāhana*), in the mantra "O Pitṛs, come to eat the oblation" (*pitṝn haviṣe attava*), the word *attava* ("to eat") is to be modified to the word *svīkartave* ("to accept"). (2) In the utterance of *svadhā*, in the mantra "Salutation to you, O Pitṛs; [grant] food" (*namo vaḥ pitara iṣa*), the word *iṣa* ("food") is to be modified to *āmāya* ("for raw flesh/food"). (3) In the dismissal (*visarjana*), in the mantra "In strength, in strength... (*vāje vāja*), where it says "being satisfied, go by the paths traveled by the gods" (*tṛptā yāta pathibhir devayānaiḥ*), the past passive participle suffix *-ta-* in the word *tṛptāḥ* ("satisfied") is to be replaced by the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) as *tṛpyata* ("be satisfied"). (4) Although the modification of a Ṛgvedic verse (*ṛgyūha*) is prohibited by the rule, "Indeed, that syllable of the Ṛc becomes putrid which one modifies" (*pūyati vā etad ṛco ‘kṣaraṃ yad enad ūhati*), nevertheless, such a modification occurs on account of the specific statement in the verse "In strength, in strength, O Vāta... (*vāje vāje ‘vate*). (5) In this same manner, in expressions such as "this food" (*idam annam*), one should understand the modification to be "this raw flesh" (*idam āmam*), and so forth. (6) Regarding "other rites," the meaning of Marīci’s statement is that there is no modification in mantras such as "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering" (*viṣṇo havyaṃ rakṣasva*).

(7) "Clothing, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth should indeed be given according to one's ability even in the case of both *āmāśrāddha* and *siddhānna-śrāddha*; for the rule that applies to a *siddhānna-śrāddha* is the same rule that applies to an *āmāśrāddha*," according to the statement of Sumantu.
(1) But when many Brahmins are not available, then the Śrāddha should be performed even by one alone;

in the absence of food or in the absence of twice-born ones, at a great festival (mahālaya) which has the nature of a sacred ford (tīrtha), food is offered to a single person, while the water-offerings (arghya) and the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) are given separately for each. 526.
Because of this statement:

(1) when not even a single person can be found, then the *śrāddha* should be performed upon a bundle of *darbha* grass, and one should cast the food into fire or similar elements; for in the absence of a recipient, a man, having completed the entire ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), [should proceed thus].
Or, having placed darbha-grass mats upon the seats, he should remain composed in meditation.
One should perform the ritual procedure joined with the primary and secondary injunctions;
in the absence of all [materials], one should cast it into the fire, or give it to a cow, or else into the waters.
There is no loss whatsoever for one who has obtained it, especially in the case of that which is ancestral.

Thus it is stated by Devala. (1) Regarding the phrase "connected with the primary and secondary directions," the meaning is that one should personally utter the questions and responses such as, "Is the *śrāddha* completed? and "It is well completed. (2) This applies to the case of a *śrāddha* consisting of cooked food (*anna*). (3) However, in the cases of raw food (*āma*) or gold (*hema*), having performed the entire *śrāddha*, one should give that material to a Brāhmaṇa at a later time. (4) Furthermore, this *āma-śrāddha* should be performed immediately upon reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in the forenoon, provided that it is possible.
The *āmaśrāddha* is performed in the forenoon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday,
the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi*) in the morning.

Thus it is stated by Hārīta. (1) However, in the case of an accidental occurrence, it was previously stated that [the rite] may take place even at another time, in accordance with the specific cause characterized by such an occasion. (2) If, however, one is unable to perform the *śrāddha* at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) by any means whatsoever, then the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) with barley flour (*saktu*) and so forth must certainly be performed.
