For this very reason, the *Devīpurāṇa*, while discussing the *śrāddha*, states that since the offering of the rice-balls is already implied: "But the offering of the rice-balls is commended and indeed dear to the ancestors. (529 = 381)
(1) Thus, moreover, the "mere lump" has been stated separately. (2) Otherwise, there would be the threefold fault of enumerating other [unauthorized] limbs. Devala says:
When the day of the śrāddha has arrived, if there is an absence of both wealth and provisions, one should offer merely a ball of food; or indeed, one may even remain without eating at all.
Thus it is said. Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"He who, practicing deceit regarding his wealth, shall not offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas)... [531]

(1) In the statement of the ancestors (*Viṣṇupurāṇa* 3.14.22c–d), only the *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) is mentioned. (2) By this very indicative mark, the offering of the *piṇḍa* at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) is also a primary rite, just like the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha.
(3) And the substances for the *piṇḍa* are as follows:
In the Devīpurāṇa:

"The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) should be performed with roasted barley flour (saktu), or with parched grain (saṃyāva), or with milk-rice (pāyasa); it has been declared by the sages that it may also be done with oil-cake (piṇyāka) or with iṅguda fruit. (532)

(1) Or there is the reading “guḍena vai. (2) *Saṃyāva* is a preparation made from wheat. (3) *Piṇyāka* is sesame paste. (4) *Iṅguda* is the fruit of the *tāpasa* tree. (5) In this context, it should be understood that each subsequent item is to be used only when the preceding one is unavailable. Satyavrata says:
“But with vegetables, roots, fruits, and cooked food, or with clothing, cattle, land, and gold...”
Or, through a conversation with the waters, one may bring about the gratification of the ancestors. || 533 ||

(1) Regarding the consultation with a Brahmin (*viprasaṃvāda*): in the absence of [other] Brahmins, one should say to a Brahmin, "May the *śrāddha* performed by me today be effective," and the Brahmin should reply, "So be it. Such is the form [of this consultation].
(2) And regarding the size of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), Aṅgiras says: "One should offer rice-balls according to the prescribed rule, measuring either a wood-apple (*kapittha*) or a bilva fruit."
Or [the size] of a hen's egg, or equal in measure to Āmalaka fruits.
"Or one endowed with faith may give even those equal in size to a *bādara* fruit. (534) Thus it is said.
(1) Even when unable to do so here, offerings of a subtle measure should also be given;
"one should offer a *piṇḍa* at Gayāśiras even in the measure of a *śamī* leaf. (535)
From this indicative mark (liṅga);
and furthermore—
Sesame, food, water, incense, a lamp, milk, honey, and ghee mixed with sugar—this is called the eightfold offering (aṣṭāṅga). || 536 ||
Likewise:

"The washing, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), the subsequent re-washing, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the formal declaration regarding the food—this is the sequence for Śrāddhas performed at sacred bathing places (tīrthas). (537)
Thus says Vṛddhaśloka:

(1) At a śrāddha performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas); however, one should give those cakes to a cow, a goat, or to Brahmins, or even cast them into fire or water. || 538 ||
The interpretation stated by Yājñavalkya in verse 1.256ab should not be followed; rather, there must be an actual casting [of the pindas] into the water:
"In a *tīrtha*-śrāddha, one who is composed should always cast the pindas into the sacred ford (*tīrtha*)."
Facing the south is proclaimed to be the direction of the ancestors (pitryā dik).
Because of this statement,
it was explained in the context of the *śrāddha* that the prohibition applied by Nanda and others does not apply to the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
However, when one is unable to perform even the offering of rice balls, then the libation (*tarpaṇa*) must also necessarily be performed.
Bowing with devotion, he will offer a handful of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds upon the ground, dedicating it to us.
Having obtained it from anywhere at all, or even from cows for the daily cow-offering (gavāhnika), [one should perform the rite]. || 540 ||
Because of the statement regarding the ancestors (*pitr̥*) joined with the word "also" (*api*) in ViPu 3.14.27–28b:

(1) this being so, the summary is as follows—(2) one who is capable should perform all three: libation (*tarpaṇa*), the *śrāddha* rite, and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*); (3) one who is incapable [of all] should perform libation and the rice-balls; (4) one who is even more incapable may perform libation alone.

Furthermore, when many intermediate holy sites (*avāntara-tīrtha*) located within a single great pilgrimage site (*mahātīrtha*), such as Kāśī, can be visited on a single day, then even on that one day, many *śrāddha* rites must be performed according to the sequence of their respective occasions (*nimitta*), due to the distinction between those occasions—just as one performs both the *darśa-śrāddha* and the *uparāga-śrāddha* [on the same day]. As for the statement of Pracetas:
"One should never perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day;
nor should one perform the *na-hanti*, the fire-oblation (*homa*), Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), or the water-libation (*tarpaṇa*). (541)
(1) Thus, that [prohibition] refers to the case of a *śrāddha* performed for the same cause. Regarding this, Jābāli says:
"Having performed a *śrāddha* for a specific person, one should not perform another *śrāddha* for that same person on that very day;
however, an occasional (*naimittika*) *śrāddha* must be performed when the occasion arises in its proper sequence. (542)
Kātyāyana also says: "Two or many omens may arise on a single day; the rites performed in response to those omens should be carried out according to the sequence in which they occurred. (543)
Elsewhere it is also stated:
"But one should not perform a *śrāddha* on a single day for more than one occasion.

(1) However, regarding fasting (*upavāsa*) and tonsure (*muṇḍana*), they are performed only once, because they are prescribed as being delimited by the specific adjuncts of pervasive holy sites (*tīrtha*) such as Prayāga and Kāśī.

(2) However, where by performing a *śrāddha* at a specific sub-tirtha (*vyāpyatīrtha*), the *śrāddha* for the encompassing tirtha (*vyāpakatīrtha*) is also accomplished, there is no repetition for each individual occasion (*pratinimittam āvṛttiḥ*). (3) Rather, because no distinction is perceived as to which [specific rite] has been performed and which has not—due to the identity of place, time, and agent, and the non-difference of the materials and the deities—the accomplishment of the various *śrāddhas* occurs through a single performance (*tantrataḥ*). (4) This is, for example, the case with rites occasioned by the Gaṅgā-veṇī and Prayāga, and those occasioned by the Gaṅgā, Kāśī, and Maṇikarṇikā, and so forth.

(5) "But surely, because of the statement, 'And it must be performed only when [the place] has been reached' [324], one would first obtain the *śrāddha* occasioned by the encompassing (*vyāpaka*) holy site (*tīrtha*) precisely upon reaching [it] within a limit of five *krośas* or more; whereas upon reaching the location of the encompassed (*vyāpya*) holy site, that occasioned by it would come later. Thus, due to the difference in place and time, how can there be a single performance (*tantratā*)? (6) It is not so. Just as the lifelong injunction mentioned in the texts is restricted by the specific occasions of evening, morning, full moon, and new moon, so too, by way of delimitation through various principal holy sites such as Maṇikarṇikā, there is the instruction for the initial bath, *śrāddha*, and so forth.

[Page 138] This is because the scope of the causal factor known as "attainment" (*prāpti*), which is mentioned in the statement "only by those who have attained [the goal]" due to the force of the sentence, is restricted. For instance, there is the speech of Vyāsa in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"Listen, O highly wise Lomaharṣaṇa, I shall tell you how the pilgrimage must first be performed with joy by those who go on pilgrimage."

Having first bathed with his clothes on in the waters of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī pond, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods, as well as to the Brāhmaṇas, according to the prescribed rules.

(1) And so forth. Likewise, because the attainment of Kāśī as delimited by the preeminent holy site named Maṇikarṇikā serves as the instrumental cause, there is no distinction of place or time; thus, the principle of "tantratā" (unification) is logical. (2) The same applies to Prayāga and other such sites.

(3) "But if [the place] characterized in this way is the occasion (*nimitta*), then since there is no difference in the occasion itself, the contingency of distinct *śrāddhas* does not arise; so for whom would there be a commonality (*tantratā*)? (4) True, however, even in the case of the *śrāddha* at Maṇikarṇikā and other such places, because of statements that teach the excellence of distinct fruits, its attainment also constitutes the occasion for a distinct *śrāddha*. (5) For example, in the case of the full moon and new moon sacrifices, there is the delimitation of the occasion by the name "living" (*jīvana*), and yet, according to such injunctions as "He who [performs] the *iṣṭi*," there is also the status of being the time for independent *iṣṭis*; likewise here too, by virtue of two types of scriptural statements, Maṇikarṇikā and the rest will serve both as the delimitation of the occasion and as the occasion for independent *śrāddhas*, according to the principle of the distinctness of conjunctions (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*).

(6) In reality, however, when the occasion for the rite has been restricted and one fails to reach Maṇikarṇikā or other such places due to obstacles, the occasion itself remains unfulfilled; consequently, the occasional *śrāddha* would simply not be performed. (7) Therefore, it is precisely in the *śrāddha* occasioned by reaching Kāśī and so forth that a specific location such as Maṇikarṇikā is prescribed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*). (8) Thus, because the rite is mandatory by virtue of being occasioned, even if one does not reach [the ideal] place, the *śrāddha* must still be performed—even if deficient in its auxiliary factor of location—since the occasion itself has occurred. This is the general direction of the argument. (9) Therefore, there is indeed the attainment of multiple [auxiliaries].

(10) If it is argued: "Is it not the case that *tantra* (common performance) is observed only among subsidiary elements such as the *prayāja* offerings, which are encompassed by a single injunction for performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*), and not even among independent primary rites? (11) Oh, how foolish is one who clings only to what is directly perceived! For he does not consider the state of *tantra* in the following cases: the commonality of results in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and *Rājasūya*; in the *Sāṃnāyya* offering, where the two primary sacrifices—consisting of the dedication to a deity and the renunciation (*tyāga*)—have the same recipient deity; in the *Jāteṣṭi* performed upon the birth of twin sons; in the *Pakṣahoma*, where there are multiple homas; in the *Kṣāmavatī* offerings when multiple houses are burned simultaneously; and in the Smārta *Śrāddhas* performed on occasions such as the *Saṃkrānti* or the new moon, where all the primary acts arise simultaneously because, due to the unity of place and other factors, no distinction is perceived, and thus the production of all *apūrvas* occurs through a single performance. It is precisely because he fails to observe this state of *tantra* that he asserts that *tantra* applies only to the *itikartavyatā* (the procedural details).

(12) Therefore, having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): “I shall perform the *śrāddha* for the sake of Kāśī and for the sake of Maṇikarṇikā simultaneously (*tantraṇa*),” one should perform only a single *śrāddha*. (13) However, when the preceding time has nearly arrived and the *śrāddha* has not yet been performed at the Gaṅgā, then one should also say: “and the *śrāddha* for the Gaṅgā. (14) The same applies to Prayāga, Gayā, and other such places.

(15) Some, however, say: "Since the pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*) that encompasses Kāśī and others is itself the intended object (*uddeśya*), and since pilgrimage sites such as Maṇikarṇikā—which are subsumed under it—are mentioned in that context, there is a specific inclusion known as 'falling within that' (*tanmadhyapāta*). Therefore, just as the *prayāja* offerings of the animal sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśa*) are accomplished through the *prayāja* offerings performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice, or as the obligatory *śrāddha* of the dark fortnight is accomplished by the optional *agnihotra*, so too the *śrāddha* that is subsumed is accomplished by the very same *śrāddha* of the encompassing [site] like Kāśī through the principle of incidental accomplishment (*prasaṅga*). Thus, one should simply form the resolve: 'I shall perform the *śrāddha* occasioned by reaching Kāśī.'"

(16) As for the claim that "neither a primary injunction (*tantra*) nor an incidental application (*prasaṅga* applies here); rather, there is only one *śrāddha* occasioned by the attainment of Kāśī and other sites due to the restriction of the occasion. The teaching regarding separate fruits, however, will refer either to *śrāddhas* performed within the context of the Five Tīrthas and so forth—such as at Maṇikarṇikā—or to those *śrāddhas* performed independently," (17) that is not correct. For even when the occasion consisting of the attainment of a pervasive sacred site exists, there is no reason to set aside the *śrāddha* occasioned by that [specific] site. (18) Furthermore, there is evidence for the opposite case. (19) Nor is the hearing of the mention of separate fruits restricted to the *śrāddha* performed at Maṇikarṇikā and other sites included within the Five Tīrthas and so forth.

(20) Because the bathing, *śrāddha*, and other rites contained therein, when combined with the others, are satisfied by the fruit mentioned in the injunction for the performance of the whole complex—just like the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice occurring within the *Rājasūya*—there is no lack of a fruit for the whole, and thus no desire for a separate fruit. (21) Nor is there a scriptural mention of a separate fruit concerning an independent *śrāddha*, because it would be cumbersome to enjoin another *śrāddha* for the sake of a different fruit. (22) But in our view, since the *śrāddha* occasioned by [the death] has already been established, [the rule applies]: "But because of proximity, there is no division. (Jaiminisūtra 3.3.14).

By the principle stated in *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* 2.3.13.26, namely, "One should cause one who desires food to sacrifice with this [offering]," only the connection with the fruit is established, which constitutes parsimony (*lāghava*).

Therefore, the *śrāddha* at Maṇikarṇikā and other sites is twofold, like the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice: (3) as a subordinate element alongside others, and (4) as an independent rite. Of these, the first is included within the *Pañcatīrthī* and similar rites; the second, however, is occasioned by specific circumstances (*prāptinimittaka*).

(6) In that case, since there is no reason for the omission of the subsequent [rite], it is logical that its accomplishment occurs through *tantra* or *prasaṅga* according to the method already stated.

(7) Furthermore, the fact that even a single [action] serves as the means for multiple results should be established—just like the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice—on the basis of differences in application (*prayoga*) and differences in delimiting factors (*avacchedaka*). (8) This applies everywhere; enough with further elaboration.
[p.140] Now, the determination regarding the conjunction of other *śrāddha* rites.
(9) In that regard, if the annual śrāddha falls on the same day as the arrival at a sacred ford (tīrtha), then it should be performed separately. As it is stated in the *Kālādarśa*:

"In the case of annual śrāddhas and rites prescribed for specific astrological conjunctions (*alabhyayoga*), when they coincide, one should perform two śrāddhas because of the difference in deities. (547)
(1) Even there, first is that occasioned by a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), because it must be performed immediately upon arrival and thus admits of no delay;
(2) afterwards is the annual (*vārṣika*) rite.

(3) However, as for those rites occasioned by the new moon (*dārśika*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the beginnings of the *yugas* and *manvantaras*, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), and so forth—if a *tīrtha-śrāddha* is performed with raw grain (*āma*) or gold, then these [other rites] must be performed separately; for since they are accomplished through cooked offerings (*pakva*), there is a difference in the substance (*dravya-bheda*), and thus the principle of "incidental performance" (*prasaṅga*) does not apply. (4) But when the *tīrtha-śrāddha* is performed with cooked food alone, then because there is no difference in the substance and because all the deities [of the other rites] are intended to be worshipped in the *tīrtha-śrāddha* itself, their accomplishment occurs through that *tīrtha-śrāddha* alone by virtue of *prasaṅga*—this applies to the new moon, the *yuga*-beginnings, and the *yoga*s obtainable on the new moon day.
One should offer a reply because, by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), the other [point] is also established. (548)
Thus it is stated in the *Kālādarśa*. (1) Here, the word "dārśika" (pertaining to the new moon sacrifice) is indicative of all [rites] that follow the same logic.

(2) Even the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*), if performed with raw food (*āma*) or gold, is distinct from the *tīrthika* [śrāddha], because its substance consists of cooked food (*pakvadravya*). As for the fact that the deities of the daily *śrāddha* are intended in the *nāndīmukha* and *tīrtha* śrāddhas—
Since it is established by way of logical implication (prasaṅga), the eternal śrāddha (nitya-śrāddha) should not be performed separately. || 549 ||
(1) Thus it was stated by Hemādri; that should be understood to apply when the *tīrtha-śrāddha* is performed with cooked food (*anna*). This is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"One should not perform the obligatory *śrāddha* where it is accomplished as a matter of course."
If another *śrāddha* has been performed elsewhere, one should not omit that [obligatory rite] because it is mandatory. || 550 ||
[Page 141] Thus:

(1) When, however, due to some cause or lack of capacity, one desires to perform all the rites pertaining to the full moon (*dārśika*) and so forth using raw grain (*āmam*) or gold (*heman*), then success is achieved through the *tīrtha-śrāddha* performed with raw grain or gold; such determinations are to be made by one’s own intelligence.
(2) This *śrāddha* occasioned by a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is mandatory upon reaching the sacred ford after ten months have passed.
(3) However, if [the rite] is performed or left unperformed due to a desire for a specific fruit, one should go again to a sacred ford after a year less two months;
then, one should diligently perform the tonsure and the fasting. 551 (= 278)

(1) Because it is stated in words joined with the term *yatna* (effort), and because it follows the same logical principle as shaving and other such acts; or (2) because it is included by means of the word *ca* (and);
(3) however, the elders maintain that bathing, libations, and so forth occur at all times.

Thus ends the consideration of *tīrtha-śrāddha* (ancestral rites at sacred sites), along with its ancillaries, within the section on general rules in the *Tristhalīsetu* composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara Sūri.
Now, regarding those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* at sacred fords (*tīrtha*):
there, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the water-rites (*udaka-kriyā*) for the father must be performed by the son.
In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall [inherit]; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother. || 552 ||
According to the statement of Kātyāyana, "Śaṅkha 188," it is said:
"The son, the grandson, or the great-grandson, or the brother, or the brother's descendant."
Or even the lineage of sapindas, O King, becomes worthy of the śrāddha rite. || 553 ||

(1) From this statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, it follows that sons and others possess the qualification [to perform the rite]. (2) Likewise, other general qualifications should be understood from other texts. (3) However, there is a specific rule: even one whose father is still living may perform a *śrāddha* at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). This is stated in the *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*:

At a wedding, at the birth of a son, at a śrāddha for the ancestors, at a Soma sacrifice, at a sacred ford, and when a Brahmin arrives—these six occasions [for giving] occur while the father is still alive. (554)
MaitPari, pp. 236–7:

(1) “Marriage” here refers to the second [rite] and those following, because the father alone has authority over the first. (2) “Upon the birth of a son” means at the *jātakarman* rite. (3) This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to offspring. (4) “At the ancestral sacrifice” (*pitryeṣṭi*) refers to that which occurs within the *Cāturmāsya* cycle.

(5) ‘In a Soma sacrifice’: when the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) takes place beneath one’s own cup (*camasa*) with portions of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) belonging to the third pressing (*tārtīyasavanika*).

(6) ‘When a Brāhmaṇa arrives’: upon the arrival of a learned Brahmin endowed with qualities such as being a *trimadhu* or a *trisuparṇaka*. (7) ‘While the father is living’: the meaning is that these are the six occasions for Śrāddha for a son.
(8) Thus, since Śrāddha would apply to every sacred ford (*tīrtha*), Laugākṣi states an exception regarding Gayā:
One whose father is living should not perform the Darśa-śrāddha, the Gayā-śrāddha, or the śrāddha of the dark fortnight, nor should he perform libations with black sesame seeds.

Also in the *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*: "In all great rivers and at all sacred fords, except for Gayā, one may perform the *śrāddha* according to the rules of the *pārvaṇa* rite even while one's father is still living. (556)

Regarding one whose mother has died, however, in the context of arriving at Gayā as a matter of circumstance, a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is heard in the *Pariśiṣṭa* concerning the *mātṛśrāddha*:
"The *ānvaṣṭakya* [offering], upon reaching Gayā, and that which is performed on the anniversary of death..."
A son should perform the śrāddha for his mother even while his father is still alive. || 557 ||
In this passage from the *Maitrāyaṇīya Pariśiṣṭa* (p. 237):

(1) by the phrase “when there is an arrival at Gayā,” an incidental arrival is stated; (2) when that [arrival] occurs, the *śrāddha* for one’s mother should be performed, but not by going there specifically for that purpose. For this very reason, another *Smṛti* states:
“Having gone to Gayā incidentally, one should perform the *śrāddha* for one’s mother. (558)

(1) Consequently, many authorities such as the authors of the *Kālādarśa* and the *Smṛtidarpaṇa* have held that "in a sacred site other than Gayā, one whose father is living should perform the *śrāddha* with the intention to be described; (2) however, if one goes to Gayā incidentally while his mother is deceased, he should then perform only the *pārvaṇa* for his mother; (3) but one whose mother is not deceased should not. (4) Others, however, maintain the following systematic arrangement of the texts: because the injunctions prescribing the *śrāddha* for one whose father is living are general, even at Gayā, one whose father is living should perform the *śrāddha* for his father, grandfather, and so forth, as will be described. (5) And although the *śrāddha* for the mother is accomplished in this *śrāddha* by virtue of her being the wife of the father, the statement beginning with "the *ānvaṣṭakya*" is intended to ensure the separate performance of the *pārvaṇa* rite in her capacity as "mother" and so on. (6) As for those texts prohibiting the *śrāddha* at Gayā, they mean that even one whose mother is deceased should not go there specifically for the purpose of that *śrāddha*, but only if he is traveling there incidentally. Thus they explain the settled rule of these texts.

(7) Thus, since the rule for the formulation of the statement exists in both ways, the determination is made according to local custom. (8) In either case, it is established that one whose father is still living has the entitlement to perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha*. And so, as for the claim that one whose father is living has no entitlement to the ancestral rites (*pitr-kṛtya*), [it is refuted].
For according to the Vedic revelation, one should not give anything away by bypassing a living person. || 559 ||
This is the statement of Kātyāyana in KātŚS 2.16.12 [p. 144], and that which pertains to the ancestors has not been mentioned for one whose father is still living. || 560 ||
(1) Thus, that statement from the *Nigama* refers to times other than the six [specific] periods prescribed therein.

(2) "But if one whose father is still living has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, then when the father is residing at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), the son who has arrived from another land ought to perform the *śrāddha*, since the occasion (*nimitta*) has occurred. (3) We say that it indeed ought to be performed, as there is no obstacle (*bādhaka*). (4) "In that case, why is it not performed even by one who has come together with his father? (5) It is replied: it would certainly follow from the scriptural injunction (*vacana*), but it is not practiced because it is loathed by the world (*lokavidviṣṭa*).
As it has been said:
"One should not practice even that which is dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.156c–d).

If it is asked, "Why is there no performance [of the rite] on the grounds of *prasaṅga* (incidental extension), since it is established by what was performed for the ancestors?"—the answer is: No, because there is no *prasaṅga* when the agents are different.
(3) Thus it is established that even one whose father is still living has the entitlement to perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha*.

(4) However, if brothers have separated, whether they go to the sacred site simultaneously or not, then each should perform the *śrāddha* separately. (5) But among those who are undivided, the rite must be performed by whichever one among them has gone. (6) In the case of a joint journey (*sahagamana*), however, it is to be done by the eldest alone, as in the case of the taking [of the bride] and so forth, and not by all of them. As Manu says:
"For brothers who are undivided, a single religious duty prevails."
If there were a division, then their dharma too would be separate and distinct for each.
In the *Pradīpa*:
"But those who have divided [the property] shall perform [rites] such as the annual anniversary separately;
when it has been performed by even one among those who have not divided, it is considered performed by all. (563)
(1) But if a widow has sons and has gone to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha), then she must not perform it at all;
a Śrāddha for her husband should never be performed by one who has sons. || 564 ||
Because of this statement: "(1) But for one who is childless, it must certainly be performed;
a childless wife is like a son. [p.145] || 565 ||
Because of this statement.

However, some say: "(1) Even for a woman who has sons, if her sons are not present, she should have the *saṃkalpa-śrāddha* performed through the mediation of Brahmins and others. (2) And in the *saṃkalpa-śrāddha*, the following items are to be avoided—"

Vasiṣṭha: One should avoid these six elements in the formal ritual resolve (saṅkalpa): the invocation, the utterance of "svadhā," the rice-ball offering (piṇḍa), the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the scattering of food (vikira), and the presentation of the rice-balls (piṇḍadāna). || 566 ||
(1) They say that "piṇḍa" means a remnant-ball of food. (2) The source for this must be sought. (3) Even one who has not been initiated may perform a śrāddha at a sacred ford;
and even one who has not been initiated may perform this on all festival days.
The Śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa bestows the fruits of all desires.
O King, even a Śūdra who is separated from his wife or living in exile, provided he is devoted, may perform [the rite] without mantras according to this procedure.

This is because it is stated in the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Pādma Purāṇa*, beginning with the section on *tīrtha-śrāddha* and related rites: (1) In that regard, a woman and one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) should have the rite performed through a Brāhmaṇa according to local custom, or they may perform it themselves without mantras. This is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*:
"An uninitiated person, women, and Śūdras should have the *śrāddha* performed by a priest, or they may perform it themselves without mantras."

They should perform [the rites] by means of the name and the lineage, or else with the two mantras: “Obeisance to the gods” (namo devebhyaḥ) and “Svadhā obeisance to the ancestors” (svadhā namaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ).

(1) However, the specific distinction regarding the *kṣetraja* and others is not stated here; rather, it concerns the formal adoption (*parigraha*) of the *datta*, *aurasa*, and other sons as sons. 569.
(1) Thus, because other sons are excluded as being of no use in the Kali age;
likewise—
whosoever seizes the wife or the wealth of another shall perform [the funeral rites] for that person.
Those who have abducted a woman or stolen wealth shall perform the rites of offering funeral cakes and water. || 570 ||
Thus, according to the statement of Kārṣṇājini.
(1) In this way, other qualified persons are also to be understood from other texts. (2) However, some will become clear even here in the *Sampradānanirṇaya*.
[p.147] Now follows the exception to the qualification (*adhikārāpavāda*).
(3) In that regard, the ascetic has no duty; the mendicant monk should not perform birth-impurity rites, ancestral offerings, or the ritual of water-libations for the pinda.
For by means of the yoga of renunciation, he has abandoned the vows and duties pertaining to household life and the like.
The entire lineage beginning with the clan, as well as the family of the father and mother and one's wealth; || 571 ||
Thus it is from the Smṛti:
"Even one who has fallen [from caste] should not perform [these acts]; for falling away from the duties of the twice-born is what constitutes 'falling'. (572)

Because of the prohibition by this statement; however, one who has committed an *upapātaka* (minor sin) and so forth must certainly perform it, since there is no prohibition against such persons performing obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
Thus ends the section on those entitled to perform *tīrtha-śrāddha* within the General Section of the *Tristhalīsetu*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara Sūri.
[148] Now follows the determination of the recipients at a *śrāddha* performed at sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
In that regard:
"At riverbanks, at sacred fords, on fertile ground, and likewise on mountain ridges..."
And the ancestors, together with the gods, are satisfied by what is given in secluded places.
As stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa (KūP 2.22.15):
"After the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, wherever [an offering] is given..."
In that case, the pārvaṇa rite must be performed; the ekoddiṣṭa rite is never to be done.

(1) Because of this statement, the *pārvaṇa* rite for the father and others must first be performed; (2) thereafter, the *pārvaṇa* rite for the maternal grandfather and others as well, according to the principle that "wherever the fathers are honored, there the maternal grandfathers are also."
It should be performed without distinction; otherwise, through such distinction, one goes to hell. || 575 ||
According to this statement by Gautama:
"Excluding the *karṣū-samanvita* [funeral rite], the other sixteen *śrāddhas*, and the annual *pratyābdika*, there shall be six *piṇḍas* in the remaining cases; such is the established rule. (576)
And because of the statement by Kātyāyana, "Kāt 3. 24.
14," the authors of the Smṛtiratnāvalī and others have held that, "In sacred fords other than Gayā, there is only the rite of the six deities."

(2) Others, however, having commenced the general śrāddha for [deceased] relatives such as those at sacred sites, should take a handful from the remains of the oblation and, being attentive, perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for the wives of the ancestors one by one in due order. || 577 ||
(1) Thus, based on the statement of Devala, some maintain that the *pārvaṇa* rite for the mother should also be performed.
(2) However, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated that in that case, a separate *śrāddha* for the mother is recommended. || 578 ||
(1) By saying this, it is stated that [the rite] may be performed or not performed.
(2) However, we shall explain right there that the *pārvaṇa* rite for one’s mother and others is mandatory at Gayā.
And this should be offered at the western part of the rice-balls for the father and the others. || 579 ||
Thus says Śāṅkhāyana. (1) In this way, it becomes a rite for nine deities.
(2) Others, however, say that the Pārvaṇa for the maternal grandmother and others is also separate; some great sages desire a separate Śrāddha for women. 580.
(1) Thus, because it is stated generally for women as well in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "The [rite] with nine deities, such as the father and others, and likewise that with twelve deities... (581).
And because of the statement in the *Agnipurāṇa* (115.10a-b): "(1) the word 'tathā' has the sense of an alternative; (2) and thus it becomes dedicated to twelve deities;
(3) in this matter, the settled rule is determined by the traditional practice of the learned in that region."

(4) In that case, when the mother and maternal grandmother are not present separately for the *pārvaṇa* rite, then in the invocations (*nigama*), the father and others, as well as the maternal grandfather and others, should be designated together with their wives;
for "the mother partakes of the *śrāddha* along with her own husband like nectar;
and so does the paternal grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother. (582)
Regarding *Br̥ha* (Śrā) 75 (1):
since it is stated that the mother and others possess the status of deities by virtue of being accompanied by the father and others,
[the rite] on the day of death consists of the *Anvaṣṭakā* as well as the *Mātṛ-śrāddha*.
Likewise, apart from the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, there shall be no other separate [funeral] ceremony for women. || 583 ||
(1) Thus, because Śaṅkha prohibits a separate *śrāddha* while simultaneously permitting that it should not be separate;

(2) even in the case where a separate *śrāddha* for the mother and others is adopted, if they have performed *sahagamana* (self-immolation following the husband), then one should feed an odd number of Brahmins together, dedicating the rite to both the husband and them; (3) and a single *piṇḍa* should be offered, dedicated to both—such is the performance in brief.

On the anniversary of death, the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) is performed briefly and separately; however, for a husband and wife, the Navaśrāddha is performed only when she follows him in cremation (anvārohaṇa).

Thus, according to the statement of Laugākṣi: (1) this is the meaning: when the husband and wife perform *anvārohaṇa* (ascension after death), even though the date of death (*mṛtatithi*) is the same for both, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*)—that is, the *piṇḍa* and the *śrāddha*—is performed collectively (*samāsena*), as in the case of a *śrāddha* for two ancestors, according to the method already described. (2) However, the *navaśrāddha* (the nine *śrāddhas* performed before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*) is performed separately and not collectively. (3) Here, because of the specific mention of "the day of death" (*mṛtāhani*), if there is a difference in the dates of death, there is no collective performance; rather, they must be performed separately.

(4) Here, because the separate performance is prescribed specifically for the *navaśrāddha* (the funeral rites during the first ten days), it is understood through restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) that a combined performance is intended for the *darśa*, the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*), and the *tīrtha-śrāddha* and so forth. (5) The same should be understood regarding the practice of *anvārohaṇa* (the widow ascending the funeral pyre) even when there are multiple [widows]. And as another *smṛti* states:
“If a husband and wife have met their death by ascending the same funeral pyre, one should perform their *śrāddha* separately, and offer the cooked rice (*odana*) separately for each. (585)

(1) Thus, authors such as Madanapārijātakāra hold that this refers specifically to the *nava-śrāddha* (the nine śrāddhas performed during the first year). (2) Hemādri and others, however, maintain that—in order to avoid the fault of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) and in accordance with the literal meaning of the term "*mṛtāhani*" (on the anniversary of death)—this refers exclusively to the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) śrāddha.
(3) Therefore, they conclude that at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and the like, [the śrāddha] should be offered separately.

(4) Likewise, one should also offer [the śrāddha] at a sacred site for the co-mother (*sapatnamātṛ*), the co-paternal grandmother (*sapatnapitāmahī*), and the co-paternal great-grandmother (*sapatnaprapitāmahī*).
All the wives of the fathers are mothers. || 586 ||

(1) Thus, because Sumantu has extended [the status of] motherhood and so forth even to those [other women], (2) there too, in the case of the Brāhmaṇa who stands in the place of the mother and the like, as well as in their *piṇḍa*, they are also designated, but not separately. For it is said:
"He who has many mothers should offer the *arghya* separately at the *tīrtha* during the fortnight of the waning moon, but he should offer only a single *piṇḍa*. (587)

Thus it is stated by Gālava. (1) However, the learned (śiṣṭas), considering this [rule] to pertain to those who are incapable [of performing the rites], perform the *śrāddha* and the *piṇḍa* offerings separately. (2) Likewise, a *śrāddha* must also be performed for the maternal grandfathers on the father’s side (*sapatna-mātāmaha*), because Sumantu has extended the status of "mother" to the wives of one's mother, and thus the fathers of those wives also acquire the derivative status of "maternal grandfather" by implication. (3) All of this has been stated by Hemādri in the *Śrāddhakalpa*.

(4) However, when one performs a *śrāddha* with the desire to satisfy various ancestors on a distinguished occasion such as the *mahālaya*, or at a specific sacred site (*tīrtha*) such as Gayā, then a *śrāddha* must also be performed for the co-wives of one's mother—whether they have sons or are sonless.

(5) Even for those women who have sons, because of compassion or affection toward the son of a co-wife, there exists a partial entitlement [to perform the *śrāddha*] for him as well. (6) By this very principle, the wives of the grandfather other than one’s own mother, and the wives of the great-grandfather other than the great-grandmother, are also explained. (7) By defining the stepmothers as secondary mothers (*gauṇamātṛ*), it is also established that their fathers likewise possess only a secondary status as maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) in the *śrāddha* rite. (8) However, when one desires to perform a *śrāddha* at a specific place or time with the wish to satisfy various ancestors, it is settled that one may perform it for them even by virtue of a partial entitlement.
(9) One should also perform [the rite] for paternal uncles and sons; (10) and for teachers and others:
"To teachers, gurus, and disciples, to friends and kinsmen, and likewise to all their wives, one should offer handfuls of water."
A man should always offer rice-balls to them individually during the month of Bhādrapada, at all sacred fords, and in the month of Māgha under the Maghā asterism. || 588 ||

Thus, according to the twenty-fourth chapter [of the Viṣṇudharmottara]: (1) *Jñātayaḥ* refers to paternal uncles, their sons, maternal uncles, and so forth. (2) In the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*, there is another specific detail:
"To the daughter's son, the son, the wife, those who are younger brothers born of the same womb, and those who are childless—even to these, [the gift] is given here. (589)
Vṛddha-Śātātapa also says:
"The Śrāddha should be performed with affection for all those belonging to the castes and those bearing religious marks;
by doing so correctly, a man shall attain great prosperity. (590)

(1) Those who bear the marks of a caste, such as celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and ascetics (*yatī*); (2) although these are mentioned here in general terms, only those who are kinsmen (*jñāti*) are to be understood;
(3) because of the statement in the *Caturviṃśatimata*, "and to their wives," offerings should be given separately even to the wives of paternal uncles and others;
(4) and for all of these, the rite is exclusively the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
Indeed, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is performed only for one's parents;
for paternal uncles, brothers, and maternal aunts, it is always the *ekoddiṣṭa*. || 591 ||
According to the statement of Jātukarṇya:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, wherever it may be offered—
to a brother, a sister, a son, a husband, or a maternal uncle."
For a friend or for a teacher, the śrāddha is of the ekoddiṣṭa type, not the pārvaṇa.
And because of the statement by Sumantu:

"In the preceding sentence, the mention of 'mother' refers to a stepmother, since the *parvaṇa* rite for the biological mother was stated previously, and because of the association with paternal uncles and others. || 593 ||
Thus says Hemādri.
As for the statement:
"And likewise for paternal uncles, brothers, and mothers who are childless..."
For a maternal grandfather who has no son, the śrāddha and other rites should be performed just as for a father. || 594 ||
Thus, (1) this is for the purpose of establishing equality by way of necessity, not for the purpose of equality with the *pārvaṇa* rite.
(2) Likewise, it has been stated regarding those entitled to perform the rite that "he who takes away another's property must also give to him.
(3) Here, Satyavrata states the sequence for the inclusion of the *pārvaṇa* rites:
The first gift is for the paternal ancestors, followed by that for the maternal ancestors; thereafter, it is for the maternal grandfathers, and for the son of the paternal uncle. 595.
Chāgaleya said:
On the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), the offerings should be made exclusively [to the ancestors]; on occasions of prosperity (vṛddhi), they are prescribed at the beginning.
Indeed, in all cases, the Mothers should be placed in the middle and never at the end.
As for the statement:
"The father and maternal grandfather first, and the mothers immediately after them;
this is the sequence prescribed for the libation (tarpaṇa), the Anvaṣṭakā śrāddha, and at a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha). (597)
(1) Thus it was cited by the author of the Smṛtiratnāvalī; however, that should be disregarded because he himself stated that its source is rootless.
(2) For this very reason, Uśanas declares a prohibition against placing them at the end:
"He who offers [the cakes] to his mothers after having placed the maternal grandfathers in between... [p. 153]
That fool goes to hell for as long as the world endures until the final dissolution.
Jābāli:
That man who places the Mothers at the end in the Śrāddha rites goes, being a fool, head-first to the Kālasūtra hell. (599)

(1) Therefore, the *pārvaṇa* for the mother follows immediately after the *pārvaṇa* for the father. (2) By this same logic, the *pārvaṇa* for the maternal grandmother and others also follows the *pārvaṇa* for the maternal grandfather and others. (3) As for the sequence for the wife and the rest, it is exactly as stated in the rules for libations (*tarpaṇa*).

(4) Here, the *pārvaṇa* rites for the father and the maternal grandfather are obligatory (*nitya*), since the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by those alone. (5) Other *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, however, are performed out of desire (*kāmya*) and should be performed according to one's capacity; they are not all mandatory. (6) But at Gayā, even the *pārvaṇa* for the mother is mandatory, as we shall explain in that very context.
(7) Thus, when many *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are to be performed simultaneously, the cooking should be done by way of a single performance (*tantra*). Accordingly, Atri states:
"If there should be a *śrāddha* for many or even for two on the same day..."
Having performed the cooking according to the tantra, one should perform the śrāddha rites separately. || 600 ||
Pulastya said: At the Mahālaya, at the Gayā-śrāddha, or on the anniversary of death,
having performed the cooking by a single ritual procedure (tantra), one should perform the śrāddhas separately for each individual.

(1) Regarding that as well, Marīci states the sequence for the Pārvaṇa and Ekoddiṣṭa rites: "If the Ekoddiṣṭa and the Pārvaṇa should both occur on the same day, one should perform the Pārvaṇa there first and then conclude with the Ekoddiṣṭa. (602)
(1) And this applies when one has the capacity. (2) But in the case of incapacity, there is a single performance (*tantra*) for both the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites.

(3) Here, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, if one has the capacity, there is a separate feeding of Brahmins for each. (4) However, in the case of incapacity, all the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are performed even with a single Brahmin. (5) For this very reason, the *Caturviṃśatimata*, beginning with "To the teacher, the preceptor, and the disciple" [588], continues:
"And at all sacred sites (*tīrtha*), in the month of Māgha, and under the Maghā asterism... [p. 154]
One should honor all [the deities], beginning with the teacher, within a single Brahmin. || 603 ||
Thus it has been said:

(1) However, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍadāna*) is indeed distinct in the *tīrtha-śrāddha*, because that is its primary element. (2) For this very reason, the statement specifies the unity of the Brāhmaṇas alone. (3) Even in the *pārvaṇa* rites for the ancestors (*pitṛ* etc.), if one has the capacity, then there should be the feeding of one Brāhmaṇa for each deity. (4) But the rite for the gods (*daiva*) is common (*tantra*) to all *pārvaṇa* rites;
however, it would not be common when there is a difference in time, nor indeed when there is a difference in place.
Therefore, from this tantric procedure, simultaneity is understood. || 604 ||

(1) Thus, because the author of the *Saṃgraha* teaches that the *daiva* and *tantra* rites are performed together when there is identity of place and time; (2) however, when there is incapacity, then in the *pārvaṇa* rites for the ancestors and so forth, one should feed one person in place of each triad of ancestors (the three paternal and three maternal), and in the *daiva* rite as well, only one person according to the *tantra* method—this is the settled conclusion.

(3) However, when one goes on pilgrimage having been prompted by another through means such as conciliation or gifts, although he himself is the agent, he should nevertheless first perform the *śrāddha* specifically for his father and other ancestors, in order to ensure the attainment of the full fruit arising from the pilgrimage for the qualified person (*adhikārin*). (4) Accordingly, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) should be made thus: “For the sake of [the benefit of] the sacrificer’s father, grandfather, and so forth. (5) Subsequently, since the incidental arrival at the sacred site—which serves as the occasion for the *śrāddha* for his own ancestors—has already occurred, [he performs it] for the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*).

"He who goes for the sake of another obtains a sixteenth part [of the merit]. (605) For the purpose of obtaining the full fruit as awakened by this statement, one should perform the *śrāddha* even for one's own father and others. Although, due to being within one's own jurisdiction, the *śrāddha* for one's own ancestors would logically occur first as being more internal (*antaraṅga*), nevertheless, because there is no status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) [for them] in the pilgrimage, and because they do not present themselves immediately after it since the pilgrimage belongs to another, the *śrāddha* for one's own ancestors occurs only later.
(3) This has been established in detail by Hemādri in the *Śrāddhakalpa*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

(4) For this very reason, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, regarding a certain merchant who went to Gayā at the instigation of a deceased ancestor by means of donating his own wealth, it is stated that the offering of the *piṇḍa* for the deceased (*preta*) comes first, and thereafter the offering for one’s own ancestors:
"Having first gone to Gayāśīrṣa, [one should offer] the *piṇḍa* to the King of the Dead (*pretarāja*)."
Then, with joy, he gave [the wealth] to his ancestors together with his kinsmen. || 606 ||
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa* as well, referring to this very same subject, it says:
"There, he performed the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased ancestors in due order, and immediately thereafter, he established his own heirs as the fathers. (607)
A widow, however, should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite for her husband and the *pārvaṇa* rite for her own father;
likewise, she should offer to three ancestors beginning with her husband, and similarly to her own paternal ancestors.
A widow should perform the Śrāddha ceremony at the proper time, remaining diligent and unwearied. || 608 ||

Thus, from the *Smṛtidarpaṇa*: (1) "In the same way" means from exactly three [ancestors]. (2) "At the proper time" means in cases such as a pilgrimage (*tīrtha*) or a *mahālaya* rite where offerings to multiple deities are prescribed.
In this context, the *parvaṇa* śrāddha for one's own father is performed only when he is without a son or grandson. || 609 ||

Thus it is stated in the *Divodāsīya*. That is not correct, because by the word "like a son" (*putravat*) in the statement, "The wife of one without a son [is like a son]," there is an expression of equality with the performance of the *śrāddha* rite due to conformity with the context; and because a son has the authority for the *pārvaṇa* rites for his own father and maternal grandfather; and because, with respect to a woman without a son, her father and others take the form of the husband and so forth, while her maternal grandfather and others take the form of the father and so forth; and because it is understood that whether they have sons or are sonless, their own fathers and others have authority in the *tīrtha-śrāddha* and other rites just as a son does.
(2) And because there is no qualifying statement to the effect that it applies "only to those who are childless."

(3) "But surely, since he has the right to perform the *śrāddha* for his son in the capacity of being the son's maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and so forth, she too should have that right precisely in that capacity, and not in the capacity of being a father (*pitṛ*) and so forth. (4) No; because even for a single person, there is a difference in the delimiting form (*avacchedaka-rūpa*) of the relationship according to the different relatives involved—just as with the *paridhi* (the enclosing stick)—since one is intended (*uddeśyatva*) toward another only in the specific form in which one stands in relation to them. (5) Even by that much, the equality of the action described in the *vati*-sūtra is maintained. (6) Consequently, just as those who are intended toward a son in the capacity of father and so forth may also be intended toward her in the capacity of husband (*bhartṛ*) and so forth, so too will those intended toward her in the capacity of maternal grandfather and so forth be intended toward him in the capacity of father and so forth. (7) Indeed, it is precisely for the sake of such an intendedness in this form that the statement "beginning with her own husband" (*svabhartr-prabhṛti*) was uttered.

(8) Therefore, for a widow, the *pārvaṇa* rite for her husband and the *pārvaṇa* rite for her father are mandatory. (9) He uses the word "unwearied" (*atandritā*) precisely to indicate this necessity.
As for the verse:
"But that woman who, out of folly, performs the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha for her husband... [p.156]
The husband is not satisfied by that; rather, having committed it, he shall go to hell. || 610 ||
(1) This statement is intended to praise the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), and not for the purpose of prohibiting the *pārvaṇa* rite altogether.

(2) However, she whose father-in-law is living should perform [the rite] for her husband, his father, and his grandfather; (3) if both her father-in-law and his father are living, she should perform it for her husband, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.

(4) Some say, "The same applies even when one's father and others are living. (5) However, those who follow authoritative tradition state, "While one's father is living, because the door [of the ritual] is closed, the *pārvaṇa* rite for him is indeed omitted."

(6) However, for one whose mother-in-law has died [but whose husband is alive], the *pārvaṇa* for the mother-in-law and others may or may not be performed. (7) And in this way, there is a rite for nine deities. (8) Some say that for a woman whose mother has died, there is also the *pārvaṇa* for her own mother and others, making it a rite for twelve deities. (9) Others say it is a rite for fifteen deities by including the *pārvaṇa* for her own maternal grandfather. (10) Still others say it is a rite for eighteen deities together with the *pārvaṇa* for her own maternal grandmother and others. (11) It appears reasonable that these three views apply to the case of one who is sonless. (12) Even in those cases, if the preceding [deity] is still living, there is simply an omission due to the disappearance of the causal link (*dvāra*).
(13) However, there is no occasion at all for performing *śrāddha* for the father-in-law, maternal grandfather, and others.

(14) If the *pārvaṇa* rites for the mother-in-law and others, as well as for one’s own mothers and so forth, are not performed, then it should be stated that the *pārvaṇa* rites for the husband’s father and [one’s own] father are to be performed with their respective wives as appropriate. (15) For others, however, *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are to be performed according to the circumstances. (16) In this matter, the local customs of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in each region are themselves the boat for crossing the river of doubt; enough said.
(17) Regarding one whose father is still living, Manu states a specific rule:
"But while the father is still living, one should perform [the rite] for the ancestors alone," so says Manu (3.220a-b).
In another Smṛti:
When one has grown old, at a sacred ford, when one has renounced the world, or when one's father has died,
the son himself should give to those very same persons to whom his father would have given.
(1) By the word "himself" (*svayam*), the status of being the primary officiant is expressed.
(2) However, in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*, it is stated that one whose father is living should offer [the śrāddha] to his grandfather and great-grandfather alone:
"O best of the Bharatas, it should not be offered while [the father] is living, because..."
Therefore, one whose father is still living should perform [the rite] with only two [verses]; of this there is no doubt.
[Page 157] Thus it is said. Viṣṇu, however, has stated another distinction:

"If one should perform a *śrāddha* while his father is living, he should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it. If both his father and grandfather are living, he should perform it for those for whom his grandfather would have performed it. If his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living, he should not perform it at all."

He should perform [the rite]. He whose father is deceased should, having placed a *piṇḍa* for his father, offer [one] each to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather. He whose father and grandfather are both deceased should, having offered two *piṇḍas* to them, offer [one] to the great-grandfather. He whose grandfather is deceased should [offer] to him.

Having placed the rice-ball (piṇḍa) for the great-grandfather, one should offer [the remaining two] to the two ancestors beyond him. He whose father and great-grandfather are deceased should, having placed the rice-ball for his father, offer to the two beyond the great-grandfather.
"In the same manner, a discerning person should perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers;
according to the rule, with the omission of the mantras, and for the remaining [ancestors], without mantras at all.
(Viṣṇusmṛti 75.1–7 = 487)

(1) The expression "while the father is living" (*pitari jīvati*) is an exclusive specification (*asādhāraṇanirdeśa*). (2) The meaning is "only while the father is living. (3) For this very reason, it is stated that "one should certainly not perform [the rite] when all three are living. (4) Likewise, later on, it says, "The same applies to the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmahānām*). In this regard—as when the father is living, the son of those whose father would perform [the rite] should perform it, so too...

For those whose maternal grandfather is living, just as one should not perform [the rite] while the three beginning with the father are living, so too one should not perform it while the three beginning with the maternal grandfather are living; all such matters are to be extended by analogy (atideśya). 615.
Thus Śūlapāṇi has explained. (1) The author of the Kālādarśa also says the same.

(2) “The same applies even when the mother is living, due to the equality of the underlying principle. (3) Consequently, one whose father is living, having offered to the three ancestors beginning with his father’s father, should—if his mother is deceased—offer to his own mother and so forth; if the mother is present, he should offer to the three beginning with his paternal grandmother, and then to his maternal grandfather and so forth; if the maternal grandfather is present, he should offer to the three beginning with his mother’s paternal grandmother—this is the established conclusion. (4) Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural injunction beginning with ‘to those very [ancestors]’; (5) because the words ‘mother’ and ‘maternal grandfather’ are relative terms, and since the mother and others related to the son, as well as the maternal grandfather and others, are denoted by the terms ‘mother,’ ‘maternal grandfather,’ etc., they are essentially one and the same; thus, it is possible to explain that ‘those who are the deities of the father are indeed the deities of the son. (6) Therefore, for one whose father is living, the *śrāddha* is to be performed precisely for the mother, maternal grandfather, and others related to himself.”

(7) However, this is untenable: because in the interpretation that "from those denoted by the word *yat*" and "to those denoted by the word *tat*," there would result the fallacy of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) for the words *yat* and *tat*; (8) and because, regarding the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and their forefathers (*pitāmaha*), since the literal sense of the scripture is possible, there would result the fallacy of two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti*). (9) Furthermore; here, the reference in the sentence is made precisely by the words *yat* and *tat*, and that too as being correlative to the ancestors—as in "from whom [the father]," rather than as being correlative to oneself. (10) And thus, where could there be the attainment of the mere maternal grandfather and others through the force of a relative term (*sambandhi-śabda*) applied to the son? (11) In the statement concerning Viṣṇu, however, by the word "thus" (*evam*), only the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather.

(12) Therefore, for one whose father is living, the deities at the *tīrtha-śrāddha* are those connected to the father—namely the mother and so forth—and likewise those connected to him—the maternal grandfather and so forth—but not those connected to oneself. (13) However, for one’s own mother, a single-offering (*ekoddiṣṭa*) is performed because she is the wife of one’s father; and for one’s own maternal grandfather as well, because he is the father-in-law of one’s father. This is because at the *tīrtha* of one’s own father, there is authority for that very *ekoddiṣṭa*, and because the rule “to whomsoever the father would give” applies without distinction.
(14) In this regard, even one whose father is living should perform the *śrāddha* at a *tīrtha* only if he maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*), and not if he is without them (*anagnika*).
A twice-born man whose father is still living shall not perform the śrāddha rite without the sacred fire;
however, one who maintains the sacred fire should perform it for those same ancestors for whom his father would have given.

Thus, according to the statement of Sumantu: (1) "One who maintains the sacred fire" (*sāgnika*) refers to one who possesses either the *śrauta* or *smārta* fire. Therefore, the authors of the *Madanapārijāta* and others maintain that only one who maintains the sacred fire and whose father is living has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha*. (2) The authors of the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*, Divodāsa, and others maintain: "Even among those who maintain the sacred fire, this applies only to those who subsist by the *Maitrāyaṇīya-sūtra*, and not to all; for the aforementioned statement, 'These six [rites] are for one whose father is living,' is heard specifically in its own *pariśiṣṭa*. (3) Both of these two views are untenable.
A twice-born man whose father has died should perform the Śrāddha rite day after day,
whether he maintains a sacred fire or not, especially at holy places.

This is because it contradicts the statement of Uśanas. (1) As for the *Saumantava* text, its meaning is simply this: one who is without the sacred fire (*anagnika*) should not perform the *śrāddha* according to the procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, whereas one who possesses the fire (*sāgnika*) should offer to the father, grandfather, and so forth, according to that same procedure. (2) Furthermore, although the statement "these six" is heard only in the *Maitrāyaṇīya-pariśiṣṭa*, it must nevertheless be explained as being common to all Vedic schools (*sarva-śākhi*), since it is shared with the statement of Uśanas—"at a *vṛddhi* [rite], at a sacred ford," and so forth—as previously cited. (3) Moreover, if the *Maitrāyaṇīya* passage were restricted solely to those of that school who possess the fire, what would become of the second marriage and other rites mentioned in that very passage?

[159] This investigation into the qualification (*adhikāra*) has also been undertaken here as a relevant digression. Thus, once the qualification of one whose father is still living is established, if he goes [to the sacred site] solely for the sake of that fruit—being commissioned by his father like another person impelled by the giving of wealth and so forth—then, because the father alone possesses the qualification, he should perform a single *śrāddha* using a formula such as “of the sacrificer’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. However, since his own arrival at the sacred site—which is the cause of the *śrāddha*—has occurred incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*), he must subsequently perform the *śrāddha* using a formula such as “of the father’s father, grandfather, and great-grandfather,” because (5) the deities differ; for by the rule, “one should give to those to whom the father gives” [GDS 612], the status of being a deity is understood precisely through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of being the father’s father and so forth. Furthermore, in the previous *śrāddha*, just as when there is a different agent such as a servant other than the son, the status of being a deity is determined solely by the limiting adjunct of being the sacrificer’s father and so forth. Moreover, (7) the word “himself” (*svayam*) indicates that the qualification belongs to himself, and because a simultaneous performance (*tantra*) or incidental performance (*prasaṅga*) is not possible between two distinct qualifications.

(8) However, when one goes to a sacred site (*tīrtha*) for the sake of his own merit alone—whether authorized by his father or not—then, in order to fulfill the requirement of personal eligibility (*svādhikārikatā*) implied by the word "himself," he should perform only a single *śrāddha* using a formulation such as, "For my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.

(9) There is also another distinction: when one whose mother has died goes to Gayā for the sake of his father, then in the first *śrāddha*, he must perform an *ekoddiṣṭa* for his own mother in her capacity as the sacrificer’s wife (*yajamānapatnī*), because his father has authority only for an *ekoddiṣṭa* for her.
(10) However, in the second *śrāddha*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone must be performed for the mother, because she is the wife of the father; this follows from the very reasoning previously stated.

(11) Furthermore, since it is declared in the section on eligibility (*adhikāra-prakaraṇa*) that the *mātṛ-śrāddha* must also be performed when proceeding to Gayā in connection with a pilgrimage, the *pārvaṇa* rite for the mother and others must also be performed [on other occasions], as in:
"In the *nāndīmukha*, in the *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of death..."
One should perform the śrāddha for one's mother together with [the offerings for] the paternal grandmother and the others. || 618 ||
(1) Because of the statement of Śātātapa, "Thus," one has authority for that [rite] only as a *pārvaṇa* performed for oneself.

(2) However, when one whose mother has died goes to Gayā by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga*), then at the first *śrāddha*, an *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed for one's own mother in her capacity as the wife of the father. (3) But the second [śrāddha] is indeed a *pārvaṇa*, performed in her capacity as a mother and so forth.

(4) According to the view of the *Kālādarśa* and other authorities, however, since one whose father is living has no authority to perform *śrāddha* at Gayā, there is no second *śrāddha* for one who has gone there for the sake of his father. (5) But it is stated in this context of authority that for one who goes there by incidental connection, there is no first [śrāddha].

(6) At a sacred site other than Gayā, however, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite alone should be performed for the mother—either as the wife of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or as the wife of the father—as appropriate; the *pārvaṇa* rite is not to be performed, because there is no scriptural injunction to that effect. This is the distinction. (7) Likewise, for paternal uncles and others, whether at Gayā or another sacred site, one whose father is still living should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite according to the circumstances, either as the brother of the sacrificer or as the brother of the father. (8) However, a *śrāddha* performed specifically in the capacity of being a paternal uncle and so forth does not exist at all, due to the absence of any scriptural injunction.

(9) According to the Kālādarśa and other systems, however, there is no entitlement even by virtue of being a father’s brother or similar relation, because one whose father is still living lacks inherent eligibility for the *gayāśrāddha*.

(10) [Objection: "But in this way, if the father and others themselves become the preceptor (*ācārya*) and so forth through the mere difference of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), would it not follow that one must perform the *śrāddha* again and again even for those same ancestors under those very same conditions? (11) [Reply: It is said: Because such scriptural statements as "to whomsoever the father himself should give" [612] and "having gone to Gayā on some occasion" [558] would otherwise be inexplicable, performing the *śrāddha* repeatedly due to the difference in limiting conditions is not a fault. (12) However, the scriptural injunctions regarding the *śrāddha* for the preceptor and others find their fulfillment by referring to preceptors and others who are distinct from the father and the rest; therefore, they do not necessitate a further *śrāddha*.

(13) Moreover, once the first *śrāddha*—occasioned by the specific and proximate status of being a father and so forth—has been performed, it is impossible to perform another *śrāddha* occasioned by the general and proximate status of being a teacher and so forth. (14) This is just as, when the loudness required by the status of being a *nigada* has been applied, the low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) required by the status of being a *yajus* becomes impossible.

(15) Furthermore, just as the rule regarding low-voiced recitation finds its application in other *yajus* mantras, the scriptural injunction for a *śrāddha* for a teacher and others finds its fulfillment in the case of a teacher who is distinct [from the father]; thus, enough of this prolixity!

(16) Thus it is established that even one whose father is living should perform the *śrāddha* at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for the ancestors (*pitṛ-devatā*) alone. (17) But when one whose father is deceased has a living mother, then there is simply the omission of the *pārvaṇa* rite for the mother. (18) However, as appropriate, the qualification "together with their wives" (*sapatnīkānām*) must be applied to the ancestors, such as the father and so forth. (19) Likewise, when the maternal grandfather is living, there is the omission of his *pārvaṇa* rite. (20) When the maternal grandmother is living, it is exactly the same. (21) However, the qualification should be made as before. As it has been said:
"In the group of fathers, in the group of mothers, and likewise in the group of the maternal grandfather..."
If one should live, he must abandon whatever belongs to his own faction. || 619 ||

(1) Here, the phrase "in the group of ancestors" (*pitṛvarge*) refers specifically to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and similar occasions, because for one whose father is living, the *pārvaṇa* rite for the father’s father and others has been prescribed by a specific scriptural statement regarding sacred sites (*tīrtha*). (2) The same applies to the "group of mothers" (*mātṛvarge*).

(3) Likewise, having performed the *śrāddha* and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) separately for each deity mentioned for each respective person, the general rice-ball (*sāmānyapiṇḍa*) should be offered; as Devala says:
Then, having taken the funeral ball (piṇḍa), one should offer it as common to the entire circle of kinsmen, both those who have attained the conditioned and the unconditioned. || 620 ||
(1) "Iti" refers to the mantra that is about to be recited. And that mantra is:
"Those who have died in the paternal lineage, and those who have died in the maternal lineage;
and those other kinsmen of the teacher, the father-in-law, and relatives who have died."

Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, those whose sacred rites have fallen into neglect, as well as those born blind and the lame; [may they all attain satisfaction].
May the funeral offering given by me reach those of my family who were deformed, those who died in the womb, and those known or unknown; may it remain inexhaustible for them.

Thus [it is said]. Here, even though there are three verses, they constitute a single mantra, because the meaning of the sentence is completed by that much alone. And likewise, the sage Jaimini has stated that a single mantra exists because of the unity of purpose: "A single sentence is that which, when divided, would remain syntactically expectant" (Jaiminisūtra 2.1.46).
Because it has been stated in MS 2.1.14.46; and because of the singular number in Devala’s statement, “having taken the *piṇḍa*”;
likewise—
Those who are born from my paternal lineage up to Brahmā, as well as those born from my maternal lineage;
those who have been my slaves in both families, as well as my servants and dependents.

To my friends, companions, animals, and trees—those touched and those seen, and those who have rendered me assistance, as well as those who were associated with me in other births—to them I offer this funeral cake (svadhā-piṇḍa). || 623 ||
(1) Thus, with these two verses, another *piṇḍa* should be offered. (2) Here too, as before, there is the unity of the mantra.
(3) Having thus performed the offering of the *piṇḍas*, one should complete the *śrāddha* according to the rules prescribed in one's own *sūtra*, up to the point of the Brahmins' departure.

(4) However, for one who is unable—due to illness or other reasons—to perform this entire collection of *śrāddha* rites and the individual offering of each *piṇḍa*, or for whom such time does not exist, he should perform an abbreviated *śrāddha*. (5) And that is done as follows: having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), "I shall perform an abbreviated *śrāddha* due to inability."
Oṃ! Father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather;
mother, grandmother, and likewise great-grandmother.
To the maternal grandfather, his father, the great-grandfather, and the others—to them this pinda offered by me may indeed reach as an inexhaustible offering. (624)
"With this mantra, one should offer a single pinda.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the recipient in the *tīrthaśrāddha*.
Thus ends the section on *tīrtha-śrāddha* (ancestral rites at sacred sites) in the General Section of the *Tīrthasetu*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara Sūri.
Now follows (2) the procedure for the casting of bones (*asthi-prakṣepa*) at a sacred site.
Regarding that, the fruit of casting bones at any sacred site (*tīrtha*) according to the prescribed rule is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: [p.162]
Having bathed and then sprinkled [the ground] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having combined it with gold, honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
and then having placed it within a vessel made of a lump of clay, one should look toward the direction inhabited by the hosts of departed spirits (pretas).
Saying, “Homage be to the Dharma,” he should enter the bathing place and cast [the flower] while saying, “May He be pleased with me.
Having bathed and likewise emerged, and having looked at the sun, he should then give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
When this has been done, for one staying in the city of the departed, there shall be a journey to heaven equal to that of Mahendra. || 625 ||
(1) *Pañcagavam* means the five products of the cow (*pañcagavyam*).

(2) Although it is stated here that the attainment of heaven occurs without distinction [in all sacred sites], nevertheless, due to the relative gradation of the sacred sites (*tīrtha*), one should understand that there is a difference in their nature (*vaijātya*) therein. (3) But regarding the Gaṅgā, there is a specific distinction; as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"At whatever time the bones of men are cast into the Gaṅgā by people..."
Starting from that time as the beginning, his residence shall be in the heavenly world. || 626 ||
(1) Since no upper limit is stated here, the end of the kalpa alone is the limit, as it is appropriate. (2) Likewise, the attainment of the world of Brahmā is also heard [in scripture]:
Yama says—"The bone of a person of auspicious deeds which is cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā..."
For him there is no returning again from the eternal world of Brahman.
Likewise, Yama [says]: "As long as the bones of humans remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā..."
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the world of Brahmā.

"Yama [is attained] on the ninth day," and so forth. (1) The attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) should be understood as resulting from specific sacred sites (*kṣetra*) such as Prayāga, since the general attainment of heaven has already been mentioned.
(2) In that regard, there is a specific time:
Gautama states that one should not perform the casting of bones into the Gaṅgā when the preceptor has passed away, when Venus has set, or during an intercalary month.
Likewise:
"The casting of bones, the Gayā-śrāddha, and the śrāddha of the dark fortnight—one should not perform these in the first year, unless the sapindikarana has been performed. (630)
(1) However, there is a reading in some places: "even when the *sapiṇḍana* has been performed.
Likewise:
"The casting of bones, the *śrāddha* at Gayā, and the *śrāddha* of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣika*)."
One should perform the funeral rites for someone at the very first auspicious moment. || 631 ||
(1) Some recite the fourth quarter as: "yadi syād bhaktimān suta.
(2) However, there is no fault within ten days;
for him whose bone sinks into the waters of the Gaṅgā within ten days—
One shall obtain a fruit equal to that which comes from dying in the Gaṅgā. || 632 ||
Thus it is stated. Furthermore, there is another distinction mentioned in the Purāṇa:
"Having abandoned both his mother’s family and his father’s family, that lowest of men..."
Having taken bones belonging to another family, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
(1) And this refers to the sphere of greed for wealth and the like. Likewise:

"Even those who sometimes carry the bones born of their mother's and father's lineages to the Gaṅgā, being overcome by compassion—even for one who is a true kinsman—for them too, the sacred fords (tīrthas) yield fruit. (634)
Now,
I, Śaunaka, shall explain the procedure for the purification of bones in due order.
Having gone outside the village, one should then perform a bath along with one's clothes.
The wise one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), using the respective mantras for each.

(1) The meaning is that one should sprinkle that ground where the bones have been buried. (2) "With those respective mantras" refers to the mantras for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), such as "ā pyayasva" and others which reveal milk, curd, and so forth. [The sequence is:
prayer with the *upasarpa* and other mantras, then digging, then the removal of the earth, and finally the collection of the bones, in due order. (636)

(1) For the four verses beginning with “upa sarpa,” Śaṅkha is the seer, the Pitṛs are the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the metre.
