(2) Their application (*viniyoga*) is as follows: for the first verse, in the prayer for the ground; for the second, in the digging; for the third, in the removal of the earth; and for the fourth, in the taking up of the bone.
(3) Having thus taken the bones and gone to a body of water, one should perform the ritual bath according to the rules.
Then, one should perform the purification of the bones with the mantra beginning, "Come hither, O Indra."
Having touched [the object] repeatedly, one becomes pure by bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
the wise man should perform ten such ablutions while reciting the respective mantras.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water with *kuśa* grass,
ash, clay, honey, and *gaurasarṣapa*— these are indeed the ten mantra-baths.
One should sweep the bones with *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra "ato devā," and then [the mantras] "eto nv indram," "śucī vaḥ," and "na tam aṃhaḥ."
The wise man who recites the Pāvamānī hymns, the verse "mamāgne," and the Rudra-sūkta in their proper order becomes pure; it cannot be otherwise.
Then, one should diligently perform the Hemaśrāddha dedicated to the ancestors;
thereafter, one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) and perform the libation with sesame seeds (tilatarpaṇa).
Deer-skin, woolen cloth, darbha grass, cow-hair, hemp,
birch-bark, and palm-leaf— this is known as the sevenfold wrapping.
[165] However, in some places there is the reading: “Cow-hair, birch-bark, palm-leaf, and silk—these are the seven wrappings for the bones.
One should place gold, pearl, silver, coral, and likewise lapis lazuli within the midst of the bones; in this way purification occurs, and not otherwise.
Then the wise practitioner should perform a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds and clarified butter;
he should offer one hundred and eight oblations while reciting the hymn beginning with "udīrate."
Having gone there, no fault of contact exists at excellent bathing places;
one may perform urination, defecation, and ritual sipping of water while carrying bones.
In the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"The righteous Dhanañjaya, devoted to his mother,
took his mother’s bones and then stood upon the path to the Gaṅgā."
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then indeed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
having smeared it with the yakṣakardama ointment, and having worshipped it with flowers;
Then, having wrapped [it] with a cloth for the eyes, then with a silken cloth,
then with a cloth of excellent fragrance, and then with a madder-dyed garment.
(1) Having placed the merchant’s mother’s limbs— wrapped in fine white Chinese silk, or else in a Nepalese woolen blanket, or in pure clay— within a copper casket, the merchant [set out].
Untouched by low birth, pure, and sleeping on the bare ground—
Vyāsa says: (KāKh, 1.30.42–46b)
Silken cloth, silk from the *kauśeya* worm, madder-dyed cloth, white cloth, woolen blankets, hempen cloths, and likewise, upper garments of deerskin. || 639 ||
(1) And there is an option regarding these means of wrapping and the sequences of wrapping.
[p.166] Now follows its practical manual (*prayogapaddhati*).

(2) Having gone to the place where the bones are buried, one should bathe with one's clothes on and sprinkle the site of the bone-burial with milk using the verse *ā pyāyasva*; with curds using *dadhikrāvṇo*; with cow-urine using the *Gāyatrī*; with cow-dung using *gandhadvārām*; and with clarified butter using *ghr̥taṃ mimikṣe*. Then, having recited: “*upa sarpa*... [of these four verses, Śaṅkha is the seer, the Pitṛs are the deity, Triṣṭubh is the metre; the first is for praying to the earth, the second for digging, the third for removing the soil, and the fourth for taking up the bones]”—having performed these acts in sequence with these verses—one should bathe in a body of water together with the bones, wash the bones with the *Pañcagavya* and the hymn *eto nv indram*, and then bathe them with pure water. (3) Thereafter, one should perform ten purificatory baths (*daśasnāna*) for the bones along with the bones: with cow-urine using the *Gāyatrī*; with cow-dung using *gandhadvārām*; with milk using *ā pyāyasva*; with curds using *dadhikrāvṇo*; with clarified butter using *ghr̥taṃ mimikṣe*; with *Kuśa*-water using *āpo hi ṣṭhā*; with ashes using *mā nas toke*; with clay using the mantras mentioned in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* beginning with *bal̥itthā parvatānām*, or with clay using the mantras beginning with *aśvakrānte rathakrānte*; with honey using *madhu vātā*; and with pure water using *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.

(4) Having thus performed the ten ablutions, one should perform the cleansing of the bones with *kuśa* grass using these mantras: the hymn beginning with “eto nv indram,” the hymn beginning with “śucī vo havye,” the hymn beginning with “na tam aṃhaḥ,” the hymn beginning with “iti vā iti me manaḥ,” the *pāvamānī* verses beginning with “yad anti yac ca dūrake,” the *ṛc* beginning with “mamāgne varcaḥ,” and the Rudra-hymn.

(5) Then, one should perform the *hiraṇyaśrāddha*: for one for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, it is a rite for three deities; for one for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed, it is an *ekoddiṣṭa*. (6) And this *śrāddha* is dedicated to whichever deity [is represented by] whose bones [are present].

(7) Immediately thereafter, having likewise offered balls of roasted flour (*saktupiṇḍa*) and performed the libation of sesame seeds (*tilatarpaṇa*) in the same manner, and having smeared [the body] with *yakṣakardama* and other unguents, worshipped it with flowers, and wrapped it with one of the four previously mentioned types of skins (*ajina*) and so forth, one should place gold, pearls, silver, coral, and sapphires within the bones. (8) Then, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter while reciting the hymn beginning with "udīratām. (9) "udīratām": Śaṅkha is the seer, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deity, and the *triṣṭubh* is the meter.

(10) Then, having placed the bones in a copper casket, being pure and untouched by Cāṇḍālas, outcasts, or the like, he should go to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). (11) Having bathed at that *tīrtha* with the bones and placed them in a cup made of *palāśa* leaves, he should make this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the attainment of the world of Brahmā without returning again, I shall perform the casting of the bones of [Name], of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), at this [Name] *tīrtha*. Having washed the bones with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and mixed them with pieces of gold, honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, he should place them in a lump of clay. Standing in water reaching up to his navel and looking toward the south, he should cast them into the *tīrtha* with the mantra: "Homage be to Dharmarāja; may he be pleased with me. After bathing and coming out of the water, he should look at the sun, bow down, and, recollecting Hari, give silver according to his ability for the sake of the ancestral rite (*pitṛkṛtya*), saying: "For the perfection of the casting of bones performed for the attainment of the world of Brahmā of [Name], of such-and-such lineage, I bestow this silver, whose deity is the Moon, upon a Brāhmaṇa. (12) And all of this, excluding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), is to be done with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

(13) And this should be performed at any sacred ford (*tīrtha*); (14) especially at the Gaṅgā, according to the verses cited previously; (15) even there, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) maintain it should be done especially at Prayāga; (16) when this is done, the fruit has already been stated.

(17) Regarding this, Divodāsa and others maintain that "having performed this [immersion of the bones], the entire ritual procedure (*tīrthavidhi*) must be carried out. (18) Others, however, hold that "because the immersion of the bones would result in a contradiction due to the conjunction of the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*anitya*), because the immersion does not fall within the scope of the *tīrthakṛtya* (the rites at a sacred site), and because there is a prohibition against delay in the *śrāddha* and other rites—whereby delay is not permitted as in the case of bathing and similar acts which are not mandatory—and because there is no scriptural statement requiring it immediately after [the *śrāddha*], and by the maxim that 'guests are to be seated at the end,' the immersion of the bones should be performed immediately after completing the bathing and other *tīrthakṛtya* rites. (19) Those learned in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*), however, say: "When one has gone to a sacred site with the aim of obtaining the fruit produced by the immersion of the bones, that [immersion] itself must be performed first; for delay in the *śrāddha* and other rites caused by the intended purpose is permitted by the scripture, and since the *tīrthakṛtya* is an incidental consequence (*nāntarīyaka*), it cannot cause delay in the intended purpose. (20) For this very reason, even the ritual bathing occasioned by the sacred site (*tīrthanaimittika*) occurs only afterwards. (21) But he who, while traveling with the aim of obtaining the fruit of the sacred site, happens to carry the bones along incidentally, should immerse them only after all the *tīrthakṛtya* rites have been completed. (22) This being the case, in this matter, the learned (*śiṣṭa*) alone are the authority.
Thus ends the "Rite for the Casting of Bones" in the general section of the *Śrītīrthasetu*. [p.
168] Now follow miscellaneous rules regarding sacred fords (*tīrtha*), according to Devala:
The libation for the ancestors and the gods, the performance of the śrāddha rite accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
and the gift of a cow at every sacred ford— this is the prescribed rule for ordinary people when they are self-restrained.
The offering of vṛṣadāna is prescribed for those possessing distinguished marks and signs;
one should perform bathing, anointing, and worship of the deities.
The gift of land to Brahmins, or for one who performs worship of the gods—this rule applies everywhere during a procession of the gods. || 640 ||
Likewise:
"The sight of the gods is meritorious; better than the sight is the touch;
better than the touch is worship; and superior even to that is the bathing with clarified butter."
The wise declare that bathing with the waters of the Gaṅgā, accompanied by the recitation of mantras eight times and abundant fragrant substances, is equal to a bath of clarified butter.

(1) The mention of "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) is an indicative mark for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). (2) In the act of worship, whatever fragrances, flowers, and so forth are not prohibited for their respective deities should be accepted. (3) However, there is a special rule regarding the Sun:
"He who [offers] even once with a specific half-portion of substance and the water of the Gaṅgā..."
And with [the offering] measuring one māgadha-prastha, placed within a copper vessel.
One should offer a respectful oblation to the Sun together with one's own ancestors;
joined by sons and grandsons, one is glorified in the heavenly world. || 642 ||
Regarding the eightfold *argha* offering, it is stated in the *Skānda*:
"Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, honey, and the curd of cows."
Red karavīra flowers and red sandalwood as well—
this is declared to be the eightfold water offering (argha), which is exceedingly pleasing to the Sun.
Regarding the circumambulation, however, there is this distinction:
one should offer one [circumambulation] for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, and three for Vināyaka.
Four [circumambulations] should be performed for Viṣṇu, and half a circumambulation for Śiva.
Likewise—one performing the circumambulation of Śiva should not step over the *somasūtra*. (645)
(1) We shall explain the measurements for the *somasūtra* and so forth, as well as the absence of defects regarding Viśveśvara and other [shrines], in the section on Kāśī.
(2) There is also a distinction regarding the salutation (*namaskāra*): whether in front, behind, on the left side, nearby, or within the inner sanctum (*garbhamandira*).
One should not perform recitations, burnt offerings, or prostrations in a temple of the deities.
If it appears at the front, one meets death; if at the back, it is said to signify decline.
If it is on the left side, there will be destruction; on the right, it grants all desires. (646)
(1) O Śivā, it should be performed even before [the deity]:
"When the bound soul falls prostrate like a staff upon the ground before the Lord of Beasts, all his sins fall away; they do not rise again as long as he remains there. (647)
Furthermore, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Removing the garlands from a deity, sweeping the temple of a deity, and bathing all the deities are recorded as having the same fruit as the gift of a cow. (648)
(1) Sweeping consists of cleansing and so forth, as well as raising up that which has fallen.
Likewise, in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "One should never touch substances such as food, fruit, or water that belong to Śiva."
One must never step over flower offerings; one should throw everything into a well.
That man who, out of greed or delusion, makes use of Śiva’s property even to the extent of a fly's foot, is cooked in hell until the end of the kalpa. || 649 ||
Regarding the *brāhma* [oblation]:
"One should cause that which is attached to the limbs of Brahmā to be given to the Brahmins, and that which is attached to the limbs of Viṣṇu to be offered;
and that which is attached to the limbs of Rudra, one should burn it all in the fire at that very moment."
Furthermore, whatever one might offer to other gods, that should be bestowed upon the poor; and whatever has been offered to the Mothers, that should be given to Brahmins.
But that which has been offered to Gaṇeśa and the others should be given to the Vāḍavas. || 650 ||

(1) However, we shall state the exceptions regarding Viśveśvara and other such places. (2) Furthermore, one must refrain from accepting gifts and the like at a sacred site (*tīrtha*). As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"A sacred site is destroyed for the sake of livelihood; a vow is destroyed for the sake of livelihood."
And likewise, speech that is untrue, as well as that which speaks with malice;
One should not accept gifts at a sacred bathing place, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
for even a creature overcome by lust protects its own mother.
To accept a gift at a sacred ford is indeed the selling of that sacred ford;
for if the Gaṅgā were sold, Janārdana himself would be sold.
"When Janārdana has been sold, the three worlds have been sold. Furthermore:
"But that twice-born man who, out of greed, should be fond of receiving gifts for a sacred field—for such a wicked soul, there is neither the next world nor this one."
Those Brahmins who, weak in knowledge, accept great gifts,
are born as Brahma-rākṣasas in the form of trees.
One should not become fond of receiving gifts by relying on the power of the Vedas;
for it is through ignorance or negligence that one is consumed by the results of action, and not otherwise.
Standing at the gate of a king, one should not engage in the sale of the Vedas;
having killed a cow, that lowest of the twice-born would eat its supreme flesh.
But if a Brāhmaṇa, distressed for a livelihood, accepts [the gift], he should give one-tenth of what he has earned; in this way, it is not lost.
In the *Kūrma-purāṇa*, beginning with the words "one should not accept," it is stated:
"Whether in one's own business or the business of another, or even in the worship of the deities... [PrKh 1.28.30c–31b, 43–44, 47e–48b, 31c–f, p. 171]
That sacred ford is fruitless for him as long as he continues to enjoy its fruits.
Therefore, a twice-born man should not accept gifts at sacred fords or at holy shrines; he should remain vigilant regarding all such occasions. 653.
(1) These two statements are also recited in the *Mātsya-purāṇa*.

(2) In this regard, as long as a person who has accepted [gifts] at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) enjoys the wealth received there, the ownership (*svatva*) continues to persist over the wealth acquired at that site; for that long, no fruit characterized by a ten-millionfold increase and so forth accrues from giving gifts and other acts at that sacred site.

[The Kalpataru states: "It produces [a result]; however, by the abandonment of that wealth, it certainly produces its own fruit. (4) Regarding this, some say: "This [attenuation] occurs even when [the sin] was committed unintentionally due to the insistence of a master and so forth; but in the case of intentional [sin], there is no fruit at all from the sale of a sacred site (*tīrtha*). In the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa* of the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Whatever sin has been committed elsewhere, it becomes attenuated at a sacred site (*tīrtha*)."
Elsewhere, no other founder of a religious sect can ever remove one's sin. || 654 ||
In the Bhārata (PraKh 1.28.51):
"He who, having conquered desire, anger, and greed, should dwell at a sacred ford."
By that [pilgrimage], there is nothing that would not be attained through visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, *Uttarakhaṇḍa*:
"One should not commit a sin at a sacred ford; one should abandon making a livelihood from sacred fords."
Acceptance of gifts at a sacred ford must be renounced; the sale of dharma must be renounced.
A sin committed at a sacred ford is difficult to digest, as is the acceptance of gifts there;
indeed, everything done at a sacred ford is difficult to digest, and one who acts in such a manner goes to hell.
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, chapter 31, verses 70–71:
"The forest deities protect the renunciant who has gone to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)."
My messengers specifically do not go into the presence of those who belong to Yama.
Even if one always frequents a sacred ford, if one dies elsewhere, one will become a wise twice-born man, a knower of the Vedas, in an auspicious region and family. (657)
Likewise, GaPu 2.26.17, 19 states:
"But whatever sin has been committed in the home is purified by bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha)."
And there, O bird, one should always give imperishable gifts.
If one commits a sin there, it is indeed like an adamantine cement;
he shall suffer for it without doubt as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure. 658.
Likewise, GaPu 2.26.25–26 states:
"The deity is never found in wood, nor ever in stone."
For the deity exists within existence; therefore, one should take refuge in existence. || 659 ||
In the Nāradīya (GaPu 2.28.11):
"Visiting sacred fields and resorting to holy pilgrimage sites."
O Brahmin, sacrifice is indeed manifold, yet it does not protect one who has abandoned right conduct.
Devala said:
One should not speak of a river while among rivers, nor of a mountain while among mountains;
likewise, while staying at sacred fords (tīrthas) or shrines (āyatanas), one should not praise anything else.
Likewise:

"In whichever places there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) or whatever river is most meritorious, one should meditate upon that even with the mind; otherwise, there is the contemplation of other desires. (662)
(1) This concerns the subject of bathing. (2) Both of these refer to locations other than the Gaṅgā; as it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"At the time of bathing at other holy sites, people mutter the name of the Jāhnavī [Gaṅgā];
for apart from Viṣṇupadī [the Gaṅgā], what else is capable of purifying sin? (663)
Also in the *Brāhma*:
"In other sacred sites, men are made to remember the Gaṅgā;
therefore, there is no sacred site equal to the Gaṅgā within the entire cosmic egg. (664)
(1) Whatever has been performed, such as pilgrimages and the like, should be offered to Viṣṇu. As it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]:
"Whatever holy places there are, and whatever gifts, vows, and austerities, all of those indeed become perfected by offering them at the feet of Viṣṇu."
In this world, they do not offer various meritorious deeds to Hari;
here they become fruitless, and only labor would be the result.
Devala said:
The forest, the abodes of the gods, sacred fords, and shrines—by dwelling in these, one goes to the worlds of the inhabitants of heaven. (666)
Likewise:
"The man who is unable to perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti should resort to sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as vows and austerities. (667)
(1) For one who has gone to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for the purpose of a pilgrimage, there is a stay of three days as a general rule;
having reached the sacred ford, one who is engaged in vows, fasts, and observances, bathing for three days and staying for three nights, is liberated from all sins. || 668 || (~ 225)
This is according to the statement of Devala. (1) Furthermore, wherever a specific additional requirement has been mentioned, that too should be observed.

(2) When a river other than the Sarasvatī falls across the path of one traveling on the road, then bathing and other rites should be performed on the opposite bank; however, in the case of the Sarasvatī, they should be performed on this side of the bank. As it has been said:
"When a river is encountered along the way, bathing and other rites are to be performed from the opposite bank."
This rule regarding the path applies only prior to the Sarasvatī river. || 669 ||
But that man who crosses rivers without having first gratified the ancestors becomes exceedingly miserable, for they then become desirous of drinking his blood. (670) (= 332)

(1) This statement refers to the Sarasvatī river, because (2) since there are many such rivers, the use of the plural number is appropriate. Alternatively, (3) *taraṇa* means crossing over or passing beyond; thus, the meaning is that one should not proceed even when encountering a river along the path without first performing ritual bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and so forth. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
"One should not cross a flowing stream without having poured water [as an offering]. (671)

(1) Thus he states the prohibition against transgressing. (2) ‘Without having sprinkled’ means without having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (3) In both of these statements, the libation is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the bath as well, because the libation occurs immediately after that.
(4) A *śrāddha* ceremony should also be performed in a well-known river encountered on one’s path, since the same principle applies.

(5) This bathing on the opposite bank of rivers should be understood to apply when there is no superior *tīrtha* on this side; however, if such a [superior] one exists, the bathing and other rites should be performed on this side alone, for by neglecting it, a fault would arise. (6) But regarding the Sarasvatī, if there is a specific *tīrtha* on the opposite bank, the distinction is that one should first perform them on this side and then also on the opposite bank.
(7) Now, the "womb of the *tīrtha*" (*tīrthagarbha*) and so forth are described for the purpose of prohibiting the acceptance of gifts and other such acts. Regarding this, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"Taking the flowing current as the limit, for a distance of four cubits..."
In that place, Nārāyaṇa is the master; there is never any other master.
In that case, one should not accept it, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat. || 672 ||

(1) Here, “flowing water” (*pravāha*) is an indicative term for water in general. (2) Therefore, even at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) such as Puṣkara, or those consisting of ponds, tanks, and the like, the prohibition applies everywhere within a distance of four cubits measured from the water’s edge. As stated in the *Dānadharmaparvan*:
“On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, as far as the water extends...”
Up to that point one should understand it as the "womb" (garbha); beyond that, it is called the "bank" (tīra). || 673 ||

(1) Here, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, even if there is no increase in water due to the occasional absence of rain, the characteristic indeed consists of some increase resulting from rain that will occur [in the future], as in the case of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). || 674 ||
By this principle, a specific location is indicated;
and the limit of the shore is described in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Up to one hundred and fifty cubits from the interior, it is called the shore. || 675 ||
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "An area extending for one *gavyūti* all around the bank is called the sacred field (*kṣetra*).
Here, giving, recitation, and burnt offerings performed at the Gaṅgā are effective; of this there is no doubt. (676)

(1) On each of the two banks, the sacred field extends for a distance of two *krośas*, which is one *gavyūti*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "All sins without exception do not cross the boundary of the Gaṅgā;
they flee in the ten directions like deer upon seeing a lion."
"The boundary of the field is one *yojana* wide, consisting of both banks. (677).

(1) Herein, the prohibition regarding receiving [gifts] applies to well-known rivers. (2) However, regarding more renowned rivers such as the Gaṇḍakī and others, the learned authorities maintain that the prohibition applies even to a bank measuring one hundred and fifty cubits on either side. (3) As for the prohibition regarding a field, it pertains specifically to the region of the Gaṅgā, since the field is described in that very context.
As for that which is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Where the Gaṅgā flows, O Great King, there is the penance grove of Śambhu;
that should be known as a field of accomplishment extending for three yojanas in every direction. || 678 ||

(1) Regarding the statement that "on each side it is one and a half *yojanas*," the meaning is "three *yojanas* all around"; this is for the sake of emphasizing its greatness upon his death, not for the purpose of prohibiting its acceptance. (2) However, when the reading is "half a *yojana* all around," then it has the same meaning as [the account] of Skanda. (3) Now, there is a specific rule regarding the worship of the *liṅga* and other icons. In the *Nāradīya*:
"That man who should bow down to a *liṅga* or Viṣṇu worshipped by a *śūdra*..."
For there is no atonement for that, even by means of ten thousand penances.
Likewise, one who has touched a *liṅga* or even Lord Hari while in contact with a *śūdra* shall experience all the torments of hell for as long as the moon and stars exist.
By bowing to a linga worshipped by heretics, one enters into heresy;
by bowing to a linga worshipped by cowherds, one experiences hell.
Whoever bows down to a linga worshipped by women, or even to Viṣṇu, shall dwell in the Raurava hell for an entire kalpa, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
[176] (1) All of this refers to the case of a liṅga and so forth that has been consecrated in the present day, but not to those whose greatness is established by ancient tradition; for it is said:
"Once a liṅga has been consecrated according to the rules by those who know the mantras, from that time forward, neither a Śūdra nor a woman shall touch it. (680)

Because it has been stated right there [in that very source]: for this very reason, it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa* concerning the *Kāśī-liṅga*: "O Dear One, O Beautiful One, even those [liṅgas] that have become invisible, those that have fallen into a wretched state, and those that are broken by time—even they are worthy of worship. (681)
(1) "In a wretched state" means touched by those who are untouchable.
(2) Likewise, there is another distinction in that very same context.
O Lord of Men, women who have not been initiated, as well as Śūdras,
have no authority to install either Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara.
The man who bows to a linga consecrated by a Shudra, or even to Vishnu, experiences extreme sufferings even in this world; what need is there to mention those in the next?
Whether he be a Śūdra, one who has not been initiated, a woman, or even an outcaste, by touching Keśava or Śiva, he goes to hell. 682.
And so forth. (1) There is also another distinction:
"One should not undertake journeys to great pilgrimage sites or observe fasts and vows for a year following the death of a preceptor of high status. (683)
Likewise:
"Upon the death of a preceptor (mahāguru), one should not perform bathing at sacred fords, great gifts, eating the food of others, or the libation of sesame seeds for one full year."

The husband of a pregnant woman who knows the Veda should avoid shaving, sexual intercourse, visiting sacred fords, and performing śrāddha rites until the seventh month; after that, he may do so except at other [specific] times.

(1) ‘Śrāddham’ means a śrāddha feast. Lalla says: “The ritual for pilgrimage to a sacred site is recommended during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the half-rise of the moon or sun, on the sixth lunar day known as Kapilā, upon the setting of Jupiter (the preceptor of gods and demons), at a sacred ford, and also at the transit of the sun. || 685 ||

(1) *Uplava* means an eclipse. (2) The setting of Jupiter and Venus is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). (3) By this, the meaning is that there is no fault even during other prohibited times, such as an eclipse.
(4) They say that there is no fault even in the first year for a journey undertaken for the purpose of casting bones [into the Ganges]. Likewise, in the *Dharmavivṛtti*:
Fasting, vows, fire-offerings, bathing at sacred fords, recitation of mantras, and so forth—whatever is performed by Brahmins on behalf of someone, its fruit is fully attained by that person. (686)
Likewise:
"For those residing at a sacred site (tīrtha) and for those who have traveled to another country, shaving is not prescribed before one year has passed, except on account of a specific occasion. (687)
Likewise:
"In the midst of water, in a cow-pen, at sacred fords (tīrtha), and on festival days (parvan); and at the time of an eclipse of Rāhu, there is no impurity (sūtaka) whatsoever. (688)
(1) This should be understood as referring to the possibility of departing quickly for another place regarding the practice of giving and so forth.
Likewise:
"A gift given at home yields tenfold merit; in a cow-pen, it becomes hundredfold."
A thousandfold [merit] is gained at sacred fords, and it is infinite in the presence of Śiva.
And furthermore:

Regarding whichever deities are at whichever holy places, whichever twice-born ones are at whichever holy places, and whichever water is at whichever holy places—one should have no doubt concerning them. (690)
[178] (1) The intention is that even if these are impaired, there is no fault.
Likewise:
"The deity is not on the mountain peaks; the deity is not in the abode of Viṣṇu."
Even the god, consisting of bliss, is seen in heaven through his own being.
Wherever there is firm devotion, whenever it belongs to that great-souled one, there Mahādeva extends his grace to him. (691)

(1) And so forth. Enough said! Thus ends the section on miscellaneous duties regarding sacred fords (*tīrtha*) within the General Section of the *Tristhalīsetu*, composed by Nārāyaṇa, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara Sūri—the crest-jewel among illustrious scholars.
The General Section is hereby completed.
From here onwards, the section concerning Prayāga will follow.
